# Dashboard Design System

The dashboard is a React + TypeScript application, built by Vite from
`dashboard/` into `static/dashboard`, which the engine binary embeds. It talks
to the engine over ONE WebSocket: state arrives as pushes, and anything needed
on demand is a query on the same socket (see
[API Endpoints § the live stream](api-endpoints.md#live-stream)).

This page documents the **visual system** and the **rules a change has to keep
holding**. What each screen answers is [Information architecture](#information-architecture);
how it is built and shipped is [How it is built](#how-it-is-built).

---

## The one rule

**Colour carries STATE, never IDENTITY.**

A hash of a name carries no information (rename the seat and its colour changes), and an eight-family palette shared between "which agent", "which phase" and "which event category" makes one amber mean three things on one screen.

Colour is spent in exactly three places:

| | What it means | How many |
|---|---|---|
| **State** | *what a piece of work is doing*: info is working, warning needs a person, danger is stopped, success is done | 4, fixed |
| **Accent** | *what to do*: the primary action, the focus ring, the Inbox's count of what is waiting, the on filter | 1 |
| **Data** | a chart series, inside a figure that names it (a legend, or the label of a one-series figure such as a meter) | 4 + a neutral residual |

Everything else (a seat, a unit, a **phase**, an event category, an
integration's state, a node, a tool origin) is **neutral**; its identity is its name, icon and position, which are stable, legible and do not run out at eight.

A phase is a category, so it is its **word** on the neutral pill (`@crewlethq/tokens` 0.5.0 removed its three hues): beside a state badge the
state must be the one coloured thing on the row. Inside a figure a phase is a
series like any other, drawn in the hue of the **band** the engine folds it
into (`tokens.PhaseBand`: execute and the executor's launches are Execute, review is
Review, delegated workers are Workers, the rest Auxiliary), so one
phase is one colour on every chart. `contract/spend.ts`' `PHASE_BANDS` is that
fold by phase; `internal/api/queries` holds it against the engine's in both directions.

There are eight exceptions, each held to exactly what makes it one.

**First: a third-party app's own mark** on Company › Integrations
(`VendorMark`, from `@crewlethq/icons`): Slack's four colours, Atlassian's blue, GitLab's orange,
Datadog's violet, as the app draws them. A mark is identity by
definition, and a recoloured Slack mark is not Slack's. It is drawn only beside the third-party app's name, or
beside a link or reference INTO that app in operator-facing words, where it
says whose the pull request or channel is ([What prose names is drawn as
what it is](#what-prose-names-is-drawn-as-what-it-is)); nothing reads state
from it, none of its hues is reused as a token, and the
integration's STATE beside it is carried by the status tone. A tool the company has not set up keeps its mark at full strength:
connected-ness is the state beside it, and a drained Datadog read as a placeholder image. Crewlet's own services carry their
**product marks** (`ProductMark`) on the same terms: only beside the
service's name, the one place the brand's violet is identity rather than a
token. SSH, a protocol with no vendor, carries the kit's key mark
(`VendorMark vendor="ssh"`) in the same violet, on the same terms.
Gitlet, writing a merge commit or moving a branch, is drawn with its product
mark beside its name, where a seat would show its face. The Google Analytics logo, Google's own file in Google's
colours, is shown on the same terms under the Google Analytics data on that
integration's Settings tab, never as its icon: Google's developer branding
policy asks for it beside that data.

**Second: the organization on Company › Structure**, its Org chart and Table:
every agent seat is its own Crewlet character on a node toned in its own
colour, with the branch arriving at it (and, in the Table, its row) in
the same hue. The hue is the one the seat's profile icon
names (third exception), never a hash of a name; a person's node
and a unit's stay neutral; the tone is drawn only on Structure.
Nothing reads state from it: what a seat is doing is the state's dot, on its
mark on the chart and beside the state's word on the Table.

**Third: an agent's profile icon**: the Crewlet character and
colour its author chose, written in the seat's own `avatar` block
(see the [Role Fields Summary](../getting-started/configuration.md#role-fields-summary)).
This is identity by CHOICE, so
renaming the seat keeps it. Its six colours are the design system's node hues
(`--color-node-*`), a family no state, accent or data series draws from. A
part a seat left out is picked by the engine from the seat's handle (minted once, never changed), so agents that chose nothing are still told
apart; the dashboard picks nothing and draws the look it is served. Only an agent wears one: a person is drawn as
themself and a unit is neutral. It is drawn as the agent's own badge
(`SeatAvatar`) and its node on the two charts, and nothing reads state from
it: the status glyph on its corner and the word beside it say what
the seat is doing. It is drawn wherever the seat is, with the name as the badge's accessible name and hover title
where no word is printed beside it. The
org builder's Add dialog suggests a character no agent in the draft wears yet
and the next colour round the six; the suggestion is written into the new
seat, where its author can change it.

**Fourth: a QR code** (`@crewlethq/ui`'s `QrCode`), not colour
but a symbol a camera reads: black modules on its own white plate, quiet zone included, in the dark theme as in the light and under forced
colours. A code is specified dark on light, and some scanners and authenticator apps will not read an inverted one. Its two inks are the
`color.qr` tokens, the same in every palette; nothing reads state
from them and nothing else is painted with them.

**Fifth: a collaborator's presence colour** in an artifact (D22): the
hue a person or an agent present in it wears on the marks they make on its
content, so a reader matches an outlined cell to a face in the presence stack. It is drawn only on another
collaborator's cell outline, name flag and the ring round their badge in the
stack while they are present (`PresenceRing`, `CursorFlag`, `PresenceStack`
from `@crewlethq/ui`), always with their name beside it, never on chrome and
never as state. An agent wears the hue its profile icon names; a person is given one of the six node hues for the session, in the
order they joined, skipping hues already worn in the room, never a hash of a
name and never stored on them. Past six people hues repeat and the flag tells
them apart; the same fact is in words in every cell's description and the
presence list, so nothing relies on colour alone. The reader's own place is
the focus ring, as everywhere.

**Sixth: a colour value's swatch** (`ColorChip` at the text's size):
where words write a colour (`#ffe100`), a small square of it is drawn before
the value. It is the value itself, shown: drawn only beside the value it shows, which stays
written out (the swatch is decoration); filled only from a value that passed the design system's `#rrggbb` gate, never
from raw CSS; and drawn with an edge of its own, so a colour matching the
ground is still a swatch.

**Seventh: code read in Gitlet**: code
coloured by kind in its files, diffs and search hits; a change's state pill and
a branch chip wear the kit's code host colours, each hue a kind beside its
sign, word or glyph: never done, a fault or an action. A **JSON or YAML record**
the kit's `CodeBlock` draws with its `language` is code read too, wherever it
is: Settings › Configuration's active document and its entities, an event's
payload, a turn's records, a report or a record as sent, a call's
arguments and the company's YAML colour each key, string, number, boolean,
null and sign in the kit's syntax ink for its kind, and nothing else of the
code host's family.
The pill, the state's glyph and the chip appear only in
its change rows (a task, a seat, My work, Home's code card), its peek and the
Inbox's code notice (`codehost.test.ts`, `tone.test.ts`).

**Eighth: a diff's lines**: every diff of lines tints an added line light
green and a removed one light red, with its glyph and word beside the tint (see
[Every diff is tinted](#every-diff-is-tinted)).

**A readiness is a meter of its conditions, each in the tone of where it stands**: met in
success, measured or waiting on an agent in info, waiting on a person in warning, a failed
check or a conflict in danger, with the count beside it and the next sentence as its title and name.

A seat's badge takes one of three **status glyphs**, or none, from what it is DOING,
and that is the ENGINE'S word, never the dashboard's. Every seat row carries
`activity` (`working`, `needs`, `stopped` or `idle`) and, when stopped, a
`stopped_reason` (`paused`, `unplaced`, `budget` or `provider`), computed once
by the live projection from the seat's turn, its executor's durable record,
its pause, its placement across the fleet and its budget windows (see
[Agent States](../concepts/agent-runtime.md#agent-states)). `lib/seats.ts`
maps the word to a status, a pill's tone, a label and a state line and folds nothing in (deriving state per screen disagreed, and a run parked on a question dropped out after the old twelve-hour age-out). A source gate in `seats.test.ts` refuses any other module turning a
live call's or a run's fields into one of the state words. The two words are
the contract's `SeatActivity` and `StoppedReason`, held to the engine's by a
gate.

**The status is a glyph on the badge's corner and a word in the row, never a
line round the badge.** The kit's `status` (`lib/seats.ts`' `statusOf`, which
passes the engine's own word through and drops idle) draws a small round
badge on the lower-right corner: the state's fill carrying a play for
working, a question mark for needs you and a square for stopped, so shape says it to a reader who cannot tell the fills apart. A ring in the
state's hue round a plate in the agent's own hue put two colours on one
small mark and framed what the agent was doing louder than who it is, so there is no ring and no coloured edge down a roster card's side. Where
the row has room it also says the state in words: a decision row opens
its second line with "Needs you" or "Stopped" in the state's ink, an Inbox
row carries its pill, a Structure row its dot and word, a profile its state in
the engine's word. A badge drawn alone (a sidebar row, a work card's holder,
a spend row) carries the glyph and, where it names itself, the state in its
accessible name. A stack of badges carries none: each overlaps the one
before, and the sentence beside it says what they are doing.

**A reviewer's face in a change's row wears the kit's verdict corner** in place of a status:
a check on the success fill for an approval, a mark on the danger fill for changes requested,
each said in its title too. It is held to Gitlet's rows (`SeatAvatar.test.tsx`); elsewhere a verdict
stays words, except a review's disc on a change's timeline and a reviewer's mark on
its rail (`change/timeline.test.ts`).

| Status (pill tone) | `activity` | Label |
|---|---|---|
| `working` (`info`) | `working`: mid-turn, or its executor is running in its box | "Working"; the state line names the phase and the item ("Executing ENG-412"), a parked turn's too, with no round, for as long as its executor works in its box, delegated workers included (they run under its executor, whose calls the engine does not stream) |
| `needs` (`warning`) | `needs`: its executor waits on a question only a person can answer | "Needs you", "Needs you · executor parked" |
| `stopped` (`danger`) | `stopped`: paused, placed on no node, its budget window refusing, or its provider unreachable | "Paused by Jane Founder · 12m" (the pauser by the name the chart gives their handle; a token nobody bound, by its own name), "Not placed on any node", "Stopped · budget", "Stopped · provider" |
| **none** — a neutral pill | `idle`, no row from the engine yet, or a human seat | "Idle · last turn 24m ago", "No state from the engine yet" |

A handle is written `@pm`; a seat with none (a builder seat the engine
has not derived one for yet) gets nothing rather than a bare `@`. So no markup prints `@{handle}` itself: every handle goes through
`handleLabel` in `lib/seats.ts`, and `app/source.test.ts` refuses JSX text
ending in `@` before an expression and a template inside markup that does the
same. A live round that has not moved in two minutes
is stale, in ten stalled, except while the turn is **parked** on its
executor in its box, which is silent by design for as long as it takes:
the executor's phase card then reads "running in its box", because the
stage travels with the live call off the seat's own turn.

A failed last turn does not colour a seat. The seat takes its next wake like
any other; its `last_error` is shown where the seat is read about, not as a
stop.

**Where a seat runs is which node holds it**: the peek's **Running on** fact
(**Runs on** on the profile's Setup card), never the human seat's **Held by**:
"this node · node-a", "another node", or "no node", read off this
node's own health push (the seats it holds) and the engine's `unplaced`. Which peer holds one held elsewhere
is Settings › Nodes' to say: labelling one seat fleet-wide would make
opening a peek a company-wide read.

An idle seat is deliberately untinted: a tinted tile read as activity, and the fix is no hue, not a duller one.
`warning` and `danger` are separate because a seat parked on a question and a
seat that fell over have both stopped, and only one is a failure.

### A confirmation says its consequences and changes one way

Every dialog that confirms consequences or changes uses the kit's confirmation pattern: a `ConfirmModal` with `consequences` (checkbox choices and muted facts, a named secret or setting as a code chip, danger only where something is destroyed) and `changes` (each seat or record once, its fields as rows, the old value struck and the new one tinted), or `ConsequenceList` and `ChangeGroups` inside a `Modal`; a screen that assigns models, owners or roles row by row is an `AssignmentList`. No dialog hand-builds its checkboxes or before and after sentences (`app/source.test.ts`).

### Every diff is tinted

Every diff of lines the dashboard draws is the design system's `DiffView`,
which `components/DiffView.tsx` hands the screens' props (`hunks` for its
`sections`): Settings › Configuration's Diff lens, a Doclet page's History and
its editor's view of a colleague's save, a principle saved while being
written, an artifact's versions compared, an assistant's proposal, an MCP
server's changed tool under review, and every Gitlet change and commit. The
dashboard keeps no diff renderer, sheet or line comparison of its own
(`components/DiffView.test.tsx`).

In light and dark, an added line is on the diff family's
light green row and a removed one on its light red row, the numbers on a band
in the sign's ink, an edited run on its word tint and a gap on the hunk row;
the design system measures the text on each tint at 4.5:1 or more. The diff
family is never a state: a removed line is not a failure and an
added one is not done. A line's kind is said three ways, each enough alone:

- **The glyph gutter**: `+` for an added line and `−` for a removed one, with
  *Added* or *Removed* read in its place (a minus sign is announced as
  anything from "minus" to nothing).
- **The tint**: the diff family's row, on the card rung the diff paints for
  its own ground, where the design system measures it.
- **The word underline.** Where a removed and an added line are one line
  edited, the run of each that differs is underlined (`changedRuns`): ONE
  run, between what the two lines share at their start and at their end, in
  whole words, and none when all they share is spacing and
  punctuation. A word-by-word diff would mark every word the edit moved past:
  prettier for a small edit, unreadable for a rewritten paragraph.
  Which two lines are one line edited is read off the change, never guessed
  from their words, because an underline says they are one: a setting's old
  and new value under one path (a value of several lines, an object or a
  list, is a small text of its own, its lines paired by the text's rule
  below); in a text, the lines in the same place of a
  change that removes as many lines as it adds (the shape git's own
  `contrib/diff-highlight` pairs), or one line against several, the first
  of each. Any other change of a text underlines nothing (two lines
  or more a side with unequal counts, where every pair after a line added
  is two neighbours).

**A change read as prose is the design system's `DocumentDiff`**, the one
place a diff is not of lines: the newest change on Doclet's landing, where a
reader asks what changed rather than which lines did. `lib/proseDiff.ts`
compares two versions of a page by block and then by word, with the line
diff's own comparison (`compareSequences`) and bounds, and
`components/ProseDiff.tsx` renders each block with the dashboard's markdown
renderer, its changed words in `DocumentDiffAdded` and `DocumentDiffRemoved`.
It carries no tint: an added run is underlined
on the raised rung and a removed one struck in the tertiary ink on the sunk
rung, each said in words.

Two texts are compared by the design system's line diff, `compareLines`,
which every diff, preview and merge of a text uses: the shortest edit
between their lines (Myers' algorithm, as git's diff), in linear
space, over lines interned to numbers, the stretch the two share at their
start and end walked once, so cost follows what changed rather than text length. It is bounded, and
says so: past 20,000 lines a side in what changed, or 4,000 lines removed and
added, two texts are NOT compared, and the diff is a sentence saying which in
place of every row.

A diff of a text is numbered in both versions, in Geist Mono at the document's
13px. A diff of SETTINGS (a configuration's paths, an artifact's files) is
keyed instead: each line names its path where a text's carries its numbers,
and a setting that changed is its old value removed and its new value added,
so the underline finds what moved inside it. A hunk opens with a row saying
how many unchanged lines it skipped, because a silently closed gap makes a
document edited at both ends look rewritten in the middle. A diff is
unified, or split (older text beside newer, each removed line beside
its replacement) only where it is at least 640px wide (the kit's
phone breakpoint, read off the diff's own width); a keyed diff is always
unified. Past 1,000 rows it is windowed: only the blocks of 100 rows within a
view of the screen hold their rows, measured against the diff's own scroller,
and the rest keep the height they last had; under it every row is mounted,
which keeps find-in-page and a screen reader's reading of the whole diff. The
threshold is provisional: it is decided by the first paint of a 1,000-row
split diff, held to 100 ms, which needs a browser the dashboard's
suites do not run. Whether to add one, keep the value unmeasured, or lower it
to the window's own 300 rows is the maintainers' call.
The window bounds the reading too: line pairing is settled from the change's shape, and a pair's words are
tokenized for its underline, and a line's code coloured, only once one of its
lines is drawn.
In Gitlet a host hands it each line's coloured spans (`tokens`), asked as a
row is drawn: from the blob under 256 KiB, else from the hunk's first line, so
past it a hunk opening inside a comment may colour wrong until it closes.
A coloured diff paints plain until its blobs are read, then walks each once.

**A host can write on a diff.** A change's review is read in its diff, so the
component takes what a host anchors to a line (`notes`, drawn under that
line, and under its row across both sides of a split diff, once) and lets a
host pick lines (`onPick`): each line's own number (its newer one, else its
older, the number a finding names) becomes a button, Shift extending the
host's pick from where it began, and a picked line (`picked`) takes the
selected tint in place of its tints, with an accent bar at its start. What is drawn under a line and what a pick does are the host's; a
diff given neither draws as before. A host that opens on
a line (a failed check's) hands the diff the line to bring into view
(`reveal`) rather than searching the page: past the window's first
block the line has no element until its block is drawn, so the diff scrolls
to that block's box, bringing it within the window, then centres the
line, once.

A picked line in a diff and in a Gitlet file take one look: the selected tint
in place of the line's tints and band, its sign, its run's underline and an
accent bar at its start.

`components/DiffView.test.tsx` holds that every diff is the design system's:
no module writes a `diff-view` class or declares a line comparison of its own,
no sheet styles one, and the adapter draws the kit's tinted lines. The design
system's own suites hold what `DiffView` draws, its line diff and the contrast
of the text on each tint.

A diff a host lets expand opens each hunk with the host's row (git's header and
its controls) in place of the skipped count, each under the line above it;
Gitlet reads the hidden lines from the blob by its id. Stacked, each file is its own DiffView.

### Code is coloured by kind in Gitlet

A file Gitlet draws under 256 KiB, and its blame, colour each token in the
kit's syntax ink for its kind (`lib/syntax/`, one fetched grammar a language),
its state walked from line 1; a larger or plain-text file is plain.
A README's fenced block is coloured by its info string's first word; an
unknown one is plain.

Lines paint plain and colours follow; a file opened past line 1
waits for the lines above it, read by its blob's id, so no line changes
colour. `styles/codehost.test.ts` keeps the inks to `gitlet-code.css`.

A diff's lines take the state of their blob's line, read by its id, under
256 KiB, and of their hunk's first line past it; a changed run keeps the code's
own text. A search hit is coloured on its own line.

A diffstat's figures take the diff family's sign inks and its squares its mark
inks, still told apart by shape, and a tree's file status its file ink, beside their words.

Outside Gitlet a JSON or YAML record is coloured by the kit's `CodeBlock`
itself, handed `language="json"` or `"yaml"`: its own tokenizer, one span of
text a token and never markup, plain past 256 KiB. A block whose text may not
be JSON (a tool's result, a model's words) is handed no language and stays plain.

---

## The palette is measured, not asserted

`@crewlethq/tokens` is the one source of colour, type, space and motion. The
dashboard declares none of its own: `dashboard/src/main.tsx` imports the palette, the themes, the
density scale, the faces and the document baseline, in that order, above every
other import (imports evaluate in source order and components carry their own stylesheets, and
the baseline must be what a component rule outranks). The dashboard's own sheets (`tokens.css`, `base.css`,
`components.css`, `frame.css`, `screens.css`) come last. The rest are each a
screen's own, imported by the module that draws it so it arrives with
that chunk: `create.css`, the create pages'
(`routes/artifacts/new/CreateShell.tsx`), `charter.css`, the Principles
editor's, `brand.css`, the brand's, and `folders.css`, the folders'. Each lands after every other sheet, so it selects
only its own classes (`styles/classes.test.ts`), and never a kit class
(`TestNoLazyStylesheetCarriesTheDesignSystem`).

**There is no alias layer.** Every stylesheet in `dashboard/src` reads the
package's tokens under their own names (`--color-text-tertiary`,
`--spacing-4`, `--size-control-md`, `--shadow-focus`), and `tokens.css` keeps
only three values that are this application's own (a row list's inset, the
toolbar's band and the sticky offset under it). A short name is a
second name for one value: it hides a token the package renames and is where the two disagree. `styles/tokens.test.ts` refuses a stylesheet of ours that
DECLARES any `--color-*` or `--shadow-*`, and reads every `var()` against the
installed package.

The rule table and the colour maths are the package's own,
`@crewlethq/tokens/test/palette`, so the design system and this application
cannot disagree about what a floor is.
`dashboard/src/styles/palette.test.ts` runs them over the INSTALLED
stylesheets in that same import order, for **every theme the registry lists**
(the default, and each named theme over it under the profile its entry
declares), in **every theme state** (dark on the bare root, light by media
query, light by attribute) and over **every composited surface a token can
land on**, including a hovered row inside a nested panel, where a ramp anchored to the panel fill quietly falls under its floor. The engine
measures as well as the package so that a tokens release that lowered a ratio
cannot arrive through an auto-merged bump unmeasured by `make
check`.

What is measured, and the floor each clears:

| Claim | Floor |
|---|---|
| `--color-text-primary` on every surface | 7:1 |
| `--color-text-secondary`, `--color-text-tertiary` on every surface | 4.5:1 |
| `--color-text-muted` on a panel | **between 2.8 and 4.5**, because it is decoration, and a step that crept up to 4.5 would invite itself into a table cell |
| every `-ink` step as TEXT on every surface, and on its own `-soft` tint | 4.5:1 |
| every fill step as a MARK on the page surfaces it sits on | 3:1 |
| `--color-text-on-accent` on the accent, `--color-text-on-danger` on the danger fill, `--color-text-on-scrim` on the scrim | 4.5:1 |
| the focus ring against every surface | 3:1 |
| the four state hues, pairwise, under normal / protan / deutan vision | ΔE 10 |
| adjacent data hues, in series order, under all three | ΔE 9, and ΔE 15 under normal vision |
| every data hue against the reserved danger hue | ΔE 14 normal, 8 dichromat |
| every other hue against the accent, under all three | ΔE 10 normal, 8 dichromat |
| the neutral ramp's chroma | ≤ 2.2, or inside the tint a theme declares, with the accent carrying twice the chroma of its most tinted rung |
| text, inks, the muted step and the card's hairline in the high-contrast theme | 7:1, 7:1, 4.5:1 and 3:1 |

**A measured token is only as good as where it is spent.**
`--color-text-muted` clears its floor as decoration, so words a reader has to read ("(optional)", "not set", "none", "not reported
by this engine", a seat's goal, an event's category, every text box's placeholder) take `--color-text-tertiary`. The floors are measured by
`@crewlethq/tokens`' own `runPalette` over all four states of the cascade,
driven from `styles/palette.test.ts`; a second implementation would be
two ideas of what "4.5:1 on every surface it can land on" means. WHERE a
step is spent is this page's rule, kept by a reviewer; mechanically, `styles/tokens.test.ts` fails on a `var()`
naming a token nothing declares, because an undeclared custom property does not
fall back: it takes its whole declaration with it.

**The fill/ink split is enforced by that measurement, not by convention.** An
`-ink` step is text; a fill step is a mark or a background. Mixing them shipped role badges at 1.63:1 (an inline
`background:` with a hue token and the default text colour on top).
Only `--color-brand-accent` is ever a fill behind a word, under
`--color-text-on-accent` (plus the danger fill behind a destructive action's
label, `--color-text-on-danger`, measured at 4.5:1; a theme
whose accent is light labels it dark, so the danger fill and the scrim have
labels of their own; and, in Gitlet, a change's state pill, below). A state
is a soft tint carrying its own ink step, never a solid block with a label on
it, which also lets the state fills be light enough to read as marks
on a dark ground.
In Gitlet a change's state is the one state drawn as a solid block with a label
(the seventh exception): the kit's `--color-change-*-fill` under its `-label`,
pairs the package measures.

### The ground

**Dark first.** The design system paints dark on the bare root and light under
`@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) :root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and
`:root[data-theme="light"]`, so a browser reporting no preference gets the
palette the product is drawn in, the OS setting works, and an explicit choice
wins in both directions. The package's suite compares the two light blocks
key for key. The dashboard adds no theme block of its own (`tokens.css`
declares no colour at all).

### Mode and theme

**Two choices, never one.** The **mode** is light, dark or the machine's, and
is the `data-theme` attribute the design system's contract names. The
**theme** is one of the named palettes `@crewlethq/tokens` ships (Crewlet,
the default, and nine more in five groups), each a full token set with a dark
and a light half, and is the root's `data-palette` attribute: the mode chooses
the half, so a theme never changes the mode and the mode never the
theme. `main.tsx` imports `css/themes/all` after `css/themes`, so every theme
is in the first sheet and switching needs no request and nothing new for the
content security policy. The default paints the bare root.

**One id is stored, nothing else.** `lib/prefs.ts` keeps the choice under
`crewlet_palette` (`lib/storage.ts`), validated against the registry the
package exports, so an id no build ships (a removed theme, a hand edit)
reads as no choice. A reader who has
chosen no theme gets the default, or High contrast while their machine asks
for more contrast (`prefers-contrast: more`); any choice, the default included,
wins over the machine. `bootTheme()` paints the stored mode, density and theme
before React mounts, so nobody sees the default flash,
and a storage event from another tab applies what that tab
chose, so two tabs never disagree.

**A list previews; choosing applies.** The preferences popover's theme list
and the palette's Change theme step repaint the whole frame in the theme their
highlight comes to rest on (at once for a key, once the pointer has rested on
a row for 120 ms), through `previewPalette`, which writes nothing; the list
closing, emptying, its step being left or the pointer leaving it puts back the
theme in effect, so a preview never outlives its list.
There is no Appearance page: the popover is where a reader sets how this
browser looks. Every pick, from either, applies through one helper
(`app/appearance.tsx`), which says "Theme set to Abyss" in a toast with an
**Undo** that puts back the previous choice, including no choice.

The dark ground is deliberately **not** `#000`: an operator reads this page for
hours, and pure black behind near-white text halates. It is also barely blue: tinting every neutral
with `rgba(176, 152, 255, …)` made the whole product read violet and left the accent
nothing to separate itself from. A near-neutral ground with one saturated
accent is what makes the accent mean "here".

**Four opaque rungs, and each is painted by what it names.** `--color-surface-
frame` is the window and its navigation — the sidebar stands on it; `--color-surface-background` is the SHEET, the page column
everything is read on, and a bar inside the page (the page bar) stands on it
too; `--color-surface-subtle` is a card, which is what the kit's `Card` paints;
and `--color-surface-elevated` is the one step a card can show: a block inside
a card, a grid's head, a chip, a well. Below them `--color-surface-inset` is a
translucent recess that reads as a well on whatever it lands on. A card is
found by its HAIRLINE as much as its rung: the sheet-to-card step is nearly
flat on purpose, and a page of cards each lifted by a large step is a relief
map.

A numbered ramp cannot state which rung a thing stands on, so collisions went unseen (sidebar, cards and grids painted the page's colour behind a 1px border; the calendar's out-of-month cells painted the card's). `styles/surfaces.test.ts` measures the
rungs against the installed palette (all four a different colour from every
other in every state, the frame under the one sidebar, the sheet under the
page, the card rung under the kit's `Card`) and refuses an interaction
state (`:hover`, `:focus`, `:active`) that paints a structural rung rather than
an overlay.

### Type

Two self-hosted variable faces, **Geist** and **Geist Mono**, the `latin`
and `latin-ext` subsets, 83,736 bytes for the four files, embedded like every
other asset and served from `/static/dashboard/fonts/` beside their OFL text.
They arrive from `@crewlethq/tokens` (0.5.0 replaced Inter and JetBrains
Mono). Self-hosted because a CDN would be the ONLY external runtime reference: on an air-gapped
engine, a supported deployment, every face would fall back to a system font the
design was never measured against. `TestTheBuiltDashboardIsWhole` requires
exactly the four Geist faces in the built stylesheet, each under `fonts/`.

The document's line is the kit's: 13px on 1.45.

Nine sizes, `--font-size-2xs` … `--font-size-3xl`, are **the only
sizes in the product** (194 `font-size` declarations over 14 literal pixel values made the old scale fiction, and its density control resized only some steps).

There is ONE micro-label register (`.t-label`), declared once and never
overridden. Numbers are tabular everywhere: a live token count that changes
width as it counts makes the column beside it jitter.

### Space, radius, elevation

A 4px base scale, with the package's `--density` multiplying every spacing and
size token (rows, controls, gaps) so compact mode changes every
surface. A row is `--size-row-md` (36px), a control `--size-control-md` (30px),
and the sidebar's rows `--size-nav-row` (30px), all the kit's own steps rather
than literals. Four radii and a pill. **The card is flat:** it
is found by its rung and its hairline, and a shadow is spent only on what
stands OVER the page: a popover, a dialog, the command palette. The focus
ring is the package's `--shadow-focus`.

The sidebar's inset is split in two, because a
sidebar row has two edges that want different things. `--size-nav-gutter`
insets the sidebar and is where a row's own background, hover and active
tint begin, so it decides how much of the sidebar's width the click target
covers.
`--size-nav-row-pad` insets
the content inside that row. Every glyph in the sidebar lands on the sum
of the two, and anything with no row of its own (the brand lockup, the group
labels) adds them rather than carrying a literal. So rows can be widened without moving one glyph: shrink the gutter, grow the pad by the
same step, and the vertical line the mark, the group labels and the item text
share does not move.

---

## Information architecture

**One sidebar, and three nouns that keep it one.** The sidebar lists where a
reader can go (fifteen **workspaces**, in three runs and a foot) and the
few objects they keep coming back to: the views and artifacts they pinned and
the pages they starred. A workspace's own **sections** are paths drawn as tabs
in its page header (Settings draws its twenty-one as a column of five groups, and
lists nothing that lives elsewhere; Worklet draws its as the lenses of the scope
its trail names),
and its objects (a unit, a
container, a node) are rows on the section that lists them.

Trees are not the sidebar's to hold (a unit list is a tab of Structure, a node
list a section of Settings): a per-workspace second column moved the reader's place on every navigation.

### The grammar, stated once and asserted

- A **sidebar row** is a workspace, or a live shortcut to a pinned view, a
  starred page or a running turn. A project is not one: it is a **scope** of
  Worklet, named and switched in Worklet's trail
  ([Worklet's scope](#worklets-scope-is-named-and-switched-in-the-trail)).
- A **section** is a **path segment** inside a workspace, drawn by one
  renderer: `tabs` in the page header, `lenses` beside Worklet's scope in the
  trail, `column` for Settings, or `panel` for Chatlet, whose screen draws them
  at the head of its Rooms panel. Chatlet draws no tabs because the header
  draws them on a section's own page and never on an object's, and a room is
  the object page a chat reader spends their time on, so Activity, Threads,
  Drafts and sent and Saved head the panel, drawn from the same table, and the
  frame draws nothing for them.
- An **object tab** is a `tab=` query on an object's own page (a seat's
  Overview, Work, Turns…), bound to 1–9.

Nothing is two of those. A section is never a sidebar row and never a query; an
object tab is never a path. A filter (a reason, a scope, a status) is none of
the three and lives in the page's own filter bar. `view=` and `lens=` remain
where a screen switches how ONE object is read (a list's saved view, the
configuration's active / history / diff), which is an object tab by another
name.

`app/nav.ts` holds the one table, `WORKSPACES`, with each workspace's sections;
`DESTINATIONS` (the palette's "Go to") is derived from it. `app/routes.ts`'s
`resolve(path)` is the one route table: the screen dispatch, the breadcrumb,
the stars and recents a reader keeps and the tests all ask it, and a stored
path that stops resolving is dropped when read. `router.test.ts` holds
the grammar against the definitions (every destination resolves to the
workspace it declares, chords are unique, no reserved segment has the shape of
a key the engine mints) and holds the table below against the resolver in
both directions.
### A filter is a chip; an arrangement says what it is set to

The grammar above says where a control lives. This says what a control is. Nothing is both:

- A **filter** narrows the answer. It is added from one **+ Filter** menu at the end of the chip row and drawn as a removable **chip**. A filter that is off has no chip, so an unfiltered list's row is "+ Filter" alone. Removing a chip clears the one URL key it names.
- An **arrangement** decides how the same answer is drawn (shape, grouping, order, grid columns, board lanes put away) and is drawn as a control that says what it is set to, so it reads without opening anything.
  - On screen: the five shapes are a segmented row of glyphs ahead of the saved views (the kit's `SegmentedControl`, also the Artifacts gallery's List/Cards switch). **Group by** and **Sort** sit at the far end of the chip bar, each showing its value; the default order is named for what it is ("Manual", "Recently updated", "Start date"), never "Default".
  - Set once and forgotten (second axis, grid columns, what a board's cards show, lanes put away): the **Display** menu. A menu button cannot say what several things are set to, so the three used all day stay out of it. Its way back to "this view's own shape" is offered only while a SAVED view runs in another shape.

  **A board's arrangement is what its cards show** (`card_hide=`, the facts put away): size, priority, labels, due date and tokens, each a box in the Display menu, ticked while drawn. Only DESCRIPTIVE facts are offered. The key, holder, title and STATES (blocked, "blocks N", open asks, the flow badge, the live band) are what a board is triaged by; a board that could hide them would report a quiet project that is not one.

  **An item in progress says why it is not moving** with the engine's [flow](../guides/worklet.md#why-an-item-in-progress-is-not-moving):
  - A badge (`FlowTag`) on a card, a list row and above the task's title. It gives the state's end where known ("Held · until 13:00") or how long it has held ("Stuck · 9h"); cause and the wait's words on hover. A cause that is the whole story is the badge's word ("No assignee", "Assignee left"). The ordinary `moving` draws none.
  - Instants are on the company's clock, as Worklet's dates are: a wait until a start names the day it opens; a clock time names its zone where the reader's clock is another.
  - The sentence speaks in the assignee's terms (a person picks an item up, an agent takes a turn on it) and names the project's stuck window where the screen holds the project.
  - A card's live band is drawn on an item whose flow reads `working`, its words lent by the assignee's own row; no screen pairs a running turn with an item or compares a start with its own clock.
  - The task's rail has a **Flow** row with where its hold is lifted beside it (the seat's page for a stopped seat, the models for a model limit, Assign for an item nobody holds); its history draws the recorded flow among the changes.
  - An answer read without the seats' live state says "live state unread" beside its rows.
  - A project's About states its **Stuck after** window; Edit project sets it.
  - The facts are one declaration (`CARD_FACTS` in `components/work.tsx`) that the menu and the card both read.

  **A screen whose grid has an optional column has a menu to reach it.** The kit's `ColumnChooser` is drawn by the work list's Display menu and by the projects directory's own **Columns** button beside its segment; `optional` with no chooser is a column nobody can turn on (the directory's Unit column shipped so, taking `sort=unit` with it). One implementation, because two rules are easy to get wrong separately: an empty `cols=` is the DEFAULT set, not an empty grid; and the value written back is in the columns' DECLARATION order, not click order, because `cols=` carries an order as well as a selection. Each screen keeps only which columns exist (per shape on the work list, per grid elsewhere); the choices are DERIVED from the columns the grid draws, so a new column appears in its menu with no second edit.

`URL_HOMES` in `lib/work.ts` declares, per key, the control that owns every URL key the work list carries: chip, arrangement, or one of three that are deliberately neither and carry their reason at the entry. `routes/worklet/toolbar/grammar.test.tsx` holds it against the SCREEN in both directions, reading the key set out of `ItemsView.tsx`: every key the list puts on the address has a home, and every home is a key the list writes. A key with no home is a narrowing reachable only by editing the address (`unit=` was, while Clear walked past it); a key with two is two controls for one fact that disagree when either writes.

The one control outside both is the **scope** picker (**Show**: Open / Recent / Closed / All, at the row's far end beside Group by). It is always set to something: as a chip it would be permanently present (not a chip) or absent on its default (hiding the control that decides whether finished work is on screen).
- Its last value is NAMED (`all`), not `""`, because the router deletes a key set to `""`.
- **Recent** is the one scope that is not a status group: open work plus whatever finished since the start of the week, sent as the engine's `closed_since=sow` so the week is the COMPANY's, not the browser's. The engine refuses it beside `show_closed`, so the chosen scope replaces whichever of the two a saved view carried.
- A **board opens on it**, every other shape on Open: a board's last lane is Done, and under Open nothing can fall into it. A view that said anything about finished work keeps what it said.

**A key that is there and empty is not a key that is missing.** Narrowing a board to one column writes `group=<value>`. The column holding rows with no value on the axis (Unassigned, Untagged, No parent) has the empty string as its key, on every axis, which is what the engine reads with `Params.Has`. No word can be reserved that some axis will not one day hold, so the spelling is PRESENCE: the address carries `group=` with nothing after it, `URLSearchParams` round-trips it, and every reader asks whether the key is there. As a plain string it was lost end to end (the query builder dropped an empty value, `useParam` could not tell it from absent, the address writer deleted it), so the Unassigned column's "N more →" loaded the whole board.

A **saved view** is neither: a query somebody arranged and put somewhere, so it is an option in the strip. The five shapes are not options beside it: a shape draws any query, and mixed into one strip the two read as one kind of thing. That is also why `view=` and `shape=` are two keys: switching a saved board to a list must not throw the saved filters away.

**A narrowing the SCREEN is, is not a filter either: it is LOCKED.** One list serves three screens, two of them that list narrowed to something the reader did not choose: `#/worklet/{KEY}` (the work in one project), and `#/me`'s Queue (work one person holds) and Asked by me (work one person waits on an answer about). A locked narrowing:

- is **applied under everything else**, after every reader key and saved-view default, so nothing widens the list past what the screen is about;
- is **not offered** in the Filter menu: a row there would write a key the lock overwrites, a control that does nothing;
- draws **no chip**: a chip that will not come off reports a state the reader cannot reach;
- is **not in the URL**: the screen's own key addresses it (`#/me?handle=cto`, a project's path segment), and a second key for the same fact could differ.

So a locked narrowing does not make a list "filtered": the empty state that blames a narrowing and offers to clear it is for a filter actually on. A host screen says its own sentence about its own subject.

### The sparse state

Every screen above is designed on a company with work in it. A company's first week has each band conditional on data that does not exist yet. Five rules:

- **The landing shape is the list.** A board's information is the comparison ACROSS lanes: worst at low N, best at high N (four lanes holding one card say nothing, and the card is a 292 px object in a 1500 px field). A list degrades to one full-width row. So a container with no default view opens as a list, the board one press away (the second of the five shape glyphs ahead of the saved views). The landing shape is never conditional on how much work exists: a screen that redraws as a company fills up cannot be learned.
- **A closed-set axis draws every declared value; an open one draws what exists.** The ENGINE decides which lanes exist: `work_items` carries every column the query's own predicate admits, so a one-item company gets the denominator a comparison needs and Open draws no dead Done lane. The screen's part is the drawing: an empty lane says "Nothing here" rather than a heading over nothing. The axes it covers are in [the Worklet guide](../guides/worklet.md#views); a list, a table and a timeline draw only bands that hold rows (the bullet under "A board draws every lane the scope admits" below).
- **The view strip is always drawn.** Its first tab is the container's own list, a real destination and the only thing naming the page inside its content column. It ends in a link to the inventory, since saved views are undiscoverable until used. The container tab carries no count: the engine's total is over the FILTER, not the container, and a number an answer does not give is not drawn.
- **An empty list is a function of what was ASKED:**
  - a narrowing is on and nothing matched: "Nothing matches", with the control that clears it;
  - nothing narrows and the container has nothing in this SCOPE: "Nothing open here", naming the switch, with a number only where the container's own counts give one;
  - nothing at all: how work arrives. Drawn by whoever holds the wider fact (the page for a company with no projects, the project screen for an empty project); the list stays quiet rather than stacking a second panel.
- **The end of a complete list is said.** The bar's count is silent once everything matching is on screen and a cursor is invisible, so a complete answer with rows closes with "That is all of it · N items". It never says how many a filter hides: `total_hint` counts what MATCHED, over the same predicate as the rows, so the unfiltered total is not in the answer and synthesising it would take a second query at a second instant.

**Reserved segments cannot collide with keys.** Project and container keys are uppercase (`ENG`), item keys are `KEY-n`, everything else the engine mints is a uuid, and every reserved segment is lowercase, so `#/worklet/views` resolves before any answer arrives. The resolver recognises a key by that shape, not by elimination: the engine uppercases every container key it keeps, so a segment under Doclet holding a lowercase letter is a section or Not Found, never a container (`#/doclet/skills` does not open a container called `skills`).

The set is `RESERVED_SEGMENTS` in `app/nav.ts`, deliberately not copied here, since a prose list goes stale. `router.test.ts` holds the routes named in the table above against that list and against `WORKSPACES`, so table and code cannot disagree about which addresses exist.
### The sidebar

Four runs. First, under no label: what needs you, what reached you, what is yours. Then **Company**, what the company decides: who it is, its policies, org chart, schedules, services and apps, and last its spending ceilings. Then **Workspace**, what the company does: work, code, chat, knowledge, what it made, what is running. The engine stands beside the company's name in the head; the foot is the reader, with Settings and Preferences as glyphs beside them.

| Row | Route | Figure |
|---|---|---|
| **Home** | `#/home` | — |
| **Inbox** | `#/inbox` | the accent **badge**: unread notices under a reason the person's record counts as PRIMARY. The chrome fills a figure only for what waits on you (this, My work's, Chatlet's): most unread notices are things the company merely told you, and a count that never reaches zero reads as broken. Asked as `unread` + `primary_only` over one page, so a full page is a floor ("50+"). Moves within half a second of an `inbox_changed` frame (the frame watches the person's own record); the minute-long poll is only the fallback |
| **My work** | `#/me` | a **badge** in quiet grey (nobody asked for this, so the Inbox's asks keep the accent): open work assigned to you, the SAME figure the Queue tab carries, read once by the frame for both. The engine's total, counted in full, a floor ("200+") where the count hit its ceiling; nothing on you draws no figure. Questions put to you are counted on their own tab (Asked of me), and each reached you as an Inbox notice |
| *Company* | | |
| **Principles** | `#/company/principles` (and `#/company`) | none: mission, vision and policies are every reader's. It is the Company landing and owns the bare `#/company`, marked at that address and under its own path only: an address under `#/company` that no row holds is Not Found in the Company group and marks no row (`nav.ts`'s `sidebarRowOf`) |
| **Brand** | `#/company/brand` | none: the published brand is every reader's; publishing is an Admin's on the page |
| **Structure** | `#/company/org` | none |
| **Schedules** | `#/company/schedules` | none |
| **Integrations** | `#/company/integrations` | none; every reader opens it, an app's state and connecting are an Admin's on the page |
| **Budgets** | `#/company/budgets` | none (tokens only; the one money drawn is a growth integration's, rule 19) |
| *Workspace* | | |
| **Worklet** | `#/worklet` | none |
| **Gitlet** | `#/gitlet` | none; locked, naming Gitlet, for a reader without Gitlet access (as Worklet's row is without Worklet's), since every section reads a code question the engine refuses them (ADR-0110); a holder's answers are held to their own grant. Hidden where the company hosts no code in the engine (`code.backend` is not `gitlet`). See [The Gitlet workspace](#the-gitlet-workspace) |
| **Chatlet** | `#/chatlet/activity` (and `#/chatlet`) | the accent **badge**: what waits on you in Chatlet, i.e. unread messages that name you (or the whole room) in a named room and every unread message in a direct conversation, in rooms you have not muted; a floor ("100+") where a room counted to the engine's bound or the list was cut short, none where counts were not measured. Counted from the frame's ONE reading of your rooms (`lib/chatRooms.ts`), which the Chatlet screen draws too, so badge and list cannot differ; re-read on every live chat frame, at the room's rate while a surface draws the rooms, at most every two seconds while only the badge reads it. Locked, like Worklet, without Chatlet access; a reader who holds it but whose credential acts as no seat is answered by the screen itself, since every chat page is read as a seat |
| **Doclet** | `#/doclet` | none |
| **Artifacts** | `#/artifacts` | none, never a lock: a share alone admits a reader, and only making an artifact is gated by Artifacts access, which the gallery says to a reader without it ("Making an artifact needs Artifacts access. An admin can give it to you. What is shared with you opens here all the same.") beside its held New |
| **Live** | `#/live` | the agents working now, beside the working mark, the chrome's one pulsing dot. It sits on Live because a count says how many of something the DESTINATION holds, and Live › Now running holds the running turns, one row each |
| *Foot* | | |
| **Settings** | `#/settings/models` | none, never a lock: Spend's readings are every reader's, and a section closed to the reader is locked in Settings' own column |

Under the workspaces:

- **Pinned**: the views this reader pinned, asked for WITH the viewer (a pin is a person's; the shared strip has none) and across EVERY container (`work_saved_views`), so a view pinned from a project board shows the project's key as its lead. Each carries the total it selects, counted in the view's own container, with every task filtered on its own, never in the grammar's tree mode (where an open epic's finished subtasks rode along). A pinned row RUNS the view, `#/worklet/tasks?view=<key>` (or its project's list for a view saved on a project), rather than opening the inventory page. Then the ARTIFACTS this reader pinned, each a row to its page with its kind's glyph, listed for every reader the engine serves (a share alone admits a reader), read from the one listing All and an artifact's Pin item read (`lib/artifacts/pins.ts`), so a pin made anywhere moves the sidebar at once.
- **Starred**: drawn only when there is one. **One row is current**: a pin, a star or a running turn that opens exactly the page on screen is the current row, and the workspace row containing it gives the mark up.
- **Running**: one row per seat the engine says is working, drawn while one is: the seat's badge with its status glyph, its name, the key of the item its turn is charged to as the lead, and a link that WATCHES the turn (its Transcript, the phase it is on open, or a parked turn's executor live above its phases; see [the turn trace](#the-turn-trace-four-tabs-one-clock)). It is the way to a running turn from every screen.
  - Same set as Live's figure, in the order every list of running turns draws: longest-running first, a seat with no readable start last (the record the engine creates when its parked turn resumes carries the newest start). A turn that starts is APPENDED so the rows a reader is reaching for never reorder, and the section is LAST so nothing above it moves.
  - Four rows with a turn id, then one row to Live › Now running for the rest: **N more running**, or **N running** when no row stands above it. A working seat whose turn has published no id yet is counted there, takes none of the four places, and is not linked to nothing.
  - Home's Live now draws the SAME four rows in the same order: both are one selection (`runningShortList` in `lib/turns.ts`), not two lists under one cap.
  - A seat that needs a person is not listed: it is running nothing; what it waits on is the Inbox's and Now running's *Waiting on a person*.
  - Nothing in it ticks (no elapsed clock, no pulse per row) because the chrome is on every screen: the Live row's one dot says something runs, these rows say which.

The foot is the **user block** alone, with Settings and Preferences as icon buttons at its end: Settings a link to where its row opened (the kit's `IconButtonLink`, current on a Settings page), Preferences its popover. The head carries the company's lockup and, at the end of its line, the **engine panel**'s compact status.

**The sidebar folds to a compact rail.** Above the shell breakpoint the kit's fold control, or `Mod+\`, folds the sidebar to the kit's 76 px rail and back. The choice is the reader's, kept per reader in this browser (`app/sidebar/railShape.ts`), as a screen's kept range is. Folded, it is the kit's `CompactNav`:
- **Search** (the palette the full sidebar's field opens), then Home, Inbox and My work, each its glyph over its name;
- ONE tile for Company and one for Workspace, each opening a flyout of its places beside the rail on a point, a press or the arrow keys; the tile carries its places' badges and is current when the page on screen is one of them;
- under the foot's rule: the engine's status (dot and alarms), **Settings** as a tile, and the reader's face alone, which opens the same menu as the user block's row, with **Preferences** in it as a dialog of the same three controls.

Both shapes are drawn from one list of places, so they cannot differ in link, lock or figure. The live shortcuts (Pinned, Starred, Running) are the full sidebar's, and a shortcut is never current in the folded rail, so the place holding the page keeps the mark. The company's mark (head's row) and the fold control (the row under it) stand in the same place in both shapes. Below the breakpoint the sidebar is the drawer, always the full list, and the stored choice comes back when the window widens.

**Every "New task" is one sheet.** A work screen's page-bar New task (Home, the Tasks lens, every lens of a project) and a board lane's `+` all open the frame's single New task sheet (`dashboard/src/routes/worklet/NewTask.tsx`, mounted by the shell out of the Worklet chunk), each door telling it only what it knows.
- **Lane `+`** files INTO its lane (`app/newTask.ts`'s `presetForLane`): it presets exactly the value that puts a task there (status, type, priority, project, holder or label; for a status-group lane the group's first status) and is drawn only where the sheet can hold that value as one. So no `+` on a due band other than "No due date" (a span of days) or a unit (the project's own team), nor on lanes of work that ended undelivered (Cancelled, Closed, the closed status group): nobody files new work as already abandoned. Done keeps its `+` (work finished before anybody tracked it is recorded as done). The Unassigned lane's `+` chooses nobody, which the project routes as its own unassigned work (to its default assignee where it names one and the chart still holds that seat, else triage), and the field says which before the press.
- Where the company does not run Worklet, none of those doors is drawn (see the rule on services below).
- An applied create that came back with a caveat (the act answer's `caveats`, in a person's words) says it in its toast rather than a plain "Filed".
- **What it files**: project, title, description, type, status, assignee, priority, due and labels as ONE `create_work_item`, sending only the fields the person set (an unset one is the engine's default, never the sheet's guess); type, status words and labels are the chosen project's own.
- **Assignee** completes against the chart with the engine's `colleague` match offered first as the **best match**, its row's hint as short as every other's (`@handle · best match`): the kit's hint does not shrink and its label does, so a tier written into the hint drew the name as "Age…" or not at all. Which tier matched is the resolver's business and said nowhere; once a seat is taken the help line says what choosing it does ("Ada Okonkwo is notified and follows it"). Words typed are not a seat until one is taken from the list: while unchosen the field says so, Create is held with "Choose who “…” is from the Assignee list, or clear it", and Enter opens the list on them, so a name left typed is never silently dropped nor sent as a handle. Left empty, the field says where the task lands: the project's default assignee (applied by the engine inside the create), else triage for its lead.
- **Draft**: what the sheet holds is kept for the tab while it holds anything (`routes/worklet/newTaskDraft.ts`, in `sessionStorage`). The same door opening the sheet again brings the draft back; another door (another project, a seat's question) starts from its own preset; filing, discarding, or a sign-in that hands the browser on lets it go.
- The field's clear control is the kit's own, inside the field as a search box draws it, so the completion list (anchored to the field's box) spans everything it hangs from.
- Every field's help line is its control's description, so a screen reader hears it with the field.
- **Outcomes**: `applied` opens the new task by the key the engine minted; `pending` closes with the not-yet-applied toast; a refusal stays in the sheet in the words the engine wrote for a person (a title over its cap is "The title is too long"), or for one nobody has worded, in its kind's own sentence: never the tool's sentence to a model, which names arguments (ADR-0060).
- **Said before the press**: title and description are counted in the engine's unit (UTF-8 bytes, against `worklet.MaxTitle`, 256, and `MaxBody`, 32 KiB, held by `contract/work.ts`), counting down in the last fifth and marked invalid past the cap, saying by how much. Create is then held and the reason is written in the sheet's foot beside it (the kit reads a held button's reason to a screen reader only); Enter while held takes focus to the field holding it.
- **Enter** in any single-line field is the press, and the sheet says so itself: the kit's sheet is a form, and a browser submits a multi-field form on Enter only via its submit button, which a write control is not. A description takes its newline; Enter that a completion list took chooses from it.
- The foot says, while nothing holds the press, who the task is filed as ("Filed as Jane Founder"). The head is the title alone, as the kit's sheet head (the page bar's height) is sized for.

**Settings is never hidden, and a lock goes where the closed thing is.** A section that vanishes without access is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. ONE RULE decides every lock, `sectionOpen` in `nav.ts`, over three kinds of section (ADR-0033):
- The reader's own (their Account) needs nothing.
- The OVERVIEW needs only being signed in: Home, Company › Principles and Brand, Structure (its Org chart and Table, and every seat page's status), Schedules, Budgets, Live › Now running and Executors, Settings › Token spend. This is what every seat is doing, has spent, may spend and who answers to whom, which everybody who works here reads.
- An APP's sections need that app: Inbox, My work's Worklet sections, Worklet and Settings › Expensive tasks need Worklet; Doclet needs Doclet; every section of Chatlet is chat's; Gitlet's (Gitlet, My work › Reviews, a seat's Code section) need Gitlet, since the engine refuses every code question to a reader without it (ADR-0110), as do the places outside those that read code (Home's Code waiting on a person, a task's Changes tab, ⌘K's Code scope), each drawing what would open it, or nothing, rather than asking.
- Admin's: the company-wide TRANSCRIPTS (Live › Turns, Agent-to-agent and the Event log, Doclet › Agent diaries, a seat's Turns and Memory sections to anybody but its lead) and every other Settings page. Company › Integrations is every reader's, with an app's state and connecting kept for Admins on the page.

Rules for the locks:
- Every comparison goes through `lib/access.ts`'s `holdsAny`, which counts every app an admin carries, so an administrator never sees an app lock.
- A sidebar row is locked only when NOTHING in its workspace that the company runs is open (a section hidden for its service opens nothing), its title naming the access that would open it. A workspace only partly closed draws its locks where the closed part is; for Settings that is its column. So the foot's Settings is never locked: a person holding only the overview would read Settings as closed while its Spend readings were theirs.
- A lock is drawn only once somebody has said what the reader holds (the viewer, or the session's own answer while the viewer has not), since a lock while the first read is out claims a refusal nobody has made. That is ONE READING, `useHeldReading` in `lib/viewer.ts` (who the reader is and what they hold, from one source), which the sidebar's rows, Settings' column and the frame's refusal all take, so they can never lock one reader differently.
- The command palette says the same of a guarded destination, "needs Admin access" beside its hint, read off its address by the rule the frame's refusal reads (`nav.ts`'s `closedBy`), the workspace's access first: every section of Worklet, My work or Chatlet is offered to a reader without that app saying what opens the workspace.
- There is NO "no access yet" state: a person given no app still reads the overview, so the socket is dialled for every signed-in principal and the frame never replaces the company with a panel saying they hold nothing; a lock beside each app says what would open it.
- Only a socket the engine REFUSED (a person whose seat was taken out of the chart) offers nothing of the company: no Pinned section, and the palette asks none of its questions and lists no seat or tool. A refusal DROPS what an earlier socket sent (`Store.setAccessRefused`), so a withdrawn tab shows what a session that never held a seat does, rather than naming the company from its snapshot. An outage keeps the last state; a refusal is not an outage.

**A service the company does not run is hidden, never locked.** A company runs Worklet, or Jira in its place, or no tracker; Doclet, or Confluence, or no knowledge base; Chatlet, or the Mattermost or Slack it declares, or none; and hosts its git repositories in the engine (`code.backend: gitlet`) or does not. The engine decides from the company document and publishes it to every signed-in reader as `services` on the org projection, which the frame reads (`lib/services.ts`). Where the company does not run one, its places are HIDDEN, because there is nothing to ask an admin for and a lock would say there was (`serviceShown` in `nav.ts`):
- Without Worklet: its workspace and My work's Worklet sections leave the sidebar, the palette and the `g` chords (My work itself leaves only where the engine hosts no code either, since its Reviews is Gitlet's, `workspaceShown`), and so does every way to file or move a task: New task, the palette's Create task, Ask an agent and Assign, a seat's ask (its Message, or its Ask as a task where Message is a conversation) and Assign, and every create page's Ask an agent. Every create page stays (a design's included), since each is finished on the page by a person.
- Without Doclet: its workspace.
- Without Chatlet: Chatlet, with its Home widgets; a seat's Message is the ask.
- Where the engine hosts no code: Gitlet, with My work › Reviews, a seat's Code section, a task's Changes tab, Home's Code waiting on a person and Settings › Gitlet.
- The Inbox stays, because the seat and budget conditions waiting on a person arrive under every backend: it draws those, and one line in place of its updates.
- Home leaves out the blocks and figures that cannot arrive, and each row of the board closes up over them: a hidden block's columns go to the blocks left in its row, so no row is drawn short (saved widths are kept, and Edit Home shows the hidden block's cell saying why). The tray's lines say what each widget shows where it is placed.
- An address under a hidden place draws a notice in place (`app/ServiceNotice.tsx`): what the company runs instead, in the engine's word, and why the page asked for is not here (a New design address says a design is made by an agent working a task). Readable by every signed-in reader, and offers the service's own page under Company › Integrations (`#/company/integrations/worklet` or `/doclet`), which every reader may open.
- Nothing is hidden on a guess: it is drawn only once the engine has answered, so a deep link on a cold tab is never refused early. Until the org projection arrives every place is DRAWN as if its service ran, but no read is ASKED of a service (`useServicesAsk`; an app the reader holds counts as not held), and a service's page waits for the projection before it mounts.

**A service this node starts only once restarted is hidden the same way, and says so.** A node builds Worklet, Doclet, Chatlet and Gitlet once, at boot, so a service the company turns on while a node runs is on that node only after it restarts, and until then every question about it there is refused (`native_backend_needs_restart`). The org projection names it in `services.restart` (`lib/services.ts`' `awaitsRestart`), and the dashboard treats it as not run HERE: its row, destinations, chords and controls leave. Its address draws the notice in place with what is true instead of "not in use here": the company turned it on while this node was running, the node starts it when it restarts, and the step the reader can take, the engine's nodes (`#/settings/nodes`) for a reader who may open that page, who to ask for anybody else.

**A guarded section says so and nothing else.** Opened by a reader the engine has SAID holds none of the access it needs, a guarded section is replaced by one refusal (`app/frame/GrantRequired.tsx`), drawn by the frame before the screen mounts: "Nodes needs Admin access", who the reader is signed in as and that an admin can give it to them, and **Switch account**.
- The access is said once, in the title: a button repeating it ("Sign in as somebody holding …") does not wrap and ran past both edges on a phone.
- The reader is named from the reading the refusal was decided on (`useHeldReading`), never from the viewer beside it, which has not answered between the session's answer and the socket's.
- It names ACCESS by the word People gives it (Admin, Worklet, Doclet, Artifacts, Chatlet, Gitlet, Atlas), not a credential: a signed-in person lacks access, and "needs an operator credential" sent them looking for one they have no use for.
- The section waits for the frame's FIRST answer about the reader (one round trip, behind a placeholder), so it asks nothing it may be refused; a screen that mounted anyway drew the refusal as data ("0 nodes", four tiles of 0). That answer is the frame's one reading (`useHeldReading`) decided by the one rule (`sectionOpen`), so the session's answer decides where the viewer has not.
- One address an app's lock does not close is a WORK ITEM SOMEBODY WAS ASKED ABOUT (`App.tsx`): the engine answers the person an open ask names without Worklet access, so the item's own read decides it.
- A read that FAILED is no answer and does not hold the section (that would lock a reader out until the next poll): the screen mounts, and guarded screens draw no figure from a read that never succeeded.
- Structure is the one section that answers its own refusal, because its draft is kept in the tab's storage: replacing the builder when access is withdrawn would take the draft off screen while its writer is still there to copy it out. The builder says for itself which of its saves the reader's access reaches.

**Chatlet is guarded whole, and keeps one refusal of its own.** Every chat page is read AS A SEAT: the engine answers for the seat the session's principal holds, with no handle parameter in the chat family and no arm, an administrator's included, that reads somebody else's rooms. So the workspace's row and all three sections name the Chatlet app, and a reader without it meets the frame's refusal on every chat page, a room included. Chat's own refusal: a principal that holds Chatlet and acts as NO seat (a deployment's own token, a service account) reads nothing, not even a public room, so the screen says "Chatlet is read as the seat you hold", naming the binding that would give the credential one (`crewlet iam
bind`). A company whose chat is not Chatlet (`chat.backend: vendor` or
`none`) is no refusal: Chatlet is a service like Worklet and Doclet, so its row is hidden and an address under it says where the company talks instead, naming the vendor to a reader holding Chatlet.

**A figure beside a row says what it counts.** The kit's `NavItem` takes a figure only with the words that name it, as two props: a **badge** is how many things are waiting on the reader, a **count** is how many of something the destination holds. A figure the engine did not answer is absent, never a zero.

**Who the reader is, and how much is waiting on them, are read ONCE.** The frame asks both (the `viewer` and the Inbox count), and the sidebar, Home's status line and the Inbox's own band all draw that one answer. Per-surface asks held several of the socket's four query slots before a screen's first read could run, and the badge and the sentence beside it could name two numbers. A surface mounted outside the frame is refused rather than handed a read of its own, because that fallback would silently bring the per-surface reads back.

**The engine panel** opens from a compact status at the end of the rail head's line, beside the company's name (the kit's `AppShell.RailStatus` in the head's `status` slot): a dot and, while alarms stand, how many, beside a warning triangle. Its words are its name and title ("Engine serving, 5 alarms"), and it reserves its width, so the company's name truncates at one place whatever the engine's state, and the panel opens below it. It says the one state that decides what a reader should do, in precedence order:
1. Two are about THIS BROWSER: nobody signed in ("Not signed in": the status is then the button that goes to the sign-in, and opens nothing; see [Signing in](#signing-in-is-a-screen-outside-the-frame)), and the engine knows who this is and will not serve them ("Access refused", a seat taken out of the chart).
2. Then: the engine unreachable; the tab still connecting (neutral dot: nothing has reported, neither healthy nor a fault); draining; falling behind (amber, while the push carries `stall_lag_seconds`, sent only once the node's watched duty has missed its beat; the panel says how far, "31s behind", a figure climbing towards the lease TTL at which the node restarts itself); starting (neutral dot, while the node applies its first configuration and its posture says `wait`); no configuration; a posture diverged from the fleet (`shed`, `stuck`, `isolated`); and serving.

The dot is the POSTURE and nothing else: a serving node has a success dot whatever its alarms say. "Engine healthy" is said only when the alarm table was evaluated and nothing in it fires, "Engine serving" otherwise, because "healthy" beside a count of alarms is a claim the count refutes.

**A refusal is a statement**, repaired by an administrator rather than by a press, so its row wears nothing a control wears: the kit's static rail row, no trailing mark, pointer, hover or place in the tab order, where the sign-in row (with a key mark) and every other state's row (which opens the panel) are buttons. Every screen but the reader's own (their Account) is replaced by one panel that names who they are from `GET /auth/session`, what they hold and the engine's reason, and offers the Account, a retry, and the sign-out. A person given no app is NOT in this state: they read the overview.

**An engine that never answered who this is says so.** The frame's `GET /auth/session` waits ten seconds (`SESSION_READ_TIMEOUT_MS`, held to the engine's `auth.SessionClientWait`, twice the longest the guard holds the read). Where it ends with no answer (the deadline, or a connection that never reached the engine) and the socket's `viewer` question has not answered either, every screen, the Account's included, is replaced by one panel, "The engine hasn’t answered", with **Try again** (`app/frame/SessionUnanswered.tsx`), instead of placeholders that never resolve. A tab that has heard who it is read by, over either, keeps its screen when a later read fails.

Pressing the row in any other state opens the panel above it (the kit's `Popover`, named "Engine"): the state again with this node's name, the live node count ("2 live", or "Count unavailable" where the presence read failed, never a zero), the configuration epoch this node applied ("Applying" while it starts), uptime, and the alarms, then **Open node** (`#/settings/nodes/{node}`) and, while alarms stand, **Open alarms** (`#/settings/backups?at=alarms`, which brings the alarm list into view without moving it). While the engine is unreachable the panel says how long ago it last answered and offers **Reconnect now**, which dials at once rather than at the end of the backoff.
- Alarms are listed by name, longest-standing first. Their COUNT is the health push's (the evaluation the engine's gauge and log lines come from); their NAMES are the operator's retention report, the document Backups & retention lists them from, asked for when the panel opens and again when the count moves, because the push is public and names only the longest-standing one. The report is asked only of a reader holding the access that section opens on (Admin); anybody else, or a report not answered yet, is told the longest-standing alarm and how many more stand.
- A name is the alarm's kind read as words, initialisms kept whole ("Backup age", "Trim blocked"), and names one alarm: the engine raises each kind once, with the logs it stands on in it, and which logs those are is Backups & retention's to list (`lib/alarms.ts` holds the rule).
- A table the engine has not evaluated is "Not evaluated", never "None". The push counts the nodes holding a presence lease and does not know how many a fleet should have, so a node that is down is a smaller count and nothing more.
- On a phone the row and its panel are in the drawer, and nowhere else.

**The user block** is who this browser is: a principal the identity directory binds to a seat, which every person is (bound: name, login and seat; the seat's kind is never captioned, since every binding is to a human seat and the guard refuses any other); somebody resolved with no seat (unbound: the login, and *No seat*: an API token's session or a service account acting as itself, which is ordinary); or nobody (a **Sign in** button).
- **The reader is called by their own name, never their seat's** (`readerName` in `lib/viewer.ts`): their directory row's name, as `GET /auth/session` answers it, else their login. The seat is said beside it as the seat, its name off the chart or `@handle` where the chart is unread (before the socket's first snapshot, or on a refused socket, it draws the seat the session names). The seat's name is the chart's name for a place and often a role ("Founder"), which is wrong as a greeting or a name. Home's greeting takes their own name alone, and a person with none is greeted without one.
- **A credential that is not a person but acts as a seat is called by the seat**: a Tier A token bound to Miles's human seat is "Miles", with "via API token" under it ("via service account" for a service account), because it has no name of its own.
