The row says only the kind of credential; which one ("via API token review", "via service account ci:deploy") is the row's title (a screen reader hears it as its description) and a line under the access in the reader's menu, never the credential's spelling as the name. Which credential comes from the login's grammar (`lib/login.ts`), never the session's `kind`, which the engine answers `person` for a token acting as a seat.
- **Badge**: the seat's own initials wearing a key on its corner (the kit's `Avatar` `mark`), so the face says who and the corner says how; a credential bound to no seat keeps the key as its whole face. It is the medium step, which the kit's account row sizes its badge column around in the sidebar's foot.
- **Pressing the name opens the reader's own menu.** For anybody resolved, the row is a menu button (the kit's `AccountRow` `menu`), named by the reader and ", your menu", with a title saying what the menu holds. In the sidebar's foot the kit draws no trailing chevron: its width goes to the name beside the larger badge, and the hover fill says it can be pressed.
- **The menu says only what the row does not**: its header is the reader's access, the one line People uses ("Admin", "Worklet · Doclet", "Overview only"), then **Account** (the one workspace with no sidebar row, `place: "menu"` in `app/nav.ts`, where the password, the second factor and the sessions are), then **Sign out** and **Sign out everywhere** (the latter in the danger ink, saying what it ends). The name links to the Account, not the seat: the seat page is the company's page about a place in the chart and has no security, so a person looking for two-step verification would conclude the dashboard had none. The sign-outs stay in this menu because it is reached even by a person the socket refuses; see [Signing in](#signing-in-is-a-screen-outside-the-frame).
- **And it is the Account's row**: the Account has no sidebar row, so on `#/account` the block is marked current as a row is on its own page, raised, with the hairline, no hue.
- **A session read that failed is not nobody**: where `GET /auth/session` failed (a 503, the network) rather than being refused, the browser may hold a session, so the block says it could not tell who this is, its menu still offers the Account (whose page says what its own read finds) and the sign-out of this browser, and nobody is offered **Sign in**.
- Beside the row sits one control, **Preferences**, drawn with a palette and holding nothing else: the mode (light, match the system, dark), the density and the theme. The two switchers draw one box of three equal cells each, so glyphs and letters read as the same control; the theme is a select whose options carry each theme's two halves as a chip, its name and its tag, and whose list previews (see [Mode and theme](#mode-and-theme)).
- Preferences are per browser and none is the company's: every key the dashboard keeps in browser storage is declared in one table (`lib/storage.ts`), and a key no build reads any more is listed there as retired and removed at boot. The session cookie is the only credential the dashboard has, and nothing of it is in browser storage.
- There is no zone or date preference: every timestamp is drawn in the browser's own zone and its locale's date spelling. A **day field** is not a timestamp: a task's due and start date, and a custom date field without a time, are dates on the company's calendar (`org.timezone`), drawn as that date to every reader. The engine stores them as the company's midnight, which on the browser's clock is the evening before for anybody west of the company. So the rail, a list's Due and Start columns, a card, a change sentence, a calendar cell and a timeline column all read the company's date, the calendar the engine's standing, overdue mark and `due=` day range are cut on, while a day's arithmetic (the grid, the span between two dates) is civil and moves with no zone.
- **The build is the foot's last line**: "Crewlet" and the engine's version as its health reports it (a release's `v1.4.0`, the image of main's `main-<commit>`, a source build's pseudo-version, or `dev` and `(devel)` for a development build), quiet, under the row (the kit's `AccountRow` `build`), cut at the rail's edge with the whole string in its title. It names the last node this tab reached, so it stays through a dropped socket until the next connection's snapshot replaces it. Folded, it is a line of the face's tooltip.
- There is no company switcher: one engine runs one company.

**The lockup is the company**, beside the product's mark: "Nimbus", on one line, and the way home. The product's name stands in only while no company has been sent, which includes a socket the engine refused. The kit's default puts the product first and the company under it; here the company is the subject, and the product is in the mark and the tab.

`g` then a letter jumps to a workspace:
- the first run: `g h`, `g i`, `g m`, `g q` (Ask Crewlet, a question), `g v` (the Advisor);
- Company: `g c` Principles, `g e` Brand, `g a` Structure, `g d` Schedules, `g n` Integrations, `g b` Budgets;
- Workspace: `g w`, `g g` for Gitlet (`i`, `t`, `l` and `e` are the Inbox's, Chatlet's, Live's and Brand's, so it takes its own prefix letter: a prefix in flight takes whatever key comes next, so the second `g` is the jump's key, never a second prefix), `g t` for Chatlet, `g k`, `g f` for Artifacts, `g l` for Live;
- `g s` for Settings, `g u` for your Account.

A chord to a hidden place is not answered, as its row is not drawn. A chord rather than a modifier, because every single-modifier combination worth having is already the browser's. Two `g` sequences are not workspaces: `g r` watches the running turn when exactly one seat is working, and opens Live › Now running (every running turn) when several are, or none; and `g p` switches project ([below](#worklets-scope-is-named-and-switched-in-the-trail)). Every key the dashboard answers is in [one table](#the-keys), and `?` shows it.
### Worklet's scope is named and switched in the trail

Worklet's pages end their trail in the scope they show: **All projects**, or one
project as its key chip and name (`Worklet › FAIR Product and
Engineering`). That last crumb is the page's `h1` and the kit's `Switcher`
button at once (`app/header/ProjectSwitcher.tsx`): pressing it, or `g p` from
anywhere, opens one panel that changes the scope. Beside it sit the scope's
**lenses**, drawn as the kit's chip `Tabs`: All projects' are Worklet's sections (Projects, Tasks and History, each a path), a project's are keys on its address (Tasks, About, History and Files). Both draw alike, the lens that is on outlined by its accent hairline; Worklet keeps no row of section tabs. Worklet is plain words on its landing, where a link would lead to the page it is on, and the frame's star is not drawn on these pages. On a phone the lenses take a row of their own under the bar's line, and Worklet shrinks to its glyph.

**The panel.** A search band, a list that scrolls and a footer that does not. In order:
- **All projects**: the open work across every active project.
- A note when the listing was cut at 200 ("200 of 340. Type to search.").
- **Recent**: the last three projects opened with the current one aside, once a company has more than eight.
- **Projects**: the active ones, a 52 px key column, the name and the open count, the current scope outlined.
- Footer: **Browse all projects** and **New project…**. New project is held with its reason for a reader who cannot set a project on the org chart: a project is a key another system finds a unit or seat by, so setting one takes Admin, a unit's lead included.

Archived projects are never offered; the panel says they are listed under Projects. It opens under its button on Worklet's scope pages, centred over the page for `g p` anywhere else (nothing behind it moves until a row is chosen), and as a sheet from the bottom edge under 640 px.

**Searching.** Keys and names, ignoring case, matched letters bold. Order: exact key, keys starting with the query, names with a word starting with it, keys and names containing it, ties by key (`lib/projectRank.ts`, the order ⌘K uses too). Past the listing's cap the engine is asked as well, through the listing's own `q`, once typing rests; that also matches a project's purpose. The count is announced politely ("3 projects", "No project matches"), and a search matching nothing offers **Search tasks for “…”**.

**Keys.** `Enter` opens a row in place, `Mod+Enter` in a new tab; a middle or `Mod` click does the same, because every row is a link. Arrows wrap and pass over a held row. `Esc` closes the panel and returns focus to the button, `Tab` closes it and moves on to the lenses, and after a switch focus stays on the button of the page it lands on. `Home` and `End` move the caret in the search field, as in every editable combobox the kit draws.

**What a switch keeps** (`app/scope.ts`). Tasks and History carry over, About and Files carry between two projects, every other lens opens the next scope's first lens. Only the list's shape travels, and only with Tasks: a saved view and the filters belong to the scope they were set in, because a project's statuses, labels and fields are its own. The browser tab reads lens, then scope: "Tasks · All projects", "About · Product and Engineering".

**New project** (`routes/worklet/NewProject.tsx`) asks for:
- An owner: a team, or an agent seat above every team, that owns no project yet, each offered by its key or handle. Never a person's seat, which the engine refuses a project.
- A key (`KEY_SHAPE`, and no project or node already has it).

It then continues in Structure with that node's editor open on its **Work** tab at the tracker project field, holding the key, not yet applied. The org is what makes a project: the engine creates it when the change is saved. Setting a node's project is an admin's write even inside a unit somebody leads (a project is a key another system finds the node by), so the button is drawn for every reader and held with that reason for one without Admin.
### The routes

Only a route a screen draws is written here, and `router.test.ts` holds this
table against `routes.ts`'s resolver both ways: every address below resolves to
a screen, and every workspace and section the code declares is below.

| Route | Page | Params |
|---|---|---|
| `#/` · `#/home` | **Home** — the landing screen: the company's day, the engine's one sentence, the pulse figures and what needs a decision | |
| `#/inbox` | **Inbox**: what waits on your decision, and what reached you *(no access needed for the page: each half lists under its own app, Worklet's notices with Worklet access and Gitlet's with Gitlet access)* | |
| `#/inbox/ask/{id}` · `#/inbox/run/{turn_id}` · `#/inbox/run/{turn_id}/{id}` · `#/inbox/fold_in/{id}` · `#/inbox/seat/{handle}` · `#/inbox/condition/{id}` · `#/inbox/notice/{id}` · `#/inbox/change/{id}/{id}` · `#/inbox/artifact/{id}` | **Inbox** with one item open, by its own address ([The Inbox is where you act](#the-inbox-is-where-you-act)) | |
| `#/me` | **My work › Queue**: what one person holds, by due date or in the order somebody put it, reordered by dragging a row *(needs Worklet access, as every section of My work but Reviews does)* | `order=due\|priorities` · `handle=` (whoever leads somebody, or an admin, reading their day, kept across the sections) · on the queue, `shape=`, `cols.list=` / `cols.table=` and the filter grammar with the assignee LOCKED |

No detail route | `window=` · `actor=` · `kind=worklet\|doclet\|config\|credentials\|runtime\|identity\|artifacts` |

Read-only | |

The link the engine mints lands here | |

**There is no redirect table.** There was one, and it was always a liability: a
redirect whose old path is now a live route sends every reader of that route
somewhere else, permanently, with the address bar agreeing with them — which is
strictly worse than the dead link it exists to avoid, because a dead link is
visible. It happened once, to an address that had meant an executor before a
workspace took it over. No `v*` tag
has ever shipped a route from this tree, so there is nobody holding an old link:
an address from before the one-sidebar rebuild (one under the retired
`activity`, `cost` or `admin` heads), or from before Company and Settings were
split (one under the retired `agents` and `spend` heads, or a Settings page
that moved to Company or was renamed), is Not Found, which names what was asked for, says
where the product knows why there is nothing there, and offers the way home.

**An object's segment is decided by its shape, never by a lookup**, so every
address resolves before any answer arrives. A project or container key is
uppercase, a task is `KEY-n` or its uuid, and a page is its uuid, so a word in
one of those positions (`people` after `worklet`, `runbook` after `doclet/pages`)
is Not Found rather than an object the engine never minted, which would draw its
refusal under a trail naming a page that does not exist.

**Two of those surfaces are the engine answering a question it has always
been able to answer.** Search is the ranking a seat gets from `search_work_items` —
by the words (Keyword, BM25 over the engine's own index), by what they mean
(Meaning, the wire's `semantic`), or both fused (Hybrid, the default) — which
the operator reading the same company had no access to at all; the board's `q=`
is an escaped substring over an excerpt and answers something else. The mode is
`mode=` in the address, and an answer served in a different mode than asked
(`served_mode`, from the engine's own `degraded` value — a company with no
embeddings provider asking Hybrid is served Keyword) says so above the hits.
The phrase field never gives way to the modes beside it: the form wraps by what
it holds, so on a phone the field takes a line of its own and the modes and
Search the next. A hit's snippet is a cut of a markdown body and is drawn as
the prose it renders to, without its `**` and `#` (the knowledge search's
snippets too). The item's **Woke** tab is who one change
actually reached and under which of nineteen reasons, which is the fact no
commercial tracker records: all of them can say you were notified and none can
say why. Both readers were written, tested and swept on a retention horizon
before either reached a screen.

### An item's address

**An item is opened by its KEY, unless another task claimed that key first.**
Two tasks can hold one key (a key counter restored beside work minted after it). The engine opens the key on the claimant, on every node, so existing links and chat messages keep reaching it. The other task is flagged `key_collision`, and its key opens its neighbour: it is reached by its **id**, which the item route takes as readily as a key. Every row listing a task says which it is, beside the key it qualifies:

- `key_collision`: a board row, a search hit, an item and its links, a page's backlinks.
- `subject_key_collision`: a feed record, an inbox notice.
- `task_key_collision`: a checklist item.

A notice is addressed by its `task`, not its subject: a `prioritised` notice's subject is the person whose list a lead reordered.

`itemAddress` in `lib/work.ts` is the one place the rule is written (the key, unless flagged or empty, then the id). Every link, peek, `[`/`]` step, "this is the open row" check and copied tool call goes through it, with `itemPath` for the route and an adapter per row shape (`subjectItem`, `noticeItem`, `checklistTask`, `linkedItem`, `detailItem`) so no screen pairs an id with the wrong flag. A project's route is `projectPath` likewise: no route into Worklet is spelled at the call site. `routes/worklet/collision.test.tsx` clicks each of a pair in every shape the work list draws and reads where it went. The key is still what a row SHOWS: the address decides where it goes, never what it is called.

**A write names the task by its address too**, because the engine resolves a key for a change as for a read: a duplicate's page sending its key changed the claimant (ticks, watch, comments, asks, hand-off) and refused a field edit against the claimant's version. The task page and its peek hold the address once (`ItemEditsProvider`'s `item`, the composer's, the hand-off's) and pass the key only as the word a sentence uses; turns, history and comments are asked for by id. The grid's inline edits, the note naming who won a lost race, a link chosen in the composer (by the hit's id, linked by its address) and the trash's **Restore** follow the same rule. `routes/worklet/WorkItem.test.tsx` opens a duplicate's page and reads what every write named; `collision.test.tsx` restores each of a pair from the trash.

**A turn's task is asked for by its id.** A turn's work item (`work_item{backend, id, key, project}`) is what the turn was charged to, not a tracker row, so it carries no `key_collision`; asked for by key, a turn on the non-claimant was titled, numbered and opened as its neighbour. So a Worklet task is asked for and opened by its id (`turnItem` in `lib/work.ts`), an answer is matched to the question by either name (`answersAddress`), and once an answer has carried the flag the task is opened through `itemAddress`. A vendor's item, whose id is the vendor's, keeps its key. The seat profile's **Current turn** card, the seat peek's "Turn N", the turn page's ordinal and its **Open task**, and an Inbox decision about a parked run or a stopped seat all follow it.

### `window=` — one vocabulary for every time range

One key and one control serve every screen with a range (the live strip was a constant, `STRIP_MINUTES`), so the same hour is the same length everywhere and a link from one screen to another carries its range. The value is a duration from a closed set (`15m` `1h` `6h` `1d` `7d` `30d` `90d`), or `today`, or an explicit interval in ISO 8601's own `<from>/<to>`, so a custom window is one value a reader can copy from the address bar. The custom window's Apply is its form's submit button, so Enter in either box applies it (as a plain button Enter did nothing, for the reason the New task sheet gives).

**A screen of whole company days** (`Offer.customDays`, Spend) puts every edge on a company midnight: `30d` is the thirty company days ending today, as the engine answers `days=30`, running to the first instant after today. Never align to UTC midnights, which in Berlin ended at 02:00 tomorrow for twenty-two hours of every day. The custom dialog is prefilled from those edges, so Apply without an edit asks for the same window. The previous window is the same number of days, counted in days rather than hours across a clock change.

**`today` is the company's day so far**, cut at the first instant of the date on the company's clock (`org.timezone`, the calendar `internal/period` keeps), not the browser's midnight and not "the last 24 hours". The first instant, not 00:00: where a zone moves its clock across midnight the day starts at 01:00 (Santiago) or at the first of two midnights (Amman), and a "Today" disagreeing with the engine's day by an hour would count a turn the engine charged to yesterday. It moves with the clock like a duration, is charted in hours from its first, and its "previous" window is the same span before midnight. A screen offers it like any window; the control draws it first.

**A company zone this browser cannot read is read as UTC.** The engine takes any zone Go's time-zone database names, which a browser's can lack. Every reading of the company's clock then uses UTC (`lib/companyDay.ts`'s `companyZone`): the day and time a row is listed under, the days a window covers, the day a budget resets on (Home's "resets Mon" among them) and the snooze menu's tomorrow and next Monday, so none disagrees with another. A window the engine cut is named by its label (`2026-09` is September), which needs no clock. A schedule's next runs are the one exception and are not listed at all: instants worked out on a clock the engine does not fire on would be wrong (see [A cron expression is read, not printed](#a-cron-expression-is-read-not-printed)).

**The offered set is the screen's, not the vocabulary's.** A spend chart has nothing to say about fifteen minutes; a strip folded from the events the browser holds has nothing to say about ninety days, nor about an interval that ended last Tuesday. Each screen declares which windows it has and whether an interval is one of them; a URL naming anything else gets that screen's default, since a value the control cannot show would put a heading nobody chose over the rows and leave no way back. The control renders the offered set in the vocabulary's order, so `1d` reads the same everywhere.

`window=` is a **section**, not a filter: a reader who widened the range and pressed Back means the narrower one.

**A range is kept for its reader.** The address is one history entry's: it carries a range through a reload and a link, nothing else. The sidebar, the palette, a new tab and a sign-in landing open a screen with no range, which must not fall back to a constant. So the last named window a reader CHOSE on a screen is kept in the browser (`lib/keptRange.ts`, one record per reader in `lib/readerStore.ts`, a word per screen), for `window=` and Home's `range=` alike:

- **The address wins when it names a range.** A shared link opens the range its sender saw.
- **Where it names none, the reader's last choice is the range**, the screen's default only if they never made one. That choice is noted into the address without a history entry, so a copied address says the range shown; the address stays bare where the kept choice is the default or nothing is kept.
- **A choice is written to both, and to the address in full**, the default included: a bare address means "the reader's own", so the only way to say "seven days" to whoever opens the link is to say it. The assistant's range actions write the default in full likewise.
- **Opening a link is not a choice.** Only the control writes the store.
- **Only a named window is kept** (`7d`, `today`). Two typed instants are shown and linked, not remembered. A stored word the screen no longer offers is its default.
- **Screens that ask one question share a choice**: Token spend and its Expensive tasks page keep one window. Every other screen keeps its own, since their offers differ.

The two edges reach the engine as the half-open `since`/`until` pair every windowed question takes, except on Spend, whose named windows are whole company days cut on the company's clock: it sends `days` and offers no interval of two instants. A chart's edges are rounded **up to the bucket it draws**, so the hour in progress is on the chart and the query changes once per column, not once per second; a list's are not. An interval never moves: it is the one window stable to link to.

### Every list is one grid

`DataGrid` draws all of them: `@crewlethq/ui`'s `DataGrid`, which the dashboard binds to the address (the sort and the column set), the peek (the row it is open on) and the keymap (which grid `j` and `k` drive). No `<table>` is left except a project's Files listing: a block inside a card that already titles it, with nothing to sort, a table in the sense the element means. The retention screen's per-domain terms are a description list. A Gitlet directory's entries are a table too: head cells hidden from sight, each row stacking on a phone, with the grid's `j`, `k` and Enter. Gitlet's Branches and Tags are tables likewise: boxes titled in their first head cell, each row stacking on a phone, with the grid's `j`, `k` and Enter.

**Gitlet's lists are rows of sentences, not a grid.** Its commits, changes, repositories and pushes are drawn by `CodeList`, which keeps the grid's `j`, `k` and Enter, the peek, a phone row, Load more and the address.

**Worklet's own list and table are one grid with two column sets.** Two components over one answer meant each lacked the other's rules (one track list for the whole grid, the cap on a shrink column, the card below 640px, the cursor `j` and `k` walk), and the table drew an EMPTY band per group once a second axis was asked for, because sub-groups replace a group's rows and it read only `rows`. The shape now picks a **column set** and nothing else: same fetch, bands, head and phone layout. A set is a default (columns on with nothing chosen), an order, and how a value is drawn: the list's priority is the bare mark that opens its row, the table's is the word in a sortable column.

**`cols=` selects WITHIN the active set, and is keyed per shape**: `cols.list=` and `cols.table=`. A grid already drops names its columns lack and falls back to its default when none survive; the reason is that `cols=` carries an **order** as well as a selection, and the order is the set's own. One key read against both sets would draw the list's columns in the table's arrangement, which no validation catches since every name is legal in both. Per shape, each arrangement survives the other. The **sort** is not keyed that way: it is a fact about the QUESTION (the engine orders the whole set the same way whatever draws it), so both shapes share one `sort=`.

**The sort is in the URL**, the rule the component exists for: a sorted table that cannot be sent, does not survive a reload and comes back unsorted from Back is sorted for one person for one minute.

**A grid too narrow for its columns gives some up, and says which.** The wrap clips (that keeps the sticky head working), so overrunning columns would be cut with nothing to scroll, or, with every flexible track floored at zero, the column that is the point of the list would be squeezed away (the work list beside a peek at 1280 drew titles 70px wide). A column may declare a `floor` (the work title's is `16rem`), and droppable columns declare the order they go in (`drop`, lowest first). When the tracks overrun the box, or a content-sized column is squeezed below its fifth of the grid and cuts a value short ("T…" for a status), the next column goes, until they fit or nothing droppable is left; when the box grows, every column gets another chance. The foot says "Hidden to fit: Updated and Due", since a silently vanished column is a value the reader cannot tell was there.

- **Work sets** give up what a task's own page answers one click away: when it last moved, then the dates and sizes a reader switched on, then the due date, then the marks. Never the key, the status, the title or who holds it. The status word is drawn whole rather than cut to a column's share.
- **Schedules' grids** keep a schedule's name whole (`12rem`, for a slug like `morning-tracker-review`) in both (beside a peek at 1280 the recent runs drew it 35px wide). A run gives up its Scope first (a role schedule's scope is the seat it woke), then the tick it was for, then whom it woke.
- **People** is a column of the sheet beside a person's peek, and every flexible column it keeps has a floor (Seat and Access `8rem`; at zero the seat drew its avatar alone and the access stacked a row tall). Beside the peek it keeps what people are compared by: the name with the login as its second line, the stage and the access, which never gives way. It gives up Kind first (a row that is not a person wears a key beside its name), then the seat, which the peek names. Service accounts give up Acts as and keep their access the same way.
- **Access in ANY cell** (People list, invitations, a person's or the Account's tokens) is the one line the dashboard says it in (`AccessTags` over `accessLine`, `lib/access.ts`): one **Admin** tag for anybody holding it, never Admin beside the apps it includes; otherwise a tag per app, or **Overview only**. At most two tags plus any raw name this build does not know, so no "+n" tag is needed (eleven grants drawn whole stood one People row about 290px tall at 1280).
- **The peek's own grids** are a 385px column: a credential's name and a session's state keep `8rem` floors; its state pill and a session's start take their own width (`max-content`, short by construction, where a fifth of the column cut "In use" to "In u…" and "Session" to "SESS…"); a credential gives up Expires, then Carries, then Created.

None of it happens on a phone, where a row is a card showing every value.

**The row a peek is open on is marked, in every grid.** The grid compares ADDRESSES: a row's link is its object's page, and the open peek names an object whose page is the same `peekHref` every such link is built with, so the tint lands exactly on the row the rail describes, and the row's link carries `aria-current` so the mark is said as well as painted. A mark that is not the peek (the credential a path addresses, the revision the Diff lens reads) is the screen's own (`isSelected`).

**A band may hold bands.** A second grouping is a heading under a heading; a band carries rows OR sub-bands, never both (sub-groups replace a group's rows as groups replace the ungrouped ones). A band counts what is under it, sub-bands included, and a band whose page of rows is empty still draws its heading: "Ada Okonkwo · 0 of 3" is an answer, where an empty state drawn over it is a second and false one.

**A screen's primary grid takes `sort=` and every other one takes `sort.<name>=`.** Screens carrying two or three grids (spend by seat and recent turns, a node's leases and duties) would otherwise read one key, so sorting the lower grid would re-sort the upper and a link would mean something depending on which table the reader touched. A name rather than an index, because an index is a fact about source order and inserting a grid above would shift every link's meaning. **It is held, not remembered:** the address is the document's, so a grid in the peek rail reads the same keys as the screen under it. Every mounted grid registers the keys it reads and reports a second grid on one of them to `console.error`, which fails every dashboard case that mounts the pair (`app/frame/DataGrid.tsx`). An agent's Access tab draws one grid per integration, so each is named for its integration.

**A `shrink` column is capped, because `max-content` is not "shrink to content": it is *grow* to content, with no ceiling.** Grid resolves an intrinsic track before giving anything to a flexible one, so one long value takes what it likes and every flexible column collapses to zero (the schedules grid drew Wakes at 502px of 822px with **Name and Task at 0px**, and still ran 317px past a clipping box; the work table at 1000px drew Assignee at 220px with the **title** at zero). A shrink track is `fit-content` of a fraction of the grid: a column under the cap is untouched and only one taking more than its share gives way. One fraction for every grid, not a pixel floor per column, which would be a number invented nineteen times and again at every width.

**Below 640px (`breakpoint.phone`) a row is a card, because 390px has no columns.** The audit's six columns want 808px and the work trash's twelve more, and the wrap is `overflow: clip` (the same decision that keeps the head sticky), so everything past the viewport was cut with nothing to scroll to. Sideways scrolling is not the way out: the flexible tracks are `minmax(0, 1fr)`, so once the wrap scrolls, its content box is the viewport, the content-sized columns alone exceed it and every flexible track resolves to zero (the title column vanishing to make room for a due date).

So the head goes and each cell draws its own name beside its value. Four rules follow, which a new column keeps:

- **A column with no word in its head declares one.** `header` is what the head row draws, so a twenty-pixel column carries a mark or nothing (a work item's type, a row's actions, a pair of state tags). A card has no head, so the column supplies the word separately in `label`, drawn only here; without it the card gets a bare mark on a line between two labelled ones, which reads as a rendering fault. `app/source.test.ts` stops one reaching a screen.
- **A cell with nothing in it is not a line.** A column draws no value on a row that has none (`PriorityMark` renders null for `none`, and every mark whose rule is "nothing is drawn for no value" does the same). In the table that is an empty track under a head, which keeps the columns lined up. In a card the label is the CELL's own, so it would show `PRIORITY` alone on a line; this is the labelled form of the dashed placeholder the board card already stopped drawing. The kit's `.crewlet-data-grid__cell:empty` drops it. It is `:empty` rather than a column predicate because a container cannot ask a child that drew nothing whether it did, and the element must stay in the DOM since the wide layout's tracks are positional (dropping it would move every later value one column left). Generated content is not a child node, so the label's `::before` does not defeat `:empty`. A cell drawing a marked absence has content and keeps its line, the distinction `EmptyValue` exists to make.
- **A value wraps rather than being cut.** `.truncate` suits a cell that IS one line of a fixed column and is wrong once the column is gone: at 390px it cut the one field the reader opened the list for. What bounds the value instead is the engine: a title is at most `worklet.MaxTitle`.
- **A head longer than the label column wraps inside it.** The label is a fixed 7rem (112px), so every value in a card starts at the same place; 7rem fits the widest head on one line, CONVERSATION at 93.09px. A basis on an unbreakable line is a request, not a width: a flex item's `min-width` is `auto`, flooring it at its content, so one over-long head grew its label box to 128.03px and shifted only ITS value 16.03px right (measured at 390px on the provisioning passes: five values 136px from the card's edge and WHAT IT CONCLUDED's at 152.03px). The label wraps instead, mid-word where it must, the trade `.num-col` takes one layout over: a heading longer than its column wraps, visibly, and the column holds.
- **The sort control goes with the head.** That is the real cost of the shape and the right trade: a column head a reader cannot see is not an affordance, and `sort=` is in the URL, so a sorted list still arrives sorted from a link or from the wider layout that set it.

**A footnote may not set its column's width.** A `.fact` is a column flex box as wide as its widest child, and a note is prose where the value above it is a word. On a Doclet page's header, notes of 146px (`v1` under "set by Agent CEO · 2m ago") and 153px (`2m ago`) beside note-less facts at 66 to 75px made the gaps between the five labels 85, 162, 90, 169, as if placed at random. A note is held to sixteen characters (about two short words a line at `--font-size-2xs`, roughly the label's width), which brought the gaps to 85, 144, 90, 144. `text-wrap: balance` makes the wrap look deliberate: at a hard 18ch the two notes left "2m ago" and "a save" alone on a second line, and an orphan reads as a fault. This is not `--size-measure`, a reading measure for prose somebody sits down with; a caption under a fact is read in one glance beside what it qualifies.

**A trail of one segment is not a trail.** The Doclet page draws its ancestor chain above the header, outermost first, because a title alone does not say which team's tree a page is in. For a page filed directly in its container (most of them) that chain is the container alone: a lone accent word reading as a stray button, saying what the `Container` fact below already says as a link to the same place. The trail is drawn only once it holds what the fact cannot carry, the path THROUGH the tree.

The guard wraps the NOTE, not its contents. `PageNote` renders its paragraph whatever it is handed, and that paragraph carries its own margin, so a guard on the breadcrumb inside it swaps a stray link for an empty band, the same gap with nothing in it. A test counting links cannot see that, so the element is asserted separately.

**A person in a grid cell is a RESOLVED NAME.** A handle is the database's word for somebody (what a filter takes, a payload carries, a column stores), not what anybody is called. Every cell drawing a person resolves it through the org chart and prints the NAME, under four clauses that travel together:

- **The handle is the fallback, never a blank.** A seat the chart no longer has still names somebody, so an unresolved handle is drawn as the handle. A blank would read as "nobody", which the column has its own mark for; the facts differ: nobody holds this, versus somebody the chart has lost.
- **The hover title carries whichever one the cell does not print.** A cell printing the name titles the HANDLE (what an operator types into a filter; resolving the name must not destroy the identifier); a cell printing no word (the compact row's badge) titles the NAME, the only place the answer is. The title never repeats what is on screen.
- **Where an avatar is drawn it is initials on a NEUTRAL badge**, built from the resolved name, not the handle (handle initials make every seat starting with one letter the same mark). It takes no colour, by [the one rule](#the-one-rule): a seat is identity, carried by the name, the mark and the position. **An agent the chart holds is drawn as itself instead**: its own Crewlet character on a plate of its own colour, the look its author chose (the one rule's third exception), where its initials would be. A person, and a handle the chart does not hold, keep the initials.
  - The look is a REQUIRED input of every shared piece that draws a seat (`SeatAvatar`, `seatBadge`, `linkedSeat`, `plainSeat`, `SeatChip`, `Assignee`), so a surface cannot leave an agent's character behind by omission; `faceOf` is the one translation of a look into the kit's. Every picker offering a seat draws its face beside its name (`ChoiceFace`: a Select option's `leading`, a Menu item's `icon`, a filter row's face), and its Nobody choice the empty-assignee mark. Source gates in `ui/SeatAvatar.test.tsx` hold all three.
  - Its only other variant is STRUCTURAL, its outline: a circle for a person, a squircle for an agent. **Every** cell drawing a person resolves the kind with the name: `seatLookup` answers both, the row chrome carries both, and the two cells a screen hands them to (`SeatCell`, `SeatChip`) take the same `kind` prop, so a caller cannot thread the name and drop the kind (half-threaded, one human seat was a person in the table column set and an agent in the list, and eighteen of nineteen seat chips passed nothing).
  - A handle the chart does not hold is resolved from the RECORD: every change row and comment carries its writer's `actor_kind`/`author_kind`, and `kindWithAuthors` layers those under the chart's answer (`human` and `operator` draw a person, `agent` an agent). A credential bound to no seat needs this (an API token's session, a service account acting as itself): its write is authored under a login no chart lists, and the chart alone drew the founder who filed a task through the deployment's token as a squircle.
  - A handle with neither answer takes the kit's default, the agent's squircle (the kit has no third outline), and is never drawn as a person, since a circle would claim an answer nothing gave.
  - Inside a row that is itself a link, `SeatLabel` draws the same badge and name with no anchor of its own, so a seat column is never a processor glyph where every other surface draws the seat's badge.
  - The two places passing a literal `agent` are those where the chart cannot be wrong (a turn's seat and an executor's seat, which the engine RUNS, never a human seat), and they say so at the call.
  - A badge BESIDE the printed name is decorative, or the row reads "Ada Lovelace avatar, Ada Lovelace"; a badge ALONE keeps its accessible name, or columns drawing no word announce the assignee as nothing.
- **The KIND is marked only where it is not the ordinary one.** Who wrote something is a person and a kind (`agent`, `human`, `operator`, `system`), and `agent` is what nearly every write in an agent company is. A mark on every row separates nothing: the tag exists so writes that were NOT an agent's stand out. The word checked against is the engine's own; a cell spelling it separately once checked for a kind the engine does not mint and marked every row.

The cells this governs: the frame's `SeatCell`, the shared `SeatChip`, the Worklet's compact `Assignee`, the Projects directory's Lead and Last change, the trash's `removed_by`, the log's actor, a schedule's scope and every fire it woke, a saved view's owner, a page's watchers and commenters and a delivery's recipient. The rule is written here because the same person must look the same on every screen. `components/work.test.tsx` and `routes/worklet/shapes/Grid.test.tsx` hold the outline over the pieces and over the grid's two column sets.

### A row of numbers shares its lines

A stat row's tiles are one grid's columns, and **every figure in a row stands at one height whatever its label does**. Each tile is a subgrid over the row's three lines (label, number, sub), so a line is as tall as the tallest of it across the row: a wrapped label makes the label line two lines tall for every tile, and each other label sits at its foot, one gap above its own number. Stacked per tile, a wrapped label pushed only its own number down (beside a node's peek at 1440, "Behind on config" broke over two lines and its figure sat 18px below the other three). Where the kit folds a row to two columns (below 1024px) an odd last tile takes the whole row, and a sub wraps rather than ending in an ellipsis. `styles/stats.test.tsx` holds the span to the lines the kit's tile renders.
### A dropdown's list sizes to its options

The product has one dropdown, `@crewlethq/ui`'s `Select` in its listbox mode. Three compensating rules once lived in this tree; all were fixed in the package from `0.4.4`. The shapes recur:

- A row shrank below its content: an explicit `min-height` on a flex item replaces the automatic content minimum, so a tall list squeezed every row before it scrolled.
- An option label declared `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis` but no `white-space`; text allowed to wrap never ellipsizes.
- The panel was placed with the TRIGGER's width while its height was measured off the panel. That pinned a toolbar picker's list to its current answer, made `align="right"` compute the same as `align="left"`, and clamped a grown panel as if it had not grown, so it hung over the viewport edge.

**A rule compensating for a package expires; the consumer must notice.** The fix belonged upstream, in the `placePopup` call that already measured the panel's height. Nothing here styles `.crewlet-select__menu`, `.crewlet-listbox__option` or `.crewlet-select__option-label`, and `styles/classes.test.ts` keeps that true: a rule on a package class needs an `ALLOWED` entry with a reason.

A screen's own class on the panel is no way round it. An Agents tab widened its level picker with `menuClassName` and a `min-width`, but the built page links the app's sheet after the package's rules (`vite.config.ts`, `appSheetsToBodyEnd`), so the screen's rule lost and every level picker opened at its cell's 120px. The package owns the width: a list whose options carry a description gets a reading width (floor 22rem, measure 28rem, never wider than the window) and is never wider than the field it opened from. The Agents tab and Settings › Models & Fleets' seats keep no width rule.

### An object's own facts

`PropertiesRail` is the rail beside an object: its state, people, plan and record. It draws with `@crewlethq/ui`'s `PropertyList` (each section a description list on one subgrid, so every label shares one term column), and translates the engine's routes, turns by id and change log instants into it. The kit's suite holds the rules below. It replaced a flat `KeyValue` (event, run, turn, seat) and a separate sectioned work item rail, which differed in label widths, gaps and absent-value rules, and could not say **who** set a fact, which is what a reader of an agent-written object asks most: "moved to in progress by ada, eleven minutes ago, in turn ↗", not "In progress".

**An absent value is a decision.** Four facts share one empty cell:

- the row is **dropped**: the object has no such property (a task with no collaborators has no collaborators row);
- the row is a **dash**: the property exists and holds nothing (an unset due date);
- the row **says something**: the empty state means something ("none — reflection uses the default");
- the whole **group says something**, in one line, because every property in it is absent: `whenAllAbsent`. A section of nothing is not a row of nothing: a fresh task spent a heading, hairline and four dashes saying nothing is scheduled, most of a 420px peek. "Nothing scheduled: no dates, no estimate, no size." says it once; the heading stays (the group exists and is empty, unlike *dropped*), and the rows return when any one is filled.

The caller says which, on all four, so forgetting cannot produce a plausible wrong one. The fourth is opt-in, not inferred: a rail of annotation rows would otherwise fold into one sentence when somebody cleared them, undecided. `0` and `false` are values, rendered, never folded into "nothing set".

**One attribution per change, not per row.** A **run** of consecutive properties sharing one (actor, instant, turn) draws ONE line, naming what it covers, under the last: "Status, Priority and Type · set by agent-ceo · 21h ago · turn ↗". This is the rule [A row is not a row](#a-row-is-not-a-row) states for a feed. A row that draws no line ends the run rather than being reached over, since "Status and Type" with a Priority between them is a claim to check.

**Never an attribution under an absence.** Provenance under a dash claims the engine recorded somebody setting nothing. The exception is a change that EMPTIED the field, which the log witnessed; it reads "cleared by", not "set by". One component, shared with the header's fact line, writes the wording (it drifted when written twice: the line said "set by ada", the rail a bare "ada", which under a value reads as who wrote the row).

**A header and a rail stacked in one column are one reading.** On an object's page the rail sits BESIDE the header in a sticky side column, so the fact line (scan in a second) and the rows (study) are read across a gap. In a **peek** both share one 420px column, so the same facts in both are the same answer twice before the description. A peek whose body is a properties rail passes NO facts and the rail states every property once; a peek with no rail (a unit, a revision) keeps its fact line, the only place the object's values are stated. The caller decides, since the rule is about the frame's BODY.
### A log is an axis, then its rows

A page of rows answers *what happened*, not *when the company was busy*: the event log and the Inbox need a time axis.

**`Histogram`** is that axis, and its bars are the **engine's**. The browser holds at most a page, never the store's window, so a client-folded axis would be right for one window and absent for the rest (the spend series follows the same rule). Both halves compile their filters through one predicate in the store, so a bar never claims rows the listing beneath would not show. Every bucket is drawn, empty ones included (a quiet hour is a fact). Height is the true proportion with a floor in **pixels**, not percent, so a bucket of 4 beside one of 400 stays visibly shorter.

**A bar is a control.** Clicking one narrows `window=` to the bucket it covers: "what happened in that spike" is the question the spike creates.

**The axis is labelled.** A seven-day window with one busy day is a lone column against an empty plot, which reads as a failed load. So the first bucket, the last and an even spread between carry their own dates: five labels at most (what the narrowest layout holds), positioned over the bucket each names, not in flow, since a label is wider than its bar. A day bucket is a date with the year dropped in the reader's own year (the form every date column takes); anything shorter is a wall clock in the browser's zone, so a chart of minutes does not repeat today's date five times. Labels are **ink**, tabular, at the caption size: the chart's one accent is spent on the bars.

**What the bars count OF is a required prop.** `over` is `window` where the engine counted them through the listing's own predicate and `loaded` where the browser bucketed the pages it holds; the noun is the caller's too. The one sentence a screen reader hears reads "9,412 events in this window" on the event log and "41 changes on the pages loaded" on Worklet's.

**A log reaches older rows by fetching them.** A page boundary is not a window: telling a reader to narrow the window sends them toward fewer, newer rows. A log that fills its page offers **Load older**, holds the pages it has, and discards all of them together when the window or a server-side facet changes: pages fetched under the old question are rows the engine would never answer for the new one. Discarded, never hidden: hidden pages came back on return under a first page read since.

The first page stays live while the reader pages on (polled, re-read on reconnect and after the reader's own write). The second page's cursor was minted from the first page's last row, so a re-read first page under newer rows pushes that row out and the changes between belong to neither page: a silent hole. So whenever the first page moves under pages loaded, the range between it and the next held page is read and spliced in before the list moves; until then the list stays as drawn. The read is bounded by the pages held; a longer gap, or a failed read, drops the later pages so the reader pages on from a list with no hole.

The pager is one, `lib/usePaged.ts`, under every paged list (a list paged by a cursor in another order loses rows off its first page alike): Gitlet's Repositories, Worklet's task lists, Doclet's listings, the Inbox's Snoozed and Earlier, the artifact gallery and its folders. **An older page that fails is said beside the control that asks it, never in its place** (`PageFailed`: "Could not read the next page", with the code): the pager keeps what it holds and the cursor, so the same press retries. In place of the control a footer leaves only reload, and a refusal's banner promises a self-retry a user-requested page never gets. Live › Activity reads its first page through the same control, so a first page refused before any answered is said as the refusal, with the control beside it.

**A picker over what the engine pages asks the engine for what was typed.** Gitlet's repository picker, shared by Changes, Queue, Search and Pushes (`routes/gitlet/RepoPicker.tsx`), is a field over `code_repos`: typed text, lowercased, is asked as the listing's `prefix` once it rests (one range of the name index), and Load more pages on under it. With nothing typed, the list is the listing from its first name, the screen's row for every repository above it. A first-page-only picker cannot choose past the first hundred repositories. An opening no repository name could have is said in the list and never asked; the chosen name stays a row where the loaded pages do not hold it, so an address naming any repository reads as itself.

**A date is a band, not a wider cell.** The time column is sized for a wall clock; a full instant in the 62 px track wraps to three lines and reads as a rendering fault. A date belongs to the rows *under* it, so it is a heading between days, at the list's own inset, parked at `--sticky-top` like every band so the current day stays named while scrolling.

**A repeat is drawn once, counted.** Where a log is about one object (a turn's bands), a consecutive run of indistinguishable rows collapses into one carrying the count and the span of its first and last instants. Counted, not dropped: eight fall-throughs differ from one, and the heading above still counts what went wrong, not what the list draws. Consecutive only: the axis is time, and a merge across an intervening row would lie about when or reorder the band.

**Every row in the product takes one inset**, `--row-inline`, the step `Card.Header` pads by: a row list usually sits in a card, and per-class literals drew content four pixels inside its own title.

**`FacetRail`** is one dimension of the list, as chips that narrow it. Whether a count is over what is **loaded** or what **exists** is a required prop, said beside the chips: a number next to a chip reads as "how many there are", and "how many of the four hundred rows this tab holds" would tell the reader something false.

**The note is a caption on the numbers, so it is drawn only where a number is**, not beside a rail that cannot carry a count (a scope control, whose other scopes are rows the loaded page does not hold). A dimension that cannot be counted is not a facet rail but one of N scopes: a `Segmented`, the control the work toolbar's open/closed/everything uses.

A facet count is computed with its **own** filter lifted and every other applied: a chip says how many rows choosing it would show. Counted through its own filter, every chip but the selected one reads zero.

### The frame-level keys

| Key | Kind | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `peek={kind}:{id}` | section | the detail rail is open on that object |
| `tab=` | section | the object page's tab |
| `view=` | section | a list container's view |
| `lens=` | section | which whole reading of an object is drawn — a project's items, about and history, Settings › Configuration's active, history and diff |
| `sort=` `cols=` | filter | the grid's order and its visible columns |
| `sort.<name>=` `cols.<name>=` | filter | the same, for a second grid on the page — and `cols.<shape>=` alone on the work screen, whose one grid has a column set per shape while both share its `sort=` |

**`peek` is one key, one component, one rule.** A plain click peeks; ⌘-click, middle-click and the rail's `Open ↗` go to the page. A kind with NO page of its own, a person, whose directory row is read beside People and nowhere else (`KindSpec.peekIsPage` in `app/frame/objects.ts`), has that list WITH ITS PEEK OPEN as its address, so a new tab opens on who it was about; the rail draws no `Open` over that list, which could only close it. Inside a peek `[` and `]` step through the list it was opened from and `esc` closes it. Every list a plain click peeks from (the work list in every shape, the search, an item's subtasks) draws the row the rail holds as the open one, matched on the same reference the peek was opened with. Opening the rail **pushes** (Back closes it); moving it **replaces**, because four objects walked through one open rail are one place, as four ticked chips are one screen.

**The shell mounts the rail; no screen renders one.** A peek's BODY belongs to the kind, in `app/frame/peeks.tsx`, and the shell dispatches on the `peek=` token, so a list opens a peek by naming what it points at. (A rail taking its body as `children` meant only the opening screen could render one: of seventeen addressable kinds only a work item appeared.) A kind with no entry there is not an error (a notice is read in its own inbox, a model has no page); the rail closes rather than opening empty.

**Each peek asks its own question.** It takes an id and fetches, not the row that opened it: the row carries what its list needed, a peek answers "what is this thing", and it lets a pasted `peek=` open on arrival. For a work item the id is its ADDRESS ([An item's address](#an-items-address)), so the rail, the opening row and the row drawn as open name the same task when two share a key.

**A peek is one column, so it says everything once.** Its header carries identity and state marks; where a properties rail follows, the rail states every property and the header carries no fact line ([An object's own facts](#an-objects-own-facts)). A list inside a peek measures ITS OWN box: the kit's grid fits columns to its own width, or a 420px panel on a wide screen gets the full eight-track row and starves the title.

**`[` and `]` walk the list, so the list publishes its order** with `usePeekNeighbours`: only the list knows what is on screen, sorted, filtered and paged. A screen that publishes nothing gets a rail with no stepper.

The id is split on its FIRST colon only, so an id carrying a colon survives a query value.

### The frame

The frame is the kit's `AppShell`: the sidebar stands on the frame rung and the screen floats beside it on a sheet, inset by `--size-shell-inset`, rounded, with ONE scroller inside. Below the kit's `breakpoint.shell` (1024 px) the sheet is the whole window and the sidebar is a modal drawer: it takes Escape, traps Tab, hands focus back to its toggle, closes on navigation, and opens from the bar's toggle or `Mod+\` (`⌘\` on a Mac, `Ctrl+\` elsewhere), the chord that above the breakpoint folds the sidebar to its compact rail and back ([The sidebar](#the-sidebar)). The skip link precedes everything and lands on the scroller. None of that is written here (a second copy drifts). What `dashboard/src/app/` owns:

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| `sidebar/` | the one sidebar ([The sidebar](#the-sidebar)), with the engine panel and the user block |
| `sidebar/UserBlock` | who is signed in, at the sidebar's foot, by their OWN name, never their seat's (`readerName`: their directory row's name as `GET /auth/session` answers it, else their login). States: bound (that name, the login where it is not the name, and the seat — its name off the chart, or `@handle` where the chart is unread; the seat's kind is never captioned, since every binding is to a human seat); a credential acting as a seat (a Tier A token or service account bound to a human seat: the seat's name, "via API token" under it with the token's name in the row's title and under the access in the menu, the seat's initials with a key on the corner); unbound (name, login and *No seat*: a Tier A token's session or a service account acting as itself, which is ordinary; never a person, who holds a human seat while here ([ADR-0032](../../adr/0032-every-person-holds-a-human-seat.md))); nobody (a **Sign in** button back to the current screen). A FAILED session read says it could not tell who this is and still offers the Account and sign-out. Pressing the name of anybody resolved opens the reader's own menu (the kit's `AccountRow` `menu`, named ", your menu", marked current on `#/account`, where it stands in for the row the Account lacks): their access as header, then the reader's own [Account](#account-the-readers-own-page) (`place: "menu"` in `app/nav.ts`; never the seat, which holds none of what a person looks for there) with the password, second factor and recovery codes, sessions and personal access tokens, and both sign-outs. Those need only `GET /auth/session`, the frame's one read of it (`lib/frameSession.ts`), never one of the block's own: while the socket's `viewer` question has not answered (it never does for a person the socket refuses or never dials for), a session is offered the two sign-outs under its own login. See [Signing in](#signing-in-is-a-screen-outside-the-frame) |
| `header/PageHeader` + `Breadcrumb` | the page header: the kit's top bar with the trail (last crumb is the page's `h1`), who is working now (Home's bar only, `useWorkingNow`), the star, and last the screen's own controls (portalled in by `PageActions`); then the workspace's SECTION TABS (links in a labelled `nav`, `aria-current` on the current section, drawn only on a section's own page); then the `StateBar`. Settings draws its sections as a grouped COLUMN beside the screen instead (`SectionColumn`, the kit's `SidebarNav` inside the kit's `SectionFrame`, which lays column and screen side by side and folds the column into a section picker below 1210px, folded on every arrival so the requested section starts right under it), with a lock naming what a section closed to the reader lacks (`sectionOpen`; drawn only once somebody has said what the reader holds), each row's hint as its title, and nothing that leads out of Settings. A screen whose design keeps the star in a menu gets no star from the frame (`useOwnStar`): a Doclet page, whose More carries it, and Doclet's landing, whose pages are each starred from their own More |
| `routes.ts` + `crumbs.ts` | the route table as a pure resolver, and the trail derived from it |
| `layout.ts` | the frame's breakpoints, READ from the kit's tokens (`breakpoint.shell`, `breakpoint.phone`), and the widths the dashboard derives itself: where the peek becomes a column, where Ask Crewlet does, where Settings' column folds, where Chat's columns fold |
| `StateBar` | the answer's honesty in one place: degradation, `read_level`, `complete: false`, how far this node has applied. The two positions compared (`applied_through` against `log_seq`) are PACKED on the wire, (generation × 2^40) + sequence, so a plain `<` works across a re-anchor, and printed unpacked (`positionWords` in `components/work.tsx`): the bare sequence in a log's first generation, `generation:sequence` past it. The stride is the engine's `statelog.GenerationStride`; a gate in internal/api holds the dashboard's copy (`GENERATION_STRIDE`) to it. The first dial is the one degradation it does not draw: until this tab's socket is first answered, the page bar says "Connecting to the engine." as a status chip in its own row (`FirstDialChip`), since a strip in the flow pushed every page down on a cold load and floated under the bar over the screen's first lines; only an open artifact, whose head is not drawn until the engine answers, says it here |
| `ObjectHeader` | an object's eyebrow, title (a level-two heading in every frame: on a page the last crumb is the `h1` and already names the object, and a peek sits inside a page that has one), state marks and up to six facts, in the same order wherever the object appears; a peek whose body is a properties rail passes none ([one reading](#an-objects-own-facts)). A fact may carry a `note` saying where its value came from, only for facts a reader can reasonably doubt. A fact that is one token (an id, a build) or a set of chips (a node's roles) takes two tracks, so it is never broken mid-token or stacked chip over chip. STATE lives here, never in the page bar: see [What a mark MEANS, and where a control belongs](#what-a-mark-means-and-where-a-control-belongs) |
| `OwnPageHeader` | a screen that draws its own head in the frame's place: the frame draws the slot it is portalled into, with the state bar under it, instead of the page bar. ONE screen does, an open artifact ([An open artifact is the screen](#an-open-artifact-is-the-screen)); `FrameNavToggle` is the navigation toggle for that head to place first |
| `useTab` | which OBJECT tab is real: `tab=` is a URL string and the tab set belongs to the object (a human seat has three, an agent seat six), so the hook resolves the parameter against the tabs this object HAS. It binds `1`–`9`; the strip is `@crewlethq/ui`'s `Tabs` |
| `peekAddress` | the peek's address: `peek=` in the URL, opened by a push and moved by a replace, and the page a row links to (`peekHref`); which clicks peek is the kit's (`peekClickHandler`, `peekRowActivation`) |
| `PeekHost` + `peeks.tsx` | the one peek in the product, mounted by the shell in the kit's `peek` slot and drawn by the kit's `PeekRail` (resizable from keyboard and pointer, a column of the sheet where the frame leaves the list beside it its floor, 1158 px on most screens and 1394 beside Settings' column, a drawer under that): the body belongs to the KIND. `usePeekNeighbours` is how a list publishes the order `[` and `]` walk |
| `DataGrid` + `cells` | the kit's `DataGrid`, bound to the URL (sort and columns), the peek and the keymap; bands from a grouped answer, typed cells; a row becomes a labelled card under 640 px, or two unlabelled lines on a `compact` grid |
| `PropertiesRail` | an object's own facts, in sections, with who set each: the kit's `PropertyList`, given routes and turns |
| `Histogram` + `FacetRail` | a log's time axis (the kit's `Histogram`, given the engine's buckets and the reader's zone), and one dimension of it as chips |
| `lib/rangePicker` | the one control for `window=`: a screen's range mapped onto the kit's `TimeRangePicker` (Today as the company's day, a custom window on the reader's zone or as whole company days) |
| `PageActions` + `PageNote` | a screen's own controls, portalled into the bar; its one sentence of explanation (the kit's `PageNote`), wrapped so its last line never holds a word alone |

**Two widths are the kit's, and the rest are arithmetic.** Below 1024 px (`breakpoint.shell`) the sidebar is the drawer. Below 640 px (`breakpoint.phone`) a layout is single pane: a `DataGrid`'s rows become labelled cards, or on a grid asking `phoneRows="compact"`, two unlabelled lines: what the row IS (its `phoneLead` cells), then its marks. The work list takes the compact row (scanned by the dozen; the labelled card stood eight lines and 230px per task); the table keeps labels, since its question is a field at a time. A column whose head is a glyph or nothing names itself on the card with `label`, except a column of row actions, which says `action` instead: its button is its own name, and a `label` there read `SIGN OUT  Sign out`. The same `label` names such a column's head at every width, to a screen reader and on hover, so no column of marks is unnamed. The Settings column stacks above the screen, and the page bar's controls take a line of their own and scroll. Both are the kit's numbers, written as media-query literals that `frame.test.ts` holds against `app/layout.ts`, which reads them from the kit.

The peek is a column of the sheet wherever the list beside it keeps its 444 px floor, which is arithmetic over EVERY width in front of the list:

| Term | Width |
|---|---|
| the sidebar (`size.shell.rail`) | 236 |
| the sheet's inset (`size.shell.inset`) | 8 × density |
| the sheet's two hairlines | 2 |
| the peek, at rest | 420 |
| the scroller's reserved gutter (`scrollbar-gutter: stable`, the wider of the kit's bar and Firefox's `thin` one) | 8 |
| the screen's padding (`spacing.5`, each side) | 40 × density |
| Settings' section column, on a screen that draws one | 236 |
| the list | 444 |

That is **1158 px** on a screen and **1394 px** beside Settings' column at the normal density (1150 and 1386 compact, 1166 and 1402 comfortable). Below that the peek is a drawer over the screen. (Omitting the gutter and padding put the threshold at 1112: the Worklet list beside a peek was 396 px, and at 1280 a peek on Settings › Nodes left the nodes grid 328 px with columns cut off.)

**The shell, not a media query**, applies it, because the section column belongs to the screen and the inset and padding scale with density: a media query sees neither. `app/layout.ts` (`peekColumnMin`) does the arithmetic, the shell asks `matchMedia` for the one width right for the frame on screen, and hands the kit's `AppShell` one `peekShape`, published as `data-peek="column"` or `"drawer"`, so no width has both or neither. The column is the reader's dragged width CAPPED at what the sheet can give with the list at its floor (the rail's `reserve`, from `listReserve`), because a width dragged to 640 on a wide window outlives it.

**Beside a canvas the peek rests at 330.** A list beside a peek reflows; a chart is SHRUNK into the width the peek leaves, so every pixel the rail takes draws the whole company smaller. The org chart asks for the approved artboard's 330 (`usePeekWidth`, as a screen asks for the window's height with `useFillScreen`), and the rail rests there until dragged: a dragged width is the reader's preference on every screen, 330 to 640. The threshold above is computed at the resting 420 for every screen.

**Chatlet's columns give way by the screen's width.** Chatlet draws up to three columns: the Rooms panel when pinned, the conversation, and a pane (a thread, a room's details, a profile, a catch up). They fold by the width of the SCREEN (`@container page`), never the window's, because the sidebar, a peek and Ask Crewlet's column each take a share a media query cannot see; whether the panel may be pinned at all is taken from the chat area's own measured width. The transcript keeps a 320 px floor (`TRANSCRIPT_FLOOR` in `app/layout.ts`, the width WCAG's Reflow criterion asks every page to read at) at every step:

| Screen | The panel and a pane | The transcript |
|---|---|---|
| 1180 px and over | 280 and 400 beside it | 500 at 1180 |
| 908 to 1180 px | 248 and 340 beside it | 320 at 908 |
| 760 to 908 px | 340 beside it; a pinned panel gives way while a pane is open | 420 at 760 |
| under 760 px | the panel slides in from Menu, the pane covers the conversation | the whole area |

Beside Ask Crewlet's column at its resting width, a 1280 px window leaves the screen 558 px at the normal density, under 760: the Rooms panel slides in from Menu and a pane covers the conversation. At 1166 px, where the column first fits, the screen is 444 px. A wider-dragged column folds the columns sooner.

**A screen publishes what the chrome needs and renders none of it:** the labels the route cannot supply (`usePageLabels`), the coverage of the answer it drew from (`usePageCoverage`), a section's figure for its tab (`useSectionCounts`, a string the screen already wrote, "12" or "20+", because only the screen knows whether a number is a total or a floor), and its own controls. Twenty screens each drawing their own header is how five dropped the coverage badge.

**Only a SCREEN publishes; a body rendered inside one never does.** The frame holds one coverage slot with one setter, so a reusable body publishing from inside another screen fought its answer: on `#/worklet/{KEY}?lens=history` the project's read and the log's read both wrote it, the last poll won, and switching lenses cleared the slot over a page still showing the project. A body states its coverage INLINE beside its rows, as a peek rail and the Tasks lens do. The two never both apply: a screen publishes and draws none, a body draws and publishes none, and a component serving as both takes that as a prop.

**Every object screen publishes the name it draws, the same string.** A route addresses an object by identifier (a turn, trace or event by id, a seat by handle, a revision by ULID, a page by id), and the frame has nowhere else to learn its name. So the one name a screen resolves for its `ObjectHeader` is the one it publishes, reaching the last crumb, the browser tab (`Shell` titles it from the trail) and the palette's recents; written separately, the three drift.

**A screen with no name publishes none, and the id stands.** Every object has an unnamed case (a running turn, a trace whose spans left the window, an unsummarised revision), and its header fills the slot with a placeholder. A placeholder must not reach the label: "Turn" names no particular turn, and two in the recents are identical rows pointing at different places, worse than the ids. The crumb draws an unlabelled segment in the mono face, as it does a handle: an identifier has to look like one.

### The keys

Every key the dashboard answers is a row of ONE table, `app/keymap.ts`, and `?` anywhere shows it: the legend renders the table and nothing else, so an added key is shown with no second list. The command palette has a row for the legend too, for the reader who does not know `?` yet.

| Where it is live | Keys |
|---|---|
| Anywhere | `Mod+K` search (the same chord closes it), `Mod+.` Ask Crewlet (pressed inside it, it closes it), `/` search this screen, `?` the legend, `g` then a letter a workspace, `g r` the running turn (Now running when several run), `g p` switch project (under Worklet's trail on its scope pages, centred everywhere else), `Mod+\` folds the sidebar to its compact rail and back, and opens the navigation drawer on a narrow window |
| In a list | `j` and `k` walk the rows — on a task opened from a list, they open the next and the previous task — `Enter` opens one |
| With a peek open | `[` and `]` step through the list it was opened from, `Esc` closes it |
| On a page with tabs | `1`–`9` go to that tab |
| On an open artifact | `i` its details, `h` its versions and history, `d` its data (where it keeps any), `p` who is here, each pressed again to close what it opened; `s` Share. `Esc` from inside a panel closes it (bound by the design system's `ArtifactPanel`, and listed with the layer's Escape) |
| In the artifacts gallery and its folders | `x` starts picking artifacts (and, pressed again, stops and clears the picks), `m` moves what is picked to a folder, `n` makes a new folder where the reader is, `u` goes up to the folder above. Bare letters, since a window chord compares no Shift and no Alt |
| On a chart | `+`, `-` zoom and `0` fits, with focus in the chart (bound by the design system's canvas) |
| In the org builder | `Mod+Z` undo, `Mod+Shift+Z` redo |
| Writing a reply or a message | `Enter` sends it and `Shift+Enter` adds a line, in every box a person says something in: a chat message, a thread reply or a rewrite, a reply in the Inbox, a comment on a task, a page or a change, a question to Ask Crewlet and an agent's brief (bound by the design system's `useSendOnEnter`, which its `Composer` is built on). `Mod+Enter` sends too. An input method's `Enter` never sends, an open `@` list takes its `Enter` to pick, and on a touch keyboard `Return` adds a line while the Send button sends. Long-form editors (a description, a page, code) keep `Enter` for a new line |
| Writing a chat message | `Up` in an empty box edits your last message, `Mod+B` and `Mod+I` bold and italicise the selection |
| On a focused chat message | `E` edits your message, `T` opens its thread, `S` saves it for later, `Delete` deletes it, `Up` and `Down` move to the message above and below |
| Writing the company's principles | `Mod+Enter` saves the part being written and `Esc` stops writing it, asking first when it has changes (bound by the design system's `InlineEditor`); in the standing policies `Enter` adds the policy typed, and `Alt+Up` and `Alt+Down` move the one you are in |
| In search | `Tab` and `Shift+Tab` walk the scopes (bound by the design system's palette), `Mod+Enter` asks an agent, `Alt+A` assigns the task at hand, `Alt+C` creates a task, `Backspace` in an empty picker goes back |
| In Ask Crewlet | `Esc` stops a running answer first, then closes Ask Crewlet and never a peek beside it; `Up` in an empty box brings back the last question |
| In a dialog, a menu, the drawer or Ask Crewlet | `Esc` closes whatever is on top (bound by the design system's layer stack) |

`Mod` is Command on a Mac and Control elsewhere, and every hint is drawn in the platform's own notation with the kit's `Kbd`.

**A bare `Enter` or `Space` on a focused button or link is that control's.** The list's `Enter` opens the cursor row only when focus is not on a control the platform activates itself: a button inside a row (Restore in the trash, a ceiling's pencil on Budgets) is pressed, never skipped for the row behind it.

**A binding names a row, never a key.** A component asks `useKeymap` for the rows it answers (`{"peek.close": close}`) and the table says which key that is, so no two places spell one key two ways. `keymap.test.tsx` refuses two rows answering one press where both can be live: the page's scopes are all live together (a list, with a peek open, on an object with tabs, beside a chart), so a press is unique across them; the layer's rows (search's among them, since the palette is a layer) are their own namespace because every page key stands aside while a layer is up. Search's accelerators take `Alt` rather than a bare letter because they are pressed in its field, where a bare letter is a letter of the query; they match the physical key, since Option+A on a Mac types `å`. Rows the design system binds itself (the canvas's zoom, the layer's Escape) are in the table so the legend is the whole answer and the collision check sees them, and `useKeymap` refuses to bind one a second time. Nothing else binds a key: the suite fails a module that calls the mechanism under `useKeymap`, or listens for `keydown` itself, except the org builder's undo, which is scoped to presses inside the builder and reads its keys from the table with `matchesRow`. A row nobody binds fails too: the frame's rows are bound by the frame alone, so the suite mounts it and refuses an "Anywhere" row it did not bind.

**`/` searches what you are looking at.** A screen with a search box of its own (the seat filter, the event log, the tools catalogue, the audit log's actor, work search and a list's key-or-title box, Doclet and its page finder, Search chat) registers it with `useSearchTarget`, and `/` focuses it with its text selected to type over; on a screen with none, `/` opens the palette.

**A key waits for the reader.** A bare key does nothing while they are typing in a field, a select or anything a screen made focusable and handles keys for; only a row that says so (`Mod+K`, `Esc` out of a peek's field, `Mod+\`) fires from one. Every page key waits while a dialog, a menu or the drawer is open, because the page behind `aria-modal` is inert. A press somebody already answered (the chart claiming `+`, a menu its arrows) or one an input method is still composing is not a key at all: Enter that picks a Japanese candidate must not also open the grid row behind the field.
### The page bar wraps by what it holds

The bar holds the trail, who is working now, the star, and LAST the screen's own controls (portalled in by `PageActions`), so a screen's primary action ("New task") ends the row. Who is working shows on Home's bar only, and not on a phone (Home's greeting and figures already say it): the sidebar's Live row carries the count elsewhere, and a chip in every bar pushed a profile's controls past a phone's edge and cut Home's "New task".

A SCOPE's lenses (a project's Tasks, About, History and Files, portalled in by its page; All projects' Projects, Tasks and History, drawn by the header) sit in a second slot straight after the trail (`PageLenses`). Empty, the slot is no flex item; with lenses it takes the line's slack, and the trail sizes to its content, capped at 62% of the bar, so a long name ellipsises beside its lenses.

On a phone the bar keeps ONE action in view, the screen's primary one, leading the line, and folds the rest into **More** (⋯) at the line's end: the frame's star, whatever a screen publishes with `usePageMenu` as secondary (a project's **Edit project**, opening the same dialog its inline button does), and a task's own "More for ENG-42" (no second ellipsis). The menu is drawn only at that width, so no action is in two places at once; what a press did (star cap, a refusal) is said in a toast, since the menu closes. The remaining controls share a line with the trail or lenses when they fit (inline, a project's bar was three rows, about 105 px of chrome at 390 px).

**A wrapping flex container assigns lines BEFORE it shrinks**, so a trail at content width broke the line while free space was left. The trail's flex BASIS is therefore 0, clamped by its FLOOR: a line holds the floor plus the controls, the break comes only when even the floor cannot sit beside them, and the grow factor gives the trail the line's remainder. A threshold measured on the busiest bar would push controls to their own line on every narrower screen, sparse ones included.
