The indent STOPS GROWING at 32 levels: 64 leading spaces is most of the width of a 420px detail rail, a deeper document keeps its newlines and gains no margin, and it keeps output linear (indentation is quadratic in depth, which belongs to whichever MCP server answered; Go's decoder accepts ten thousand levels). And a LIVE result over four thousand bytes is sent as its last four thousand with a leading ellipsis, which is not a JSON document, so a long result renders flat while the phase runs and indented once it completes; the text already changes at that moment.

   `json.Marshal` escapes `<`, `>` and `&` for HTML, which would make URL arguments read `?a=1\u0026b=2` and markdown bodies `\u003ch1\u003e` on a screen rendering into a `pre`. `tools.RecordArgs` is the one encoder both the phase event and the bridged-run row use, and it writes the characters the model sent.
4. **Grouping is structural; colour is semantic.** A round is BRACKETED by a rail running from its numbered node down its own content, and adjacent rounds are told apart by a two-step alternating tint, not a hue apiece (a colour per round would read as meaning something and mean nothing, the same objection as a colour per agent). A round's node takes colour for exactly four states: normal; contains a failed call or did not finish (danger); answered in prose where the phase needed a call (caution); in flight (the accent). These answer the two questions a reader brings to a running turn, "which round went wrong" and "where is it now", and a round that printed its submission instead of calling it is the first question's other answer. The note under its words (rule 2) alone was easy to read past, so the node carries the colour. Caution, never danger, because the engine asks again or rescues the phase and the turn goes on either way.

   Bounding a round and separating it from the next are two jobs. The rail was drawn only *between* rounds and the tint only on even ones, so a single-round phase (the common case) got neither and read as a bare numeral beside look-alike rows. One bracket per round, one left edge (a disclosure head carries its own inset and the model's speech none), and 24px between rounds against 8px inside one.
5. **A running phase tails; a finished one flows.** While live the ledger is bounded and follows the newest round, but only while the reader is already at the bottom; following regardless yanks them off what they stopped to read. The ledger's frame (border, padding) is the same either way; only the height bound and the scroll come and go, so the transcript does not grow a box on going live (rule 9's defect, one level down).

   **The bound is the scroller's view, and at either end the wheel is the page's.** `620px` with `overscroll-behavior: contain` was a trap: 620px is unrelated to the view (the page bar wraps; the object header, tabs and two card heads sit above the box), so the box's bottom was often below the fold, following pinned it at its end, and containment swallowed every wheel-down there. The bound now derives from one requirement, *once scrolled to, the whole box fits in the view*: `100cqb` (the shell's scroller, a size container on every screen) less the sticky band and the card's inset below it, floor four rows for a window too short; nothing contains the wheel, so at the box's top or bottom the page carries on. The box ALONE: its caption is an uppercase label in a column the sidebar and a peek narrow, and it wraps, so subtracting one line of it promised a fit that held only while the caption did.

   The same requirement applies one level down. A tool's record is its own scroller, and one taller than the box that scrolls it is the same trap: inside a running ledger a record is at most the box less its one-word label, elsewhere at most the view less its label (the record ceiling every block of machine text shares, declared once; see
   [The document does not scroll](#the-document-does-not-scroll)), so with room for 460px of record it keeps that ceiling. The tail re-sticks when the BOX changes height (a resized window) as well as when content grows, and opening a running phase always starts at its tail (the "still following?" flag used to outlive the box).

   The engine STREAMS: a round's text arrives while the model writes it, coalesced to five frames a second, and the round in flight rides `partial_round` on the live-only progress event. It is never merged into `round_narration` (arriving and committed text are different facts); when the round commits, its narration replaces the fragment. An endpoint that cannot stream is negotiated down to the unary call once per process, and text then appears a round at a time. The round in flight is shown redacted, a line at a time as its lines complete.

   A provider that dies mid-answer keeps what it wrote, dimmed and labelled, with the retry below it: erasing read text looks like a glitch, and "wrote four hundred characters and then died" is the useful fact about a flaky provider.
6. **A round's number is the PHASE's, not one loop invocation's.** The tool loop counts from 1 each time it is entered and an extended phase re-enters it, so an unshifted second invocation made the phase read as running backwards: the live projection dropped a round numbered below the one it held (the extension vanished), the ledger merged extension round 1 into original round 1, and the completed record lost every call and narration from before the extension, on exactly the long phases that get extended.
7. **A discarded round changes nothing.** Seat state was set before the two guards that decide whether to keep a round, so a straggler arriving after its phase completed flipped the seat to "working" and was thrown away with nothing pushed to correct it. A round about to be discarded must not move the seat.
8. **A phase start does not blank a call its own first round already seeded.** `agent_phase_started` and `agent_turn_progress` travel on different subjects, so the opening round can land first; an unconditional seed replaced a call that had a model, response and tool calls with an empty placeholder.
9. **Open/closed is latched.** Once a reader opens a phase or a turn it stays open. Deriving it (open while live, closed once finished) made a transcript vanish the moment it completed, and a new failure elsewhere re-opened a different card and shoved everything below down.
10. **Time is compared as an instant.** Go's `RFC3339Nano` trims trailing zeros, so `…:07Z` sorts *after* `…:07.42Z` on a raw string compare (`'Z'` 0x5A against `'.'` 0x2E). Every list sorts through `tsKey`, and every comparator is three-way: one returning −1 for equal operands makes equal rows trade places on each render.
11. **A prompt is a document, not a wall of text, read through a map, an outline and one section.** A seat's system prompt runs to tens of kilobytes (identity, mission, policies, roster, turn contract, prefetch, workers, skills, tool catalogue), and an operator asking *what was the reviewer actually told about self-iterating?* scrolled 30 kB for a heading. A stack of closed folds per `##` was also hard to follow (look-alike rows, raw inline markdown titles, sizes that never added up, one-fact-per-line bodies collapsed into run-ons). The *Rendered* view is a designed reader (`components/PromptDoc.tsx`):

   - **The map**: one slim bar for the whole request, the system prompt's sections, a gap, then the user message's, each as wide as its share of the bytes. Neutral fills in two alternating steps that are two different greys (two tokens once held one colour, so neighbours never alternated in the dark palette), the accent only on the section being read. A half is never narrower than its segments, so a small user message beside a large system prompt does not spill past the bar on a phone. Pointing at a segment says "Your turn · 2.8 KB · 23% of the system prompt"; pressing it reads that section. It is a picture of the outline, so `aria-hidden` and no focus; the outline is the keyboard's way to the same sections.
   - **The outline**: both halves under their names and sizes ("System prompt · 11 KB", "User message · 1.2 KB"), one row per top-level section with its title rendered as inline markdown, its size and a weight bar. The bars are neutral, the selected row's too (its ground already marks it, and an accent bar a hundredth of a row wide was a stray dot). A title's link is drawn as its words in a row and in the picker (an option's children are presentational, and a click on a link there navigates instead of choosing), and as a link only in the reader. A listbox with one tab stop: the arrows, Home and End move through both halves, the reader follows, and focus moves to the row it selects. Beside the reader when the prompt view itself is at least 720px wide (a container query on the view, never the window, which the sidebar and a peek narrow), a picker above the reader below that, with the map kept.
   - **The reader**: only the selected section is mounted, so unselected text is not in the card. Its title is a styled line, never an `h` element (a quoted prompt's headings are not this page's; six phases would put eighty into one outline), and the region takes its name from it; then its size and share ("2.8 KB · 23% of the system prompt"); then Previous and Next, each naming the section it goes to (the user message's first from the system prompt's last, which the label says), staying put at the ends with the reason they cannot move, because a control that vanishes under the press takes focus with it. Each owns half the row, Previous at its start and Next at its end, a long destination wrapping inside its half (a wrapping row put Next on its own line on a phone). Then the body, with headings inside the section drawn in place under styled sub-titles, nested on their levels.
   - **Find** annotates rather than filters: every row says how many matches it holds, a polite status says "12 matches in 3 sections", Escape clears. A matching row lifts (title to the primary text step, count on the matches' ground); a row with none recedes to the tertiary step with its weight bar faded (further dimming would take words under their contrast, and in the dark palette secondary and tertiary are the same grey to the eye; a non-matching row is still choosable). **The selection follows the find until the reader takes it**: typing a query the section on screen lacks moves the reader to the next section that has it (the first, from the top), so the first thing a find shows is a match; once the reader chooses a section during that query, the next keystroke leaves them there. Enter and Shift+Enter jump to the next and previous matching section and bring its first match into view at the nearest edge of whatever scrolls it; typing never scrolls, which would move the page under the box being typed in. Matches are counted on the SOURCE, case-insensitively (what the model was told, markup included) and marked in the reader with the CSS Custom Highlight API where the browser has it (no element added); elsewhere the counts still say where. **What is marked is what was counted**: the title is marked only when it is the section's own heading line (a builder's "Task" or the untitled lead's words are not in the source), and the reader's own words (size, share, Previous and Next destinations) never are.

   **The outline is the builder's, and the headings only where there is no builder's.** Cutting at every `##` broke on other people's markdown quoted verbatim (a chat trigger's "## Triage" and "## Thread context", a pull request's "# Title", a model's "## Summary" in review evidence): each escaped its section or swallowed the rest under a title nobody wrote. Only the builder knows where its parts begin and end, so the engine sends a section map with each prompt (`system_sections` and `user_sections` on the settled record, `prompt_messages[].sections` live: per part a key, a title, a byte count and whether it opens with its own heading), and the top level of the outline IS that map, sliced by UTF-8 byte offsets; a heading inside a span structures it, nested, but cannot leave it. That includes a heading a HEADLESS part opens with (a worker's persona, an executor-written task, a trigger's text): with `headed` false, a quoted "## Goal" nests under the builder's "Task" like any other quoted heading, rather than being taken for the span's own and dropped from the reading view. A part the map does not call headed is headless whatever its first line; the engine writes `headed` on every part that opens with its own heading and leaves it off the rest. Spans are decoded without stripping a leading byte order mark, so a part opening with a pasted U+FEFF is still a slice. A record without a map (a resumed phase's) is outlined by its headings, and so is one whose map does not tile its prompt (bytes do not add up, a boundary inside a character, an empty span, a repeated key): a map that would mis-slice is not trusted (`lib/promptmap.ts`). Either way the outline is DERIVED, from the document or its builder, never a list this app keeps, so a new section grows a row and no rename leaves a stale name. It is derived once per prompt and map VALUE: every push rebuilds a phase's record from the wire (a streaming phase's five frames a second), so the map arrives as a new array saying the same thing, and an open Prompt fold keyed on the array re-sliced both halves and re-counted its find every frame.

   **Sizes are UTF-8 bytes, heading lines included**, matching the Turn screen's Context tab. Each section is a slice from its heading line to the next, separators included, so a half's sections tile it exactly; the Prompt fold's count is the two halves' sizes ("11 KB system · 1.2 KB user"), not the phase's name, which the card's tag already says.

   **The prompt's line breaks are its own.** A builder writes line by line for a model, and one fact per line read as soft wraps became a run-on. Bodies render with every newline a break, as a model's own words do (see
   [Markdown is rendered, not printed](#markdown-is-rendered-not-printed)).

   Three properties travel with it. **Each view does its whole job.** *Rendered* is for reading; *Source* is the record: each half whole, one block, byte for byte, one selection, what an operator reproduces a turn from and diffs when a model's behaviour changes. What is record-sensitive survives rendering: a fence comes out as its own block holding the exact text, so a tool schema, JSON example or contract template is byte-identical either way; reading spends only emphasis markers and list bullets. **The switch is offered on every document**, headings or none, since one decodes the markdown and one is the bytes; a prompt with no headings is one section named for the whole half, "The whole user message" ("Before the first heading", the lead run's name in a headed half, would claim a heading it lacks). And **the outline is the document's own shape**, mostly flat and sometimes not: an executor's sections are peers, but the endings block writes one `###` per earlier turn *inside* its block (`### Turn …`, `### Fire …` for a schedule's), and hoisting those would put a turn of somebody's conversation between "How this conversation's earlier turns ended" and the ask. So a heading nests under the nearest heading above it of a lower level, and the lead run before the first heading is a section of its own, the first one read, never hidden.

   Nesting is only correct because **the levels are**. `internal/agent/prompts` carried a single `#` over a run of `##`, claiming the executor's whole prompt was part of the agent's identity; and the executor's user message carried a bare `Task:` label between two headed ledgers, filing the ask inside the conversation history above it. Both are structural facts about the document, asserted there: every heading a prompt builder emits is a sibling, and every block of the user message is a peer.

   **Nothing in it scrolls or sticks.** The card hides its overflow, and a box that scrolls inside the page is a second thing under the wheel (see
   [The document does not scroll](#the-document-does-not-scroll)); showing one section at a time keeps the page short.

   The splitter is `lib/markdown.ts`'s, beside the renderer's own heading and fence constants: what a heading is and where a fenced block suspends the grammar are decisions that file already made once, and a `# install deps` inside a catalogue's shell sample is the drift a second copy starts with.
12. **A phase card reads in the order the phase happened**: what it was given (the Prompt, then the Tool surface), then what it did, then what it delegated. With the transcript first, the question every round raises (*what was this told? what could it call?*) was answered past the end of the answer, a whole scroll away in a forty-round phase. Both inputs are closed folds, so the order costs a transcript-only reader two header rows. Their own order is the request's: the prompt is what was sent, and the tool surface is the tools that went *with* it (served to the harness as its MCP server's for each run), one call described in two folds, so they sit together.

   **What it did is grouped by harness run.** Most phases are one run of the harness's loop; one that was steered, delegated or corrected is several, each a process handed the conversation so far. Rounds sit under a head per run (`RunHead`): *Harness run N*, the entry that served it, its round count, how long it lived, what it spent and how it ended, or that it is running. A run whose harness's record showed no requests is one round, and its head says so, since that round's timing is the run's.

   **What the record does not list is said under what it does.** A phase's record holds each payload to a share of one message, so a long phase's card can list fewer rounds, calls or tool names than it had: a warning under the rounds says how many rounds are not listed (the record keeps a long phase's first and newest) and how many calls, by tool; the tool surface says how many more tools it held than it names; a failed phase's live call, frozen with its record's list, says the same. A running phase's card says what its live frame left out in the live view's words (a frame republished five times a second keeps the newest calls, the record the first and newest) and how many more calls are running than the frame lists. A call's detail counts a collected run's unlisted calls in its one round's figure, never a host phase's, whose dropped calls belong to no one round.

   The error callout does not wait its turn: it is a banner, the reason the reader opened the card, so it stays above the inputs.

## A monitor is not a reader

A fleet-wide monitor showing every running phase as an expanded transcript was pleasant with one agent and a race with seven: seven seats republishing streamed prose five times a second in cards that grew as they wrote. Streaming made a bad shape worse rather than causing it.

**Reading what a model said is a one-agent activity**: one turn in focus, on that agent's own page. A fleet screen asks *which seats are working, which are stuck, what is this costing*, and that is rows.

So the screen is a table: one fixed-height row per phase, the same shape running or finished, sorted on the seat handle, which does not move. A live row updates its cells (rounds, tokens, elapsed) and **nothing reflows**, because a number changing inside a row of settled height cannot move the layout around it; that is why the table holds at fifty seats where cards did not hold at seven. The transcript is one click away, on the seat.

The rules below still apply to the seat screen, where the transcript now lives.
## A live screen that stays readable

Crowding is density and also MOTION: a phase spliced in at the top pushes everything below it down a card, mid-sentence, every few seconds. The rule, shared with the round ledger: **the page moves only when the reader is not reading**.

- **Running and settled are different lists.** A live phase changes every couple of hundred milliseconds; a finished one never changes. One list let the first's churn reflow the second. The live region is bounded and visibly bordered: motion stops at that edge.
- **The settled list does not splice rows in under a reader.** At the top of the scroller new rows merge straight in (somebody watching the feed; holding them back looks broken). Scrolled down, they are counted and offered: *"3 new turns. Show"*. Keyed on identity, never position, so a row that UPDATES in place (a round landing, a phase completing) is never held back.

  **Identity reaches across the two lists.** A running turn that finishes leaves the live region and arrives in the settled list under a key that list never admitted; it would show as *"1 new turn. Show"* though the reader was watching it. Each screen passes the keys it renders live, and they are admitted without the scroll check.
- **The live half of a screen does not wait on the stored half.** The Turns tab's query-state component renders nothing in flight and a banner *instead of* its children on failure, hiding a turn happening now until the event store answered (for good if it failed). The query's state renders beside the turns, never in place of them.

The seat screen makes the same split, and its rail shows which turn is happening now. The rail is the WORKING hue, info, the fill a working seat's status glyph stands on, because running is a state; the accent says what to do and must not draw it.

## Live › Now running and the turn list

**What a seat is doing is everybody's; what it SAID is its trail.** Now running, Executors, Structure's state lines and a seat's page are the overview, open to every signed-in reader. The engine splits what it sends into a status half and a body half ([the API's rule](api-endpoints.md#a-status-reader-never-receives-a-transcript)): a call's prompt, its answer, a tool's arguments and an executor's task, question and reply go to an admin, to whoever leads the seat, and, for an executor's parked question, to the person it is put to. Anybody else gets the status with `body_withheld: true`, and the dashboard draws each withheld value as **Not shown to you** (`WITHHELD_WORDS`, `lib/access.ts`; a run's question as *Its question is not shown to you*) with the one sentence why: what a seat says is its trail, which its lead and an admin read. Never an empty value: "the prompt was empty" and "you may not read the prompt" are opposite facts. A work item a call names is Worklet's, and is left off the row for a reader without Worklet.

**Now running** (`#/live`) is five cards in fixed places, each saying so when empty (sections that come and go with the data cannot be read at a glance):

- **Running turns** — one row per seat the engine says is working, the row Home's Live now draws (`LiveTurnRow`):
  - what it is doing and on what: the item's key, or on a turn charged to no item the trigger's summary ("Executing · Drafting the 2.4 launch brief"), not a bare verb;
  - where the turn is (Context → Execute "in its box" → Review, and "round 1 of 1" from the executor's opening frame while it launches; on a phone the round leads the call line so Review keeps its place on the stepper's one line);
  - how long it has run from the turn's own start, so a turn still gathering context is already timed;
  - the call it is making or last made;
  - the whole row links to its trace, the turn's record on its Timeline, as every row of a list of turns does; the links that say **Watch** open its Transcript on the running phase (see [the turn trace](#the-turn-trace-four-tabs-one-clock));
  - a round with no update for two minutes is marked **no update**, for ten **stalled**, in the caution and failure tones, never while the turn is parked (an executor in its box is silent on purpose);
  - what waits in the seat's inbox, as the holding node counts it with the turn's own mail left out: one count ("88 queued") whose tooltip, read out with the row, says what it is ("Queued in its inbox: 79 messages from people · 9 other notices"), and nothing when the inbox holds nothing else. Counts are MESSAGES, never people: the priority lane holds what a person wrote that the seat owes an answer to, and read "79 people waiting" in a company of four.
- **Waiting on a person** — every executor parked on a question: whose, the question, who it asks (the chart's names for the seats the engine resolved), how long it has waited, how long its box is still held, and **Answer**, which sends `answer_executor{turn_id, launch_id, choice}` for an option or `answer_executor{turn_id, launch_id, answer}` for words, as the person reading, naming the question it drew.
- **In a box** — the other executors in flight, eight before it says how many more. Each caption adds what waits in the inbox of the seat the executor holds, in a running turn's words. Empty, it says *What a finished one did is on its turn’s trace* (a settled executor's row is deleted, so promising every finished run under Runs was false).
- **Activity** — the engine's count of events over the window (`event_series`, minute bars summed exactly into the strip's cells) and the latest seven events, each the time and ONE line: the actor, then what happened. Source and category are the log's columns, a link away; the same node is said once everywhere, not as actor and source.
- **Recent phases** — the settled model calls, the only reader of `phases`, paged with the engine's cursor (**Load 60 older**). There is no second "running now" table: the running half of every phase is the turn rows above.

`seat=` (a handle), `phase=` and `failed=true` narrow every card that can honour them; the window (`15m`, `1h`, `6h`) is the activity strip's. `failed=true` is Turns' own failure-filter spelling, so an address carried between the two Live screens means the same on both. The seat menu offers every agent the chart holds, in every unit, and shows ten before it scrolls. The page carries no working count of its own: the sidebar's Live row says how many seats are working on every screen (Home's page bar does, on Home), and a second figure pushed the bar's controls off a phone's page bar. It is where the sidebar's **N more running** row lands. A seat is asked for by its handle and finishing phases are matched on the seat's own id, never a role name two unit seats can share. No spend panels or onboarding cards: spend is Spend's, and the sidebar names the screens the cards pointed at.

**Which finished phases are let in at once.** The settled list follows the rule above; already seen are every row of a page the engine answered (the first, which can land after a restored scroll position, and each older page somebody pressed for) and the phases the running rows were drawing. Only a phase another turn finished while the reader was down the list waits behind the button.

**Turns** (`#/live/turns`) opens on the axis, and the axis is the ENGINE's: `event_series` over `agent_turn_completed` with `suspended=false` (the turns that ENDED, one completion each, since a turn that parks on its executor writes a completion for the segment that parked it) over the whole window, on every node, each bar's failed share drawn at its foot. Folding it from the held page of rows drew a week from the newest two hundred turns. The list under it is paged (a hundred a page, **Load older**) in the engine's order: `sort=-started` or `sort=-tokens`, the order Spend's costliest-turns drill-down lands on. Columns: Started, Seat, What it did, State (re-run, parked, running, failure; a headed column sized to its badges), Iterations, Tokens, Took. The chart's key sits under its title, count and failed share first, so on a phone the explanatory tail gives way. Any node that did not answer either read is named above the list (`CoverageNote`).

**The list is asked for the window itself**: `since` and `until`, the window's two instants on the turn's START, and the engine's answer is the list, with no second filter here. Asking for "the last N days" (N the window's LENGTH) and filtering in the browser made a one-hour bar picked three days ago say "No turns in this window" under an axis counting a dozen. **Load older** is offered whenever the engine's cursor says there is more, on a page with no row as well, since the fleet's cursor can stop above every turn a node held.

**The seat and the failure narrowing are controls, not chips.** `seat=` is a `Select` (every agent seat the chart holds, read from the same org index every screen walks; the top-level roles alone are the founders and offered no seat) and `failed=` a three-way `Segmented` (All · Carried a failure · Clean). A chip per seat is the eighteen-pill row retired in the next section, and a chip is a two-state toggle where `failed=` has THREE values, "absent" being the default an operator opens the screen for. **The axis is not narrowed by failure**, and its subtitle says so while `failed=` is set: "carried a failure" is a fact about a whole turn (any of its own records failed), while the axis counts completion records each with only its own flag, so narrowing would count a different set of turns than the list under the same heading. It stays every turn, with the failed share at each bar's foot.

## Controls that mean what they look like

The Model screen's replaced design: eighteen controls in one sticky row (fifteen near-identical pills in two active idioms), four `--font-size-2xl` numerals a step LARGER than the screen title, and a copy of Spend's panel pushed further down by every "load older". What replaced it:

- **The row of controls is the list screen's own toolbar**, every axis one the screen declares: an always-present search box, a Filter menu offering the rest, a chip per axis a reader added, and a Sort menu over every column. A search hidden behind "add a filter" is never found.
- **The counts moved into the header badges**, and the failure count is the control that filters to failures (not an inert "4 failed" tile beside an unrelated chip). `Tag` renders as a real `<button>` with `aria-pressed` when given an action: a `<span>` with a click handler is neither focusable nor announced, and looks like the inert tags beside it. A tag that is ON keeps the ground its label was measured on, because the press is carried by its boundary; repainting the ground with its own ink is a contrast ratio of 1:1 on the one control whose state must be readable.
- **The seat filter is a picker.** The match is exact on both sides of the wire (server query and in-memory filter compare for equality), so a typed prefix returned nothing while looking like a search with no matches. `Select` is the design system's listbox; it searches once the roster passes eight (no native dropdown can) and scales past the ten seats at which the chip row disappeared.

  **EVERY choice on this dashboard is that listbox.** No dropdown, on any screen or in any dialog, is the platform's own: the list takes the theme, density, tokens and layer stack, not the OS palette in a dark dialog. What the platform gave free is earned back, by rules shared with every other list in the package: type-ahead, Home and End, disabled answers stepped over, the highlight announced through `aria-activedescendant`, Tab closing the list and carrying on to the next control, Escape stopping at the list, and a stored value the options no longer offer kept rather than swapped.
- **The spend panel is a link.** Screens are split by question; duplicating one screen's answer on another is how the two disagree.
- **A screen's toolbar is a `PageToolbar`, and its controls travel in groups.** It draws the `toolbar` class, which is not decoration: `.crewlet-app-shell__main:has(.toolbar)` publishes `--sticky-top`, and every other band sticking to the same scroller (a grid's column heads, a grouped list's group heads, an item's side rail) starts at that offset. It is the toolbar's drawn height, published by every `PageToolbar` (`useStickyBand`, measured when the bar resizes, never on scroll), so a bar that wraps on a phone keeps the heads under it, not behind its second line; one band of controls before the first measurement.
- **One rhythm for every toolbar, the work list's.** The band's own padding is the only space between its controls and the work under them, and it adds nothing above: controls start where any screen's content starts, and rows follow 8px below, stuck or not. The bar hands back the gap of the box it stands in (`--toolbar-host-gap`, which each such box names), and every control stands at the small step, 26px, in the kit's one edge. (Stacking the content column's padding and gap on the band gave 28px above and below.) A bar must reuse `.toolbar`, not restate its declarations: Worklet's filter bar did, left the property at its `0px` default, and the table header parked under an opaque band. Inside the bar, what narrows the rows is one group and what switches between answers another, because tabs draw different controls: as one flat wrapping row the scope control sat at x≈345 on List, x≈1338 on Board and x≈1155 on Calendar, and the Overdue chip wrapped to its own line ~1,200px from the count. A wrap breaks between groups.
- **A panel that rounds a run of rows clips; it does not hide.** A sticky box is held by the nearest scroller. A panel with `overflow: hidden` around the rows becomes that scroller and, growing to its rows, never scrolls, so its offset is permanently zero and the band sits `--sticky-top` DOWN from the panel's top, blank slot over the first row of its own group (the grouped work list did exactly this). `overflow: clip` rounds the corners identically and makes no scroller, as the data grid's wrap records.

Keyboard behaviour of rows of buttons and tables must match how they look:

- **A section row activates manually.** `Tabs`, and a `SegmentedControl` with `semantics="tabs"` (a lens, a window, a grouping), are one tab stop: arrows and Home and End move focus along the row, Enter or Space selects. A section pushes a history entry, and selecting on focus left one entry per keypress for Back to walk. Each tab names the `TabPanel` it controls.
- **A setting is a radio group.** The mode and density controls are `SegmentedControl` with `semantics="radio"`, as is the theme gallery: announced as a choice, not tabs with no panel, and arrows select as they move because changing a setting costs nothing per keypress. Likewise a filter that replaces the history entry.
- **The group keeps one tab stop, wherever the reader is standing.** The stop travels with the arrows, not the selection: a reader stands on an option they have not chosen while deciding, and a stop left on the selected one drops them somewhere they did not leave when they tab out and back. A change from outside the group (a click elsewhere, Back, a pasted URL) retires the arrows' position and takes the stop back, as does an option leaving `options`. It also survives a `value` the options do not carry: `value` comes off the query string, so a typo or hand-edited link arrives matching no option, and a stop that fell back only when the *held* option left gave every option `tabIndex="-1"` on `?lens=bogus`, dropping the control out of the tab order. It falls back to the first option; nothing is selected, so nothing else has a claim.
- **A sortable column is a button in its header.** A click on the `th` itself is unreachable by keyboard and not announced as a control. `aria-sort` stays on the header cell, and each column says which way its FIRST press sorts: a number and a timestamp from the big end and newest row, everything else from A (one direction for a whole table ordered every name from Z). An absent value sorts last in BOTH directions: a seat with no meter has not spent nothing, it has not been measured.

Four more controls that looked like something they were not:

- **A copy button says whether it copied.** The clipboard is invisible, so a silent control is indistinguishable from a dead one, and it was sometimes dead: `navigator.clipboard` is undefined outside a secure context, such as the `http://<node-ip>:8000` where anyone reads a machine's dashboard that is not their laptop, and `navigator.clipboard?.writeText(x)` swallowed that. The design system's `writeClipboard` falls back to the deprecated `execCommand` path, the only one working there, then says `Copied` or `Copy failed`, announced as well as drawn. The WRITE is the package's and the answer this dashboard's, on purpose: the package's `useClipboard` settles a refusal back to offering its action after a couple of seconds, and a control quietly back to offering looks never pressed. A refusal here holds until the next press.
- **A download button says whether it downloaded, and refuses rather than navigating.** An `<a>` whose `download` attribute the browser ignores OPENS the JSON instead of saving it, and a tab of text looks like something happening. `DownloadButton` tests both halves, `URL.createObjectURL` and `download`, before building anything, and says `Download failed` when either is missing. On success it says `Downloading`, not `Saved`: `<a download>` has no completion event, only the hand-off is observed, and a browser can still stop it. It names the file (`download started: turn-….json`) for a reader who cannot see the download shelf. It shares the confirmation machinery with `CopyButton`: the two sit side by side in the Turn header, so differing hold times would be a visible inconsistency. A `data:` URL is deliberately NOT the fallback: several engines cap one around two megabytes, so it would work on the small turns nobody needs it for and fail silently on large ones.
- **A caption-sized link is still a link.** `.t-caption` on an `<a>` sets the muted colour, which beats the anchor rule, so real navigations (a phase's own event, a turn card's id, a seat's last error, the spend screen) rendered as dim static text. `.t-link` is the caption register that keeps `--color-brand-accent-ink`, which the palette suite measures.
- **A link inside a sentence says so, because nothing else can tell it apart.** The anchor reset is right for chrome (a breadcrumb, a row that is an anchor, a caption-sized navigation: each a *thing* on the page) and wrong for an anchor that is a word in a line: the sentence is `--color-text-primary` and the link `--color-brand-accent-ink`, and colour alone is what WCAG 1.4.1 refuses. `.prose-link` puts the underline back, at rest rather than on hover. `.prose.md a` (rendered Markdown) and `.int-form-note a` (the sentence under a setup form) get it without asking. No scan can decide whether an anchor is inside a sentence, so `proselinks.test.ts` refuses the shape where nobody asked: an `<a>` carrying no class at all.

  **A chrome class on an anchor that is a word in a line passes that scan silently** (`.t-link` on "…No Mattermost bot for this seat. **Open Integrations**", fifteen cases). A hover underline never satisfied 1.4.1, since no keyboard or touch reader sees it. Eleven go through one component, so the fix lives there: `ScreenLink` carries `.prose-link` BY DEFAULT and takes `standalone` for the three call sites that really are a call to action on a line of their own. A default that is the common case makes the next call site right without anybody deciding.

  The scan's second question is decidable: JSX collapses whitespace around a newline, so a space between running text and the next tag needs `{" "}`. Text, then `{" "}`, then an anchor means the anchor continues prose (sixteen hits, no false positives). It does NOT catch an anchor after a literal space on the same line, indistinguishable from a caption followed by a chip; two of the fifteen were that, found by reading. A gate exactly right about a subset beats one that guesses about everything. The scan skips a bare `<ScreenLink>` on the strength of that default, a premise about a component a source scan cannot hold (deleting the default left the scan green and all eleven links unmarked), so `dialogParts.test.tsx` renders it and checks the output.
- **Select-all is a local verb on a record.** ⌘A / Ctrl+A is a *document* gesture, so on a screen about one JSON record (a turn's record, the active configuration) it took the nav, stat row and every phase card along. A `CodeBlock selectable` block is focusable and owns the chord while it holds focus; elsewhere the browser keeps it. The focus ring is required: a keyboard verb that changes meaning on click is a secret without one.

Two more a keyboard or screen-reader reader could not use, a class of defect no screenshot shows:

- **A meter needs a name, and a value inside its own range.** `role="meter"` with no accessible name announces as a bare number, and the visible legend ("94% of the meter used") is a reading, not a noun, so `Meter` takes `label`. The fill and `aria-valuenow` are clamped, because a budget *lowered* under a counter already past it would publish a value above `aria-valuemax`; `valueText` carries the true figures, so the overage is reported, not hidden. A meter with no ceiling is not drawn as one: "0 of 100" claims nothing has been spent where nobody has said the limit.
- **A tall record block is reachable from a keyboard.** A `CodeBlock` scrolls under its height cap, and Chrome and Safari reach a scroll container by keyboard only if something makes it focusable. A `selectable` block is (select-all needs it); the rest, the tall ones such as a phase card's verbatim system prompt (tens of kilobytes), were not. `focusWhenScrollable` is the second door onto the same tab stop, separate because `selectable` is an INTENT only the screen has (this block is the page's record) while the stop a scrollbar owes is an OBLIGATION the block discharges itself. A bridged run's tool log and a seat's thread take the second: named regions with a tab stop, and ⌘A keeps its usual meaning. It is measured on both axes, since `wrap={false}` scrolls sideways in a box too short to scroll down; a stop on every block would put one before each of a round's tool arguments, most a few lines. `label` is what such a block takes focus under, from either door: focus without a name is the other half of the trade.

The header carries the same facts in the same order whether a phase is live or finished (phase, decision, model, rounds, tokens, age), so the row does not change shape on completion. `decision`, `exhausted_rounds`, `empty_answer_rounds`, `rescue_fired`, `notes`, `tools_available` and `conversation_key` are all rendered. `empty_answer_rounds` keeps a seat whose model never speaks from reading as one merely rescued a lot: an empty answer is corrected in the tool loop (it once failed the provider call, walked the fallback chain and could end the turn as a red `llm_unavailable`).

**Nothing animates on a data push.** A list that re-flows as each tool-loop round lands cannot be read while running, and `agents` is pushed twice per round and once more before every tool call. Two kinds of motion are allowed, and `styles/motion.test.ts` holds every animation in the stylesheets to being declared as one, with its reason:

- **an entrance** of a surface the reader opened (the palette rising, its veil fading in), played once because somebody pressed something;
- **a steady-state pulse** on something live right now (the round in flight, a phase waiting on its first answer, the caret on text being written), running as long as the state holds rather than playing once on arrival, so a push changes WHETHER it runs and never triggers it.

An animation on a class a push adds (a new row, a changed value) is neither, and the suite refuses one by its selector. **Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` both stop.** `base.css` ends every entrance and transition on its first frame, document-wide; a pulse is not left to that rule (it would play one iteration instantly and leave the element wherever its keyframes rest), so each pulse carries its own `animation: none` and is static, in its resting look, still saying "live". No component animates from a `style` attribute, where no sheet could stop it.

**A control state is the other half of that rule, and it DOES ease.** A fill changing because somebody moved onto a row is a response and should look like one; a fill changing because the engine said something must land on the frame it is told. Almost every interactive surface (the sidebar's rows and links, a grid row, a crumb, the user block, a work row, a turn row, a feed row) snapped, and a product of instant fills jerks instead of responding. It is ONE declaration in `base.css` naming those surfaces, not a `transition:` on each (24 places to forget; the five that had one drifted to three durations). `prefers-reduced-motion` zeroes every duration, so there is nothing to opt out of.

**A control must not move under the pointer either.** A figure that resizes its cell from 9 to 10 shifts its neighbours, so every live number sits in a tabular cell with a floor; a count inside a heading's text resizes the heading, so it is its own element; a mark drawn in only one state (an unread dot) is a fixed cell, filled or not; and a filter chip ordered by a live count reorders on a poll, so chip rows are ordered by name.

---

## A turn is a story, not a log of itself

The Turn screen answers "what happened in this turn" once per fact. Rows like `started execute (iter 2)` repeated the phase card above them. Four rules:

1. **A duplicate is a row whose fact belongs somewhere else.**
   `agent_phase_started` and `agent_phase_completed` are the same phase (same
   `turn_id|phase|iteration`, which *is* the phase key), and the start says
   nothing the finished card does not. Pairing start and completion to get a
   duration is gone: it needed **both** events in one reader's hands, and a turn
   deep-linked *while it runs* asks its query before the phase starts and buffers
   only completed envelopes afterwards. So the engine measures the phase where
   the clock is and publishes `duration_ms` on `agent_phase_completed` itself.
   Every phase reports it (it answers "why did this turn cost 290k tokens" on
   self-iterating turns), and so does every **nested** call, a delegate's worker
   and the round-cap judge included, which publish no start. Zero means *not
   measured*, never *took no time*: an executor's rounds run inside its
   harness's own loop in another process, and that wall clock is on
   `executor_launched` / `executor_finished`.

   **The page says where each absorbed row went.** *Relocated* is only better
   than *dropped* if the page says so; a row drawn by no panel is
   indistinguishable from one the store never returned, which matters when
   checking a **cut** turn's event total against the panels. Every absorbed type
   names its destination ("the phase card it opens", "the turn's header and
   record"), and the page prints them under the bands as a folded **Already on
   this page** note: how many rows are not listed, what they were, where each
   kind is drawn. Absent when nothing was absorbed.

2. **Weight is meaning.** `reflection_completed` is a sentinel that deliberately
   carries no outcome; a guard breach is a turn the engine stopped. As identical
   feed rows an operator scanning for the second reads past it. So rows are
   grouped by the question they answer: **What went wrong** (above the phases,
   absent on a healthy turn), **What the turn was given**, **What else it did**,
   **What it left behind**. Anything this build has no opinion about falls
   through to a residual list, never dropped: the event registry is
   additive-only and a type a newer node publishes must still render.

   **A band entry is a query predicate, not a wish.** Every row these panels
   sort came from one read, `WHERE turn_id = ?`, and that column is filled from
   the event's own `turn_id` *field*. A type whose payload carries none can never
   be in the answer, and banding it promises what the wire cannot keep. It fails
   **empty**, the one way a panel cannot say it is broken: a turn that asked
   three colleagues renders like one that spoke to nobody. Eight types were
   banded that way:

   - **Four were the engine's omission, fixed there:** the three A2A audit
     records (published inside the asking turn's tool loop by code already
     holding its id) and one reflection record its worker did not stamp. All
     carry `turn_id` and `work_key` now, so an ask appears on the turn that made
     it.
   - **Four are facts about the event and stay out:** the scheduler's cron fire
     (the *trigger*, preceding every turn id, already rendered as the brief),
     two records saying **no** turn ran, and the curator promoting a skill off a
     cluster of many seats' turns (no single right id).

   `internal/events/types/turnbands_client_test.go` reads the dashboard's own
   declarations and fails the build both ways: on a band entry that can never
   fill, and on a kept-out type that has since *gained* a `turn_id`. It covers
   the **absorbed** map on the same terms (those rows are drawn, in the
   inventory below). The one declared exception is the live progress event,
   stream-only and in no table, kept on a roster of its own.

   *What the turn was given* draws both halves. `prompt.size` (a row of integers
   per phase, so prompt-slimming progress is measurable) sits beside
   `prefetch_summary`, which together say whether a heavy prompt is heavy
   *because* of what was prefetched or in spite of it. Per phase and per round,
   never summed: a prompt is re-sent every round of the tool loop, so a total is
   neither the turn's input bill (the tiles above report that) nor anything ever
   sent.

   Every term of the approximation gets a column, **System**, **User**,
   **Tools**, **Approx. tokens**, so the total can be checked against the row.
   *Tools* is the tool-definition array as compact JSON, definition count on its
   hover, and is usually the largest (unmeasured, a turn reported ~6,900 tokens
   on a prompt billed 205,000 input tokens). For the executor, *System* and
   *User* are the system prompt and the brief its run was launched with. Four
   fixed columns overflow a phone, hence the sideways scroll on `.num-block`.

   **One row per measurement**; the phase key is deliberately not the row's
   identity, and a repeated `turn_id|phase|iteration` is never folded into an
   `×N` chip. Since
   [ADR-0017](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/blob/main/adr/0017-a-turn-id-names-one-run.md)
   a run id is minted per dispatch, so a redelivered trigger runs under a
   *different* turn id and lands on its own Turn screen (the attempt banner at
   the top is for that); a re-run cannot put two rows in this table. A parked
   turn does not either: the executor publishes its prompt once, at launch, the
   collection re-entering the *same* phase and iteration sends none, and a
   send-back's relaunch is the next iteration, a row of its own. A row is one
   prompt this turn sent, drawn in publish order: folding reads two different
   prompts as a range of one quantity, which this panel must never say.

   The figures are **bytes**, `len()` of a Go string, and the wire keys say so
   (`system_bytes`, `user_bytes`, `tool_bytes`). They equal a character count
   only on ASCII, so under a character label non-Latin names or emoji would make
   "the count" a different quantity per company. See `PromptSize`.

3. **A healthy turn must be able to say so, and only when it can.** A set
   defined by subtraction (`type !== …`) has no meaningful empty state, and a
   section that is always full is one nobody reads. "Nothing went wrong" is a
   header badge beside the problem count it replaces. It is withheld on a
   **cut** view as on a running turn: the `turn` answer carries a `truncated`
   flag (as the `trace` answer does), because a guard breach among unread rows
   is invisible to the page.

   A turn is read oldest first, so a head-only read dropped the **ending**,
   including the two records the header reads its outcome, duration and plan
   summary off, and printed "no turn record" above the rows it did get. So the
   answer recovers the turn's last rows beside its first, and the flag names a
   gap in the **middle**. The badge reads "middle not shown".

4. **The feed's row is not this screen's row.** `EventRow` has four columns:
   time, actor, summary, source and category. On a one-turn page the actor is
   the same seat on every row and the category is an internal taxonomy, so these
   sections use a narrower row that spends the space on the event's own type.

### And the header has to read the record that has the field

`duration_ms` and `review_outcome` are on `turn_completed` (the learning
subsystem's record of the same turn, in the same query answer), not on
`agent_turn_completed`, which has neither. The screen reads both events and
names each for what it is.

More header rules:

- **A heading is a name, and a turn has none.** The title is the LEAD SENTENCE
  of `plan_summary`, not all of it: a model asked to account for four tool calls
  writes four sentences (one real turn headed itself with 280 characters at
  `--font-size-xl` semibold, three lines, pushing the fact line off a laptop's
  first screen), and the turns list, peek rail and feed card head with the same
  string. A boundary is a stop FOLLOWED BY A SPACE, keeping `1m 52s`, `v1.2` and
  `mattermost_post_message` whole, where a bare `.` split every one. `TurnBrief` prints the whole summary under "It
  set out to" whenever the lead took less than all of it, and stays away when it
  did not. Prose with no boundary is left alone (a mid-clause cut reads as
  broken); `.object-title` wears `.clamp`, bounding it at two lines. The TRIGGER
  follows the same exact comparison: the panel drops its "Woken by" prose only
  where the title says ALL of it, i.e. a one-sentence trigger. A longer one
  prints whole, the header's sentence at its front; on a turn with no plan
  summary it is the screen's only account of itself.
- **A turn's outcome is a state, so it takes a tone.** `Stat` has a `tone` for a
  value that IS an outcome: `done` positive, `self_iterate` caution, a guard
  breach critical. Not on other tiles: a token count or elapsed time is no
  state, and tinting every tile spends the four status hues on decoration. The
  tile also names the **executor's** last word (`delivered` / `no_action` /
  `blocked` / `incomplete`) beside the **reviewer's** decision, since a turn that
  delivered nothing reads like one that delivered if only the reviewer's word is
  shown.
- **The failure badge is derived from what failed, not from the phase
  records.** `phases.some(p => p.failed)` misses every turn the engine killed
  *between* phases (a refused charge, an exhausted chain, a guard that fired),
  which have no failed phase record.
- **An unlabelled identifier is not information.** The conversation key
  (`mattermost:9zd7xj4…:cnjza…`) is a property of the *turn*, not the seat, and
  is labelled and explained beside the turn's record. The header also shows
  **what woke this turn** (the trigger rides on every phase event and links to
  its own event) and **what it set out to do** (`plan_summary`).

### What a mark MEANS, and where a control belongs

- **✓/✗ is a pass/fail vocabulary, so it may not describe an absence.** A seat
  with no prior episodes, no synthesized skills and a turn that is not its first
  has four empty context blocks and a healthy prompt. The prefetch panel leads
  with what the prompt actually GOT, sized, and names the rest in one quiet
  line. The one diagnostic state, a block never *searched* because the trigger
  was a bare pointer, stays called out.
- **A section's name must not be readable as a failure.** "What it left behind"
  read as abandoned work; it is the reflection pass, and everything in it is
  something the seat now knows: **What the seat learned**.
- **"Nothing went wrong" is a badge, not a banner.** It is a property of the
  turn, so it sits beside the phase count, in the problem badge's slot; a
  full-width banner says the same at ten times the weight. Claimed only on a
  *finished* turn with a record to claim it from: "nothing went wrong" and
  "nothing was read" must not render alike.
- **A link to the page you are on is a lie.** A phase card's `event →` is a way
  out on the turn and the seat but a loop on that event's own page.
  `useIsCurrent` answers it generally, so no component needs to know where it is
  rendered; outside a Router it answers "no" rather than throwing, since a
  router should not be the price of drawing a phase card.
- **The way into a turn is a control, not a caption.** The turn card's `turn
  28e93bc3 →` is a button with its promise beside it, not a mono footer link.

**A chip's shape is a claim about what kind of thing it is.** The trigger's
integration in the phase tags' row, size and shape made `EXECUTE  REVIEW  mattermost` read as three phases. The trigger and its source are one fact on one
line; the phases are another.

**A page bar holds what you can DO; an object header holds what the object
IS.** The turn page portalled the seat, phase count, attempt, problem count and
"nothing went wrong" into `PageActions` beside Copy turn and Download turn: the
bar reached ten items and wrapped on a laptop (see [The page bar wraps by what
it holds](#the-page-bar-wraps-by-what-it-holds)), the eye travelled to the far
corner for a fact about the object forty pixels below, and two chips (`Agent CEO`, `7 phases`) repeated the fact line (`SEAT Agent CEO`, `PHASES 7`) under them, so those two were dropped,
not moved.

`ObjectHeader`'s `status` slot holds state, and the marks are derived on the
turn's view rather than the page, **where BOTH frames can reach them**, so the
peek gets them too (a rail over a failed turn must show the problem badge).

**A qualifier follows what it qualifies.** The source comes after the trigger
text, not in front: the subject first, with flex sizing deciding who gives way
on a narrow card (the message truncates, the source stays whole).

### The document does not scroll

`#screen-scroll`, the shell's main region, scrolls a page; the document never
does. The sidebar is a fixed column beside a scrolling sheet, so a page that
also scrolled as a whole would carry the sidebar off the top and leave two
scrollbars. The frame is the design system's `AppShell`, exactly one viewport
tall, and `base.css` gives `body` a fixed `100dvh`. On screen `html` keeps the
viewport's overflow hidden and `body` is a clipping containing block, so a box
positioned against nothing inside it (a visually hidden span) cannot stretch the
document and a script cannot scroll it. A press that goes to a place moves that
place's own scroller (`scrollToPlace` in `lib/scroller.ts`), never every
ancestor as `scrollIntoView` does.

Two other kinds of scroller sit inside it. A **full-height screen**
(`useFillScreen`; its doc in `app/fill.tsx` is the one list of the screens that
ask and when each withdraws) holds `#screen-scroll` still. A canvas fills it and
pans; a two-column screen lets each column scroll on its own, as a task does
with its body and rail (`.task-main`, `.task-rail`) and the Inbox with its list
and pane (`.inbox-list`, `.inbox-pane`). Each column is exactly the main
region's height, so `100cqb` is its view too, and a box inside one hands the
wheel to the column, not `#screen-scroll`. Chatlet asks for the height FLUSH
(`useFillScreen(true, {
flush: true })`, the kit's `fill="flush"`): the conversation runs edge to edge
under the page bar, so the content column drops its inset, measure and gap. And
a **box inside the page** may scroll its own content, on the two conditions
below.

The shell hands the kit that id as its `mainId`, and everything that needs the
scroller finds it through ONE accessor, `screenScroller()` in `lib/scroller.ts`:
the router restoring a position per history entry, the settled list checking
the reader is at the top before splicing rows in, and a seat's Memory section
checking whether an opened detail is in view. The id identifies the element; a
class (`.screen`, once the settled list's spelling, beside the router's
`getElementById`) is only a styling hook and could drift from it.

The router and settled list scroll that element directly rather than calling
`scrollIntoView`. The one `scrollIntoView` (Memory bringing a stacked detail's
heading into view) runs only when the heading is outside the scroller's box, and
with an unscrollable document no other ancestor exists to move.

**A box inside the page may scroll its own content, on two conditions.** A
running phase's transcript, a seat's thread list beside its open thread and its
session list beside its open transcript, the Settings column, a board lane's
body and a long record each scroll inside themselves, a second thing under the
wheel, so each must keep the page within reach:

- **It is bounded by the scroller's view, never by a literal.** The shell's
  `main` is a size container on every screen (`container: scroller / size`), so
  a box asks for `100cqb` (the window less the page bar, which wraps, the
  sheet's inset and any banner, none of which a descendant can count) and
  subtracts what covers or must accompany it (`--sticky-top`, a board lane's
  head), with a floor of four rows. The BOX must fit once scrolled to, not its
  caption (a caption subtraction held only while the caption did not wrap). A
  `px` height or `100dvh` sum is a guess: too tall on a short window, the bottom
  below the fold, and too short on a tall one (board lanes were `min(70dvh, 760px)` until the gate below saw every scroller). Whether the box sits beside
  what it serves is a container query on the screen's width (`@container page`),
  never a window media query, since the sidebar and a peek take width the window
  does not report.
- **At either end the wheel is the page's.** No in-page scroller sets
  `overscroll-behavior` to `contain` or `none` on the block axis: containment
  there is the wheel doing nothing while the page has more to show. The one
  exception is a box always wholly in view, the sticky Settings column exactly
  the view's height, where chaining would move the section beside it instead.

**A long record is bounded once, in the cascade.** Every block of machine text
the kit's `CodeBlock` draws (a tool's arguments and result, a phase's verbatim
prompt, an event's payload, a configuration, a run's transcript) reads its
ceiling from `--crewlet-codeblock-max-height`. The shell declares it once on the
two scrollers a record can sit in, the main region and the peek's body (itself a
size container for this): `--record-view`, the view less the sticky band and a
label's line, floored at four rows, and `--record-ceiling`, that capped at
`--record-max` (460px). A running ledger narrows it to its own box less the
record's label. A per-call number fails: on a shorter view the bottom sat below
the fold while the wheel was inside the block, and a sheet gate cannot see an
inline style. A block states its own only where it genuinely differs: the YAML
dialog (portaled outside both scrollers, takes the root's cap), the trace's
paired Input and Output (half the ceiling each, derived), and Configuration's
active document, the Active lens's whole content (the view's share, uncapped).

`styles/scrollers.test.ts` holds all of it. It scans EVERY rule in the sheets
that scrolls its block axis with a declared bound, and passes a literal bound
only from a roster saying why it cannot hide anything: an overlay or dialog the
fold does not reach (the secret completion list, the filter menu's list, the
composer's and the setup dialog's scrollers) or a box shorter than any view (a
finding's 9rem of chips). A roster entry that stopped being true fails too. Its
containment half keeps the Settings column as its one entry and reason. It reads
the record ceiling on both scrollers and in the running ledger, and the source
for any `CodeBlock` handed a `maxHeight` outside its two named exceptions, or a
number inside them. A sideways strip is not its subject, since it never holds
the page's own wheel.

### A card has one left edge

`tight` is a claim about height, for a card whose rows carry their own vertical
rhythm (a stack of cards, a footer strip). It is vertical-only in `Card.Body`,
on the inset the header sets; reducing horizontal padding too put content on a
different line from its heading and a code block hard against the right edge
with no room for its scrollbar. All four tight bodies align with their titles.

### Cards side by side end at one height

**Two cards that share a row end at the same foot.** A short card beside a tall one left a hole under it, because each page laid its cards out in a grid of its own and aligned it to the start, or wrapped a card in an element that a stretched cell could not hand its height to. So a row of equal cards stands in the kit's `CardGrid`, which stretches every cell to its row whatever the page aligns and hands a wrapped card the height; a card's footer keeps to its foot. A layout with its own tracks (a list beside its detail, a side column that becomes a grid) stretches its cards too. The one exception is a sticky pane, which keeps to its row's top so that it can stick. Home's arranged board packs its widgets as a masonry and is left out. Two checks hold it: every dashboard layout case measures the page as each React root unmounts and fails on cards of one row that start or end apart (`unevenCardRows`, `src/test/layout.tsx`), and `src/styles/cardrows.test.ts` fails where a sheet aligns a row of kit cards, or their cells, off the row. Neither sees a screen no layout case mounts that wraps its cards in an element which does not pass the height on, which is why rows of equal cards go in `CardGrid`.

### A card's head keeps its title whole

A head is one line: title, a subtitle beside it, the card's actions at the end.
Beside actions the kit shrinks title and subtitle together, so on a phone a
plain title broke over two lines (*Active* over *revision*) while its subtitle
was cut beside the Copy button. So **on a narrow screen a head holding both a
subtitle and actions puts the subtitle on a line of its own**, under the title
and actions, with the head's whole width. One rule for every head of that shape.

### A fact that moves is a fact nobody can scan

The turn card's source chip belongs in the header's metadata cluster with the
turn's other attributes (how much, how long, when): beside the phase tags it
read as a third phase, before the trigger text it was a label ahead of its
sentence, and after it the chip sat wherever the sentence ended, a different
spot per card. The same facts in the same places always is what lets a reader
scan a list down a column, and a source is something somebody scans.

### A budget bar is coloured by the engine, never by its fill

A budget window arrives with the engine's own `state` (`ok`, `near` or
`refusing`), computed once beside the shared counter, and every surface draws
that and nothing else: the attention queue, the live meters on Now, Spend and a
seat's page, the Budgets table and `crewlet budgets show`. There is **one
threshold**, the engine's (`near` at nine tenths of a ceiling, served as the
budgets answer's `near_fraction`); no screen divides a counter by a ceiling to
pick a colour. (Three thresholds, the Budgets table's 75%, the attention
queue's 90% and the kit `Meter` ramp's own, made one window read healthy,
nearly spent and full at once.) `refusing` is the gate's own word, no room left
for a single token, and the condition a seat is parked on, so a parked seat's
bar can never read as merely near.

The refusal stamp says when the gate last turned a call away: a refused charge,
or work turned away unsent because the window was already full (a turn's next
call, a parked delivery, a person's question, a reflection pass). It shows only
beside a refusing window; under a ceiling raised since, the stamp is history
until the next admitted charge clears it, and the window is drawn by its spend.
A window that refused a round reads past its ceiling, because the refused round
is counted like any other (the vendor billed it), and its figures say so: 102
120 of 100 000, the spend billed rather than the ceiling crossed.

Each capped window is its own bar: a scope capped by day and by month has two
ceilings, and a bar is drawn against one. `ok` is drawn in the first data hue
(the kit meter's `quantity` tone), not the accent, because the accent means
where the reader is and a window with room is a number, not a state: a meter is
a figure of ONE quantity its label names, which is all a data hue asks for.

---

### A description list is a metadata list, not a panel layout

Its grid is `minmax(120px, max-content) 1fr`, sized for compact pairs (an id, a
timestamp, a key). As a panel's content it crams everything into a narrow left
band: a line of prose in a column sized to the longest label, a byte count
stranded mid-panel. Two shapes replace it, both already in the product. **Prose
takes a micro-label above it and the full width below** (the seat's Profile
panel). **A figure goes at the far end of a full-width row**, behind a
`.spacer`, with the heading naming the unit once rather than every row (a bare
"134 B" says nothing about what was measured).

**The far end is the ledger's, not the card's.** A `.spacer` puts a figure at
the end of its box, right in a rail and wrong in a full-bleed panel (the prompt
ledger drew a phase tag at x=37 and its token count at x=645 on a 1570px
screen, and a reader tracking a row across the gap arrives at the wrong one). So
`.num-block` is `width: fit-content`, sized to its widest row, leaving the
spacer nothing to push with and putting figures where the labels end. Not a
chosen cap: a cap is a number invented to be wider than the content, still
leaves a gap and must be re-invented when a column is added. `max-width` stays
as a *ceiling* only: 100% so a phone scrolls the block rather than the page, and
38rem so prose-long labels cannot restore the gap.

- **The rows are sized as one box, not one at a time.** A row's own
  `max-content` is its own tag and chips, so once the block is clamped (a phone)
  every row falls back to a *different* width and the columns splay. The width
  belongs to `.num-rows`, the single box around all rows, and the rows stretch
  to it. jsdom computes no layout, so the test asserts ancestry: every
  `.num-col` sits inside a `.num-rows` inside a `.num-block`.
- **A fixed column is sized by its heading, not its figure.** `.num-col` is
  `7rem` because the widest label, APPROX. TOKENS, measures 103px at
  `--font-size-2xs` with `--font-letter-spacing-wide` and wrapped at 5.5rem. A
  column cannot grow for its own heading, so the heading sets the width.

`PropertiesRail` keeps the one thing this shape is for on this screen: the
conversation key, a term and its detail, labelled and printed as every row
prints a key (a schedule's parts decoded, the key as sent on its title), with a
caption saying what it names: the external conversation the turn served, or,
for a schedule's fire, the schedule the turn was a fire of, which no surface
holds. A phase card's footer prints it the same way, saying which on its title.

**A chip must not repeat the sentence beside it.** The trigger's summary is
built by the vendor's own summariser and already opens with who wrote it
("Message from Ana: …", the sender by the name the company knows them by where
the notification service resolved one, else the id it arrived with), so a sender
chip was the same fact twice, and two chips plus a link after one line of prose
is a hedge, not a header. Only the integration stays: the one thing the sentence
does not reliably carry.

### A link is a colour, and its hover is a step within the text rungs

Nothing in this product underlines on hover. `@crewlethq/tokens`' baseline does
(`a:hover { text-decoration: underline }`), and both it and a former repeat in
`base.css` are wrong here: almost no link in this tree is inside a *sentence*.
A breadcrumb, a seat in a grid cell, a caption-sized `turn 28e93bc3 →`, a whole
row that is an anchor are chrome, and a rule struck under a timestamp, a summary
and a type at once decorates three fragments that are not a phrase. (The
suppression had spread to fifteen rules in four stylesheets, each undoing the
inherited declaration: the exceptions outnumbered the default.)

**A reset has to reach the declaration it undoes.** `a { text-decoration: none }` is (0,0,1) against the baseline's `a:hover { text-decoration: underline }` at
(0,1,1), so the package won the one state a reader can see, and every link
underlined under the pointer, the sidebar's rows included. An outranked
declaration is no error, warning or build failure, and an unhovered screenshot
looks right. So the reset is written at `a:hover` as well, and
`styles/baseline.test.ts` holds it against the *installed* package, every entry
point `main.tsx` loads, not just `base`.

That gate must also be able to fail for the regression it is named after (a
first version matched selectors and ignored values, so `a:hover {
text-decoration: underline }` in `base.css` left it green). It holds four
things: the selector is answered; what answers it *is* a reset; no sheet of ours
re-decorates a bare anchor from the other side (`screens.css` imports later and
would win on order); and `main.tsx` imports the baseline *before* our reset
(equal specificity means the later sheet wins, a premise the rules cannot
carry). It is two-sided: a reset for a declaration the package has dropped is a
rule with nothing on the other side, indistinguishable from one whose
declaration nobody found.

The frame's own hover vocabulary carries it. The sidebar's rows, the section
tabs and `.crumb-link` answer a pointer by moving to `--color-text-primary`, and
a link does the same: in dark the accent ink (#a9b0ff) brightens toward
near-white, in light the violet (#4f51bd) darkens toward near-black, so in BOTH
themes hovering makes a link MORE prominent. Both ends are measured text rungs,
which rules out the obvious alternative: the accent family publishes exactly one
text step, and `--color-brand-accent`, `--color-brand-accent-hover` and
`--color-brand-accent-active` are fills that `styles/rungs.test.ts` refuses as a
colour.

**Where the colour step cannot be seen, the underline is the hover.** Under
`forced-colors: active` the UA forces `color` to `LinkText` in *both* states and
composites the 4–5% row wash onto its own `Canvas` as nothing. Measured in
Chromium with the mode on, `.crumb-link`, `.t-link`, `.cell-seat`,
`.work-col-foot a` and every prose register render pixel-identical hovered and
unhovered; only a row painting a wash that survives still answers.
`text-decoration` is the one property the mode leaves to the author (which is
why the baseline's default is right *there* and wrong elsewhere), so `base.css`
puts it back inside an `@media (forced-colors: active)` block, and the gate
requires that block to exist as long as the reset does.

**Where an underline is the only honest mark it is permanent, not a hover.** A
link inside running prose is otherwise distinguished by colour alone (WCAG
1.4.1). `.prose.md a` (rendered Markdown) and `.int-form-note a` (the sentence
under a setup form) carry it at rest, and `.prose-link` is the third register:
an anchor anywhere else that *is* a word in a line (see *A link inside a
sentence says so* above; seven anchors in five other files were outside the
first two).

All three state their hover, because the reset reaches one. `.prose-link` is
(0,1,0) against `a:hover`'s (0,1,1), so a class alone would put the mark back
everywhere except under a pointer, where a reader decides whether the word is a
link. `.prose.md a` outranks the reset on arithmetic and `.int-form-note a` ties
and wins on import order; both say it anyway so neither depends on a fact stated
elsewhere, and `styles/baseline.test.ts` refuses a register that draws the
underline without also drawing it at `:hover` (deleting one of those selectors
reads like removing a duplicate).

Stating the underline is not answering the pointer: pinning `.prose.md a`'s
colour at (0,2,1) kept the `a:hover` step from reaching it, the one anchor where
hovering changed nothing. It takes the step now, like everything else; see rule
16a.
### A row is not a row

`EventRow` is the activity feed's row, on a four-track grid: time, actor, summary, tail. The turn screen must not reuse it: the columns that carry information in a feed carry none for ONE turn. The actor is the same seat on every row, the category is an internal taxonomy, the date is a turn the header already dates. The actor also comes off the **summary**, not just out of a column: the engine builds lines as `lead(actor, …)`, so each opens with the seat's name, which four rows under that seat's heading need not repeat.

**A nested call hangs off the phase that made it** (`host_phase`, `host_iteration`, `groupTurns`, the `PhaseCard` prop). A delegate fan-out of eight is not eight siblings of the turn's own phases; the "N phases" badge and the token total must agree with the feed's card for the same turn.
- The token tile counts the turn's own phases and reports worker spend beside it (the engine's `total_tokens` / `subagent_tokens` split).
- **Auxiliary** spend inside the turn (`+N auxiliary`: turn-start context, ledger rewrites, its card) is read off the turn's `auxiliary_spend` records of the `turn` stage. Figure and notes add up to the turn list's tokens for the same turn.
- The reflection after the turn is never in it: it is the seat's learning, not the work's cost, and is drawn in the Timeline's Reflection lane.

**A launch of the executor sits inside its round.** Each `executor_collected` (one launch, as its collection read it off the box) is no phase but the work of the `execute` round that launched it. `groupTurns` files it under that round's record and the round's `PhaseCard` draws it inside, under **Its launch** (or **Its N launches**): harness, how it ended, spend, the report it wrote and its **Activity** fold.
- One round is one card however many launches (an answer carries a parked executor on; a launch lost with its host is relaunched). Its header's token figure is the round's, since the executor's record carries none; the Tokens fact counts it as the turn's own.
- A launch whose round has no record in hand stands in the round's place on its own card.
- In **Recent phases** a launch is its own row, drawn as the executor's: the `execute` word with its harness beside it, its harness's own turns under Rounds, `collected` as its outcome with the report's first line.

---

### Worklet is a workspace, not a table

Worklet's screen was a flat table beside a board of three `<div>`s and read as a database dump; it is a WORKSPACE now, each part below applies a rule of this page to a tracker.

- **A project is a SCOPE, not a shape of it.** Worklet's trail names the scope (All projects or one project) and switches it ([Worklet's scope](#worklets-scope-is-named-and-switched-in-the-trail)), each project with its key and maintained open count. List, board and calendar draw the scope you are on; a lens per shape would make "Engineering ▸ Board" a destination competing with Engineering. The counts are the engine's maintained columns, not an aggregate per poll, which is what lets the switcher and lenses carry a number.
- **A SHAPE is a drawing, a VIEW is a query, and only the query was saved by anybody.** [A filter is a chip](#a-filter-is-a-chip-an-arrangement-says-what-it-is-set-to) states the general rule; here is where the line falls.
