The initial load is the shell's scripts and stylesheet and everything they reach
through a static `import`, derived from the modules themselves rather than from
the order the crawl met them in, so a chunk the entry asks for lazily and a
vendor chunk imports statically counts as the initial load it is. A failure
lists the files largest first. The values and their reasons live beside the
test's constants; `vite.config.ts` sets `chunkSizeWarningLimit` to the raw
equivalent of the chunk budget (439 kB, at the most compressible ratio the build
writes), so the bundler warns at or before the point the test fails.

**The design system's stylesheet is one sheet, above ours.** A uilet component
imports its own stylesheet as a side effect of its module, which in a
code-split build puts a component reached only from one workspace into that
workspace's chunk — and a browser appends a lazy chunk's sheet after the
dashboard's own, so every one-class tie the dashboard's rules win would flip
the first time a reader opened that workspace. So `main.tsx` takes every
component sheet the kit and its icons ship as one stylesheet between the token
sheets and ours (`vite.config.ts`'s `designSystemSheet`, over the kit's own
single-sheet build), and every per-component import is answered empty. The
engine's suite holds the result from the built artifact:
`TestNoLazyStylesheetCarriesTheDesignSystem` fails any stylesheet a lazy chunk
brings that carries a design-system rule.

### What the client half guarantees

- **The store derives nothing.** The server computes the projection once and pushes the result; a client-side copy of the state machine or token aggregation makes a refresh disagree with what was on screen.
- **The hierarchy is the engine's, too.** A seat's handle, the unit a root seat's `unit:` reference moved it into, a unit's inherited lead, what a unit key in `manages` expands to, automatic management by a lead and which of several managers is primary are engine rules; the `org` projection carries their result in its `derived` block. `lib/seats.ts` indexes that block over the authored tree and implements none of the rules (a TypeScript copy derived a different handle than Go for "İlker Demir", and a handle keys a seat's memory). Both halves come from one document in one call, so they always pair, and the block is the authority, not checked against the tree: no screen draws a "hierarchy not reported" state. Units pair by key and seats by handle, both minted into every document a write stores, so a namesake never claims another's entry. `{}`, a node running no company, is an empty company.
- **A seat is never paired by its name.** A name is prose and two seats may share one. The roster row, every `agents` overlay, an executor's row, a phase record, a turn row and a spend row carry the seat's `agent_id` (derived from its handle, which no namesake shares), and the store merges an overlay onto its row by that id alone (`protocol/store.ts`), dropping one for a seat the roster does not carry. A seat of the org index pairs with its roster row by HANDLE (`lib/seats.ts`' `liveRowFor`), since both are cut from one chart view and a handle is unique; a URL, a filter and the question asked of the engine name a seat by handle.
- **A link kept before a rename still opens what it named.** A seat is addressed by its handle and a unit by its key (`lib/seats.ts`' `seatPath` and `unitByKey`); a rename moves neither, so there is no alias or route rewrite. A name is never an address, except for a seat the engine gave no handle, which `seatPath` links to by name.
- **What a redacted document holds is shown as what it is.** A credential field arrives as one whole `${VAR}` reference, shown as the name it is, or as the engine's mask, shown as "A literal value is set (hidden)". The mask is never printed as a value, and a credential field holding anything else (a partial reference such as `Bearer sk-${SUFFIX}`) is hidden the same way whatever the engine sent. The guarded half of a screen is drawn only while the guarded read succeeds: a refused re-read takes it off the page rather than leaving the last answer beside the banner.
- **A region that throws takes only itself down.** Without a boundary React unmounts the whole application on a render error (a seat whose `llm` was a per-phase mapping once gave a blank page). `app/boundaries.tsx` puts one around every region that draws what the engine sent, never around the frame, which is the reader's way somewhere else:
  - the ROUTED SCREEN renders "This screen could not be drawn" with the error's message and Try again, inside a frame whose sidebar and ⌘K still work. It resets when the resolved path changes; a query string alone (a filter, an open peek) is the same screen and keeps its failure on view;
  - the PEEK's body, inside the rail, so the rail's Close and the screen behind stand. It resets when the peek moves to another object;
  - the COMMAND PALETTE, whose failure is a dialog of its own ("Search could not be drawn") that closes the way the palette does; the next ⌘K is a fresh palette;
  - each LIVE SIDEBAR SECTION (Projects, Pinned, Starred, the engine card, the account block) keeps its heading and says "Could not be drawn" with Try again, so a malformed project row costs only the Projects list.
- **One REST transport, one REST loader.** `protocol/rest.ts` is the only path to a REST route: `rest.request(method, path, options)` answers the status and the `ETag` beside the body, takes a caller's `AbortSignal`, never lets the browser cache a guarded answer, and resolves a 304 rather than throwing it; the body-only wrappers sit on top. The deadline and the caller's abort cover reading the body as well as waiting for headers; a body that breaks part way is status 0 (never fully heard, so a write's outcome is unknown), not an empty success. A screen that reads a REST answer uses `lib/useRest.ts`. The one reader outside it is the org builder's session over the `/config` document: half of a conditional write, it holds the `ETag` a save sends back as `If-Match`. The loader aborts a superseded read and an unmounted screen's, re-reads when the socket comes back after a drop and, where asked, when the tab comes back or on a poll (those quietly, keeping what is on screen). A sign-in needs no re-read: it is outside the frame, so the screen it returns to mounts again. A refusal replaces what is on screen; a request that never reached the engine keeps the last answer with the error beside it; an answer belongs to its key, so a read whose key changed reports nothing until the new key answers.
- **A retry is the engine's to schedule.** A socket refusal is asked again after its `retry_after` and a REST refusal after its `Retry-After`, quietly, bounded at thirty seconds (`RETRY_AFTER_MAX_MS`). Nothing else is retried: a `retry_after` of `0`, and a `503` the engine wrote with no hint, is a node no wait repairs (a full log, no keyring, no surface), and re-asking only repeats it ([Honest empty states](#honest-empty-states)). The client has no retry constant beyond the engine's health tick: a flat one is too early for a node with a long backlog and too late for one that caught up in milliseconds.
- **A newer peer's frame is ignored and counted.** A push kind this build does not dispatch is dropped, not thrown on or guessed at, and the store counts it (`unknownPushes`), since a kind this engine sends and its client forgot looks the same; the e2e replay fails on any. A field a later build adds is declared optional in that build's `protocol/types.ts`, so an answer from a node on the earlier build takes the screen's "unknown" branch rather than reading `undefined` as a value.
- **Nothing outside `src/protocol/` reaches the network.** A screen calling `fetch` itself would be the one request with no session, no deadline and no refusal to branch on. `protocol/transport.test.ts` parses every module and refuses, outside that directory, any READ of `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `EventSource` or `WebTransport` (bare, or off `window`, `globalThis` or `self`), of `navigator.sendBeacon`, and a form that posts to a URL of its own. A read rather than a call, because `const send = fetch` escapes a scan of calls; `refetch()`, a type, a member sharing the name and a test kit assigning a stub are not reads, and the suite certifies both halves.
- **A read names its question.** The first argument of `useQuery(` and `query(` (bare or as a method, like the socket's `.query(`) is a string literal: never a variable, expression or template with a substitution. The registry gates (`TestEveryQueryARoomMakesIsAnswered`, `TestEveryQueryThisServerAnswersHasAReader` in `internal/api/queries`) read kinds at those calls by name alone and can read only a constant. `app/source.test.ts` reads the same calls by spelling, whatever they are bound to, and refuses a non-literal kind, a method named by a computed key (`socket["query"](`), which the Go reader cannot see, and an aliased import. The two calls that forward a kind (the hook's own body, the builder test kit's stub socket) are named there with their reasons.
- **Subscriptions are per-slice.** `agents` is pushed twice per tool-loop round and once before each call; waking every listener on every envelope would re-render the application several times a second for a turn.
- **A query WAITS for the socket rather than failing.** Screens query as the page boots, so rejecting when not yet connected made every deep link stay at "could not load". Queries are pure reads, so one in flight when the socket drops is re-sent on reconnect.
- **A question whose parameter is not chosen yet is SKIPPED, not sent.** Absent params are an empty params object on the wire, so `useQuery("work_project", project ? { key: project } : undefined)` reads like a guard and is not one: the engine refuses a question missing a parameter with no default, and the screen shows an error for something nobody asked. The engine classifies it `bad_params` and logs it as `stream_query_refused` at DEBUG (the caller's fault, not a warning). The guard that works is `enabled`, and a test scans for the shape that admits an empty parameter without one.
- **A refused credential is diagnosed over HTTP.** A handshake answered 401 never reaches the page as `close(1008)`: a connection that never opened has no frames, so the browser reports 1006, the same as an engine that is down. A plain `GET /ws/stream` runs the same guard with the same cookie and stops one line short of the upgrade:
  - 401 is nobody signed in: send the reader to the sign-in and STOP dialling (each dial is the same 401, two console errors each) until a sign-in in this tab re-dials, or the tab coming back dials once (which notices a sign-in made in another tab, whose cookie this tab shares);
  - 426 means the session was accepted;
  - `403 second_factor_enrolment_required` stops the dialling and sends them to the enrolment;
  - otherwise the loop keeps dialling on its backoff, except that a `503` the engine wrote (a node that cannot read its identity estate yet) times the next dial by its `Retry-After`, bounded like every hint. A `503` with no `Retry-After`, or one something in front of the engine wrote, keeps the backoff: a dial may reach another node, which is what a zero says, and the loop is the tab's only way back.
- **A frame arrives already encoded, and two tabs in the same posture get the byte-identical one.** The engine marshals a push once per POSTURE present on the node, not per connection: what a client receives is decided by its socket's posture (`live` or `degraded`) and the kind's own route (every client, one seat's watchers, or the one client that asked). Tabs in the same posture therefore never see differing frames, the property the transcript, activity feed and agent overlays are compared against.
- **A degraded node's socket stays open, and says so.** When the node's posture is `shed` or `stuck` its copy of the company is wrong rather than behind: pushes stop, queries come back `unavailable`, and the `ping`/`pong` keepalive and the 5-second `health` frame carry on. The page renders a stated condition, not a stall: a closed socket would reconnect on a backoff, learn nothing and show "retrying" as long as the node stayed degraded. `unavailable` is never flattened into an empty result, since "this company has no work" is something a reader acts on.
- **Three close codes, and what each one asks of the reader.** A refused handshake cannot carry one (see the HTTP diagnosis above); these are for an open socket, which the engine decides again against its opening credential whenever an identity record names it, a company is published, or the credential reaches its end.
  - `4401`: the credential no longer resolves to anybody (session ended or revoked). Once this tab's own requests settle, ask `GET /auth/session` once: a `401` sends the reader to sign in with nothing dialled (dialled blind, a session ended elsewhere cost three `401`s: handshake, probe, snapshot); any other answer re-dials with the cookie the browser holds now.
  - `4403`: the person resolves and may not have this surface (their seat is gone). The socket STOPS (no reconnect, no REST fallback; the same decision would refuse both) and every screen but the Account, which reads no socket, is replaced by one panel saying who they are (`GET /auth/session`, asked again on the refusal), what they hold and why, with the *Account*, a *Try again* for after an administrator has acted, and a *Sign out* (the engine keeps `/auth/` open to their session for exactly that). Drawn as the screens were, they said "not connected" with figures that never resolved, and the sidebar's foot said "Checking who you are" for good. A handshake refused `403` is the same state, read through the plain-HTTP re-ask.
  - `1013` (*try again later*): the engine will not vouch for the credential on this socket now (it could not read what decides it, an identity move named nobody, or the person's seat answers to another handle). Reconnect on a backoff and let the handshake decide and say why (`503 identity_unavailable` while the node cannot read its identity estate).

  Nothing else closes this socket for a fault. The socket never moves the session's cookie, only a REST response can, so a tab that would otherwise sit on the socket alone makes an ordinary REST read now and then, or its session idles out however busy the screen is.
- **One clock.** Every relative time on screen advances together; none is baked at render. A time with a word beside it is part of a sentence and is said in words on the reader's calendar ("42 minutes ago", "yesterday at 17:40", `lib/ago.ts`); a time standing alone, or set off by a middle dot, comma or brackets, keeps the short form ("42m ago"), as do a tag, a figure and a seat's state line ("Expires in 4h", "Idle · last turn 24m ago"). `app/times.test.ts` holds both.

### The components come from the design system

- **`@crewlethq/ui` draws it, and the engine composes it.** The palette, glyphs, overlays, layer stack, primitives, most of the chart kit, the canvas and the tree model are the design system's, shared with the console and documentation site. Everything with a peer in the package is the package's: the badge, panel, empty state, stat row, skeleton, select, tab strip, avatar, banner, disclosure, search input, button and chip, plus the ranked list, legend, stacked bar, activity strip, sparkline and the diff: every diff is the package's `DiffView` ([Every diff is tinted](#every-diff-is-tinted)).
- **What is left of `src/ui/` is of three kinds, none a second recipe for something the package draws.** A VOCABULARY the package lacks and should lack: `Tone`, the six words the engine's payloads are spelled in, and the single translation into the package's spelling. A TABLE, not a recipe: `PhaseTag` draws the package's `Tag` and adds what the package cannot know, which of the six phase strings the engine emits map onto the three hues it publishes. And components no shared design system has, because each is about a company's own data: the histogram, the facet rail, the `window=` control, the meter, and three charts with no package shape (a time series whose series may be a REFERENCE rather than a measurement, its stacked form, and the phase ramp). `src/components/` above it is COMPOSITION out of the package, each piece about this engine's domain: a seat, a phase, a turn, a configuration field.
- **The shell is the package's `AppShell`, and what sits in it is ours.** The window, the one sidebar, the floating sheet, the 52px bar and the drawer below the shell breakpoint are the kit's geometry, taken whole; the page header's two rows, the state bar, the peek as a column of the sheet and the Settings column are this product's ([The frame](#the-frame)). A screen's own half is its labels, coverage and controls, portalled into the bar; every list it draws is [one grid](#every-list-is-one-grid).
- **What a control did is said, in one region the application mounts.** The package's list, tag and notice controls announce every add, remove and move through a module-level `announce()`, which says nothing unless an `<Announcer>` is mounted. `app/announcer.tsx` mounts exactly one (the package keeps one sentence for the page; a second region repeats it): beside the frame rather than in the shell, so a sign-in does not tear it down; named Announcements rather than the package's default, which is also what the toast outlet calls its polite region; portalled into the fullscreen element while there is one. A case in `app/announcer.test.tsx` counts the regions that hold a sentence, by what they hold rather than by name.
- **One stack decides which surface a key belongs to.** Dialogs, sheets, menus and listbox popups register on the design system's layer stack (`useModalLayer`, `usePopupLayer`) in the order they opened, as do the step-up confirmation, the command palette and the narrow layout's sidebar drawer: no modal hand-rolls its veil or listens for Escape beside the stack.
  - The drawer is the sidebar itself below the kit's shell breakpoint (1024px), owned by the kit's `AppShell`; a dialog only while open. Closed, it is out of the tab order rather than only slid away, and it closes on a route change (the shell hands the route to the kit as its `navigationKey`).
  - Only the topmost surface handles Escape or a press outside: a prompt over the node editor closes on its own Escape and leaves the editor open, a step-up confirmation raised over it does the same, and an open menu closes before the dialog it sits in.
  - A modal traps Tab, moves focus in when it opens (honouring a field's `autoFocus`) and returns it to whatever opened it. If that control went with a modal that closed as this one opened (a menu entry handing over to its dialog), focus goes where that modal would have sent it; if it went from a modal still open, or is there but can no longer take focus (disabled by the action the modal confirmed), focus goes to that modal rather than behind its veil. A modal closed beneath a surface still open above it (route change, data push) leaves focus where it is.
  - A control that consumes Escape itself, such as a completion list, keeps the key. A veil press closes its modal on the press's click, not its first contact, so the dismissing tap never also lands on the control under the veil.
  - The page's own shortcuts ([every one of them](#the-keys)) do nothing while a modal is open (`isModalLayerOpen`): the page behind `aria-modal` is inert, and search opened over a dialog could navigate away, unmounting an unsaved editor or a write whose outcome is unseen. Search closes on its own chord from inside it: the palette reads `Mod+K` off its own surface's keys, because the page's binding stands aside for it, and a key pressed in a dialog raised over it never reaches it.
  - What happens inside an open menu stays there: its keys, presses and clicks do not reach the card or row it opened from, so Enter on "Delete" is never also the card's Enter.
  - The same stack decides what PAINTS above what, but only inside one stacking context (a z-index orders nothing outside its own context). So every overlay is portalled to the page's body, and the only `LayerHost` is a FULLSCREEN container's (the org builder's), never one around the frame. The drawer is painted in place one step above its own depth; an application-wide host is a stacking context at the bottom of the band and capped every popover, dialog and palette beneath the open drawer, so on a phone the Account popover and the palette could not be tapped. With one context, the palette opened from the drawer is above it and owns the keys; taking a row navigates and the drawer closes on the route change; Escape closes the palette alone and returns focus to the drawer's search.
- **Anything drawn as a button is `Button` or `ButtonLink`, never a hand-written `.btn` class list.** `Button` passes a ref, aria and data attributes, `id`, `tabIndex` and `onKeyDown` through, so a menu trigger or a list's Move control is built on it; it refuses `className` and `style`, so the variants are the only styling. `ButtonLink` is the same recipe on an anchor, for an action that goes somewhere; its `external` form opens a new tab without the referrer or opener. A control drawn as a glyph ALONE is `IconButton`, whose name is required (an unnamed icon button is announced as "button"). `styles/classes.test.ts` holds this and fails in BOTH directions: a `.btn` list beside the package's button is a class nothing declares, and a recipe left in the stylesheets is one nothing draws.
- **A shortcut hint is `Kbd`, never a hand-written `<kbd>`.** The command key is Command on Apple platforms and Control elsewhere, so a literal "⌘K" tells most readers to press a key they lack. The glyphs are hidden from assistive technology, which reads key names ("Control plus K"), since a screen reader reads "⌘" as "place of interest sign". The palette's own hints use it too. **A keycap is a hint for a keyboard, so the frame draws none where the reader's primary input is touch** (`TOUCH_MEDIA` in `app/layout.ts`, no hover and a coarse pointer, read through `lib/media.ts`'s `useKeyHints`): the drawer's search, the palette's key legend and its rows' chords drop them. It asks "is this touch?" rather than "is there a keyboard?", because no media feature can see a keyboard, and a browser that answers neither keeps its hints. The keys still work for a reader who attaches a keyboard.
- **A key an input method is composing with belongs to the input method.** Someone typing Japanese, Chinese or Korean walks candidates with arrows, accepts with Enter and abandons with Escape, and each press still reaches the page. `isComposing` decides once whether a press is part of a composition, reading both the `isComposing` flag and the key code Safari leaves on the Enter that ends one; the layer stack, the listbox keys, the multi-select and the list field leave such a press alone, so search does not close or navigate mid-word and a list field does not add half of one.
- **A canvas never takes the page's scroll.** The design system's `Canvas` fills the box its screen gives it and clips; the shell's one scroller stops scrolling while it is on screen. The screen ASKS for the window's height (`useFillScreen`) and the shell answers, rather than the screen's stylesheet reaching up at a shell wrapper.
  - A plain wheel pans only while focus is inside the canvas; Ctrl or Command with the wheel zooms toward the cursor. On touch, one finger scrolls the page until the canvas is tapped, after which it pans and a visible Done control gives the finger back; two fingers pinch at any time. `+`, `-` and `0` zoom and fit only while the viewport element itself holds focus, so an item's own keys are never taken.
  - The view fits on the first measured layout, then moves only when the operator moves it or a screen's own `fitKey` changes. Structure's chart opens WHOLE, fitted and centred, on its top ranks where the whole company would open below half size (`ui/canvasView.ts`'s `CHART_LEGIBLE_ZOOM`), and fits again after every layout action its `fitKey` names, at any width (`CHART_FIT_FLOOR`, 2%); a legibility floor (85%) opened a wide company cut at its edges.
  - The canvas is a `LayerHost`, so a menu or picker opened from an item renders in an untransformed layer over it, not scaled or clipped by the zoom; the canvas tells that layer whenever the content moves, so an open surface follows its anchor. Fullscreen belongs to the screen, which must take its dialogs and toasts into the fullscreen element with it.
- **Every dropdown is the design system's own, and no screen draws a native one.** A platform dropdown is painted by the OS and takes none of the theme, density or tokens (a dark dialog opened a light grey menu). `Select` earns back what the platform gave free and shares it with every list in the package: type-ahead, Home and End, disabled rows stepped over, the highlight announced through `aria-activedescendant`, Tab closing the list and carrying on, and a stored value the options no longer offer kept rather than swapped. It alone can do a search over dozens, a group heading, and a second line under an option (where a choice's hint belongs).
  - Choosing MANY is `TagsInput` over the same keys (a multiple select cannot be searched and loses its selection to a stray click); completing a `${NAME}` inside a longer value is `Combobox`, which filters on the name under the caret, not the whole field.
  - Search's results take those keys: its input is a combobox naming the highlighted result, and the list is the modal's whole body rather than a popup over it (`popup: false`), so Escape and the veil stay the modal's.
  - The one choice that is not a `Select` is a value picked IN PLACE from a menu an item already opens, such as a unit's lead chosen from its chart card (a list there would be a second control inside the item and a second click). Its answers are `menuitemradio` entries (a `checked` item of the design system's `Menu`) saying which is current, nested in one `group` apart from the menu's actions so a screen reader counts them among themselves; the form that edits the same value still uses the list.
- **The layout is measured, never assumed.** A chart card's width is the `--crewlet-tree-canvas-card-width` knob, declared on the builder's own root; its height is measured in the browser and fed to the design system's pure tidy tree layout, because density and the reader's font size change every card's height. Nothing is shown before the first measurement, and a relayout keeps the node the operator acted on where it was on screen.

### The org builder

`routes/org/builder/Builder.tsx` is the one component with a lifetime in the builder: the reducer over the pure model in `routes/org/builder/model/`, the check, save, live region, shortcuts, selection and open dialog. Views and dialogs are handed in (`BuilderSurfaces`, bound in `routes/org/builder/surfaces.ts`) and reach all of it through `BuilderContext`, so none starts a request or touches storage. Every surface is required: a Builder suite stands a view in with a fake, the screen binds the real ones, and `surfaces.test.tsx` mounts the builder with exactly those.

- **The posture is what the engine answers.** `GET /config` is read on mount and whenever the reader changes; its answer decides edit mode, create mode, a node that has not caught up, a request to sign in, a guarded reader, a process that does not serve the configuration, or an unreachable engine ([the guide](../guides/org-builder.md#opening-the-builder) has the table). A signed-in reader refused the configuration, on a company the org projection names, gets no refusal: the builder follows the org projection every reader holds (`model/projection.ts`) read-only, every edit and control held with the gate's own reason, so Structure is everybody's overview. Being signed in is never the test; only the engine knows whether this person's grants reach the company. The reader changes when the viewer's login does (another tab signing in as somebody else); a change mid-edit keeps the draft on screen, forgets the kept copy and checks again.
- **A managed document opens read-only.** When the viewer says another system [manages the document](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration) and the reader's credential is not one of its writers (`useManagedConfig()`), every editing control is disabled (a lead's own team included), an info callout carries the managed sentence, and no draft is collected. A check answered `403 config_managed` before the viewer says so sets the toolbar's check status to **Managed by another system**; the check's own `managed_by` decides the same way. A writer's token edits as on an unmanaged document.
- **Every draft is a dry run of the write a save would send.** The same `PATCH` with `If-Match` (or `PUT` with `If-None-Match: *` in create mode), plus `dry_run=true` and no audit summary, including a draft that changes nothing and a lead's unit (the engine refuses a lead only the WRITE of an unchanged unit). A changing draft moves its generation; an answer for an older generation is dropped.
- **A lead edits one unit as a document of its own.** A reader without Admin who leads a unit (`lib/leadScope.ts`) is opened on it, not refused: `model/scope.ts` reads `GET /config/units/{key}` as `{name, units: [that unit]}` and saves with `PUT /config/units/{key}` with `If-Match`, the unit whole, so nothing else in the model knows it is a lead's.
  - The engine answers about the WHOLE company, so its paths are moved into the draft's coordinates by where its derivation places the unit; a problem outside the unit is said about the draft, not put on whichever node sits at that path.
  - What reaches outside the unit (the company's name, the top level, the unit's own lead and place, and on every node the keys another system finds it by: a project, a space, a channel, an email, a contact identity) is refused at the reducer's recording door and drawn disabled with the reason.
  - A refusal the engine names part by part (`403` with `refused`) is a problem on each part, not a refusal of the person.
  - Until the viewer has answered and what a possible lead leads is known, nothing is read, so a lead is never shown a refusal of the company nor forgets their kept draft over one.
  - A lead of several units edits one per draft, chosen in the toolbar; a kept draft is offered only for its own unit. A lost save is settled by reading the unit back, and an update stands on the unit the node serves: revision history is admin's.
- **The tab is the view, and the canvas is handed the chart it draws.** Structure's tab decides the view (`Builder`'s `view`: the Org chart draws the canvas, the Table the rows). `chart=reporting` is the Builder's own section param, set by the Reporting view switch in the canvas's top left corner, passed to the canvas as a prop rather than read from the URL again. Each arrangement is its own canvas, so the switch is redrawn when it moves and focus is put back on it.
- **The Org chart fills the screen.** The builder asks the shell for the window's height (`useFillScreen`); it and the tab panel become flex columns of definite height, so the canvas takes what is left under the toolbar and the shell's scroller has nothing to scroll. The Table and the posture screen (before the engine answers) withdraw the request.
- **One drawing.** Nodes, marks, the agent hue and branches are `ui/orgNodes.tsx`'s, the one drawing of a seat, a unit and the company that the chart and the Table share. Branches are the design system's elbows at the weight it gives a chart of NODES, twice a card chart's, because a node is half a card's height and the branch keeps its ratio to what it joins; the builder sets no stroke of its own.
- **Fullscreen takes the builder container**, never the canvas: the toolbar, view, dialog host, a toast outlet of its own and the live region all render inside it, because a fullscreen element renders only its subtree. The application's announcer (which the editor's lists and pickers speak into) is portalled in beside them while fullscreen. The control is not drawn where the Fullscreen API is missing. Asking to sign in leaves fullscreen first, since sign-in is a screen outside the frame.
- **The selection is in the URL, by address, and the toolbar mirrors it.** `unit=` names the selected unit by key and `seat=` the seat by handle, never a name, which two units may share; a link naming one selects it, a new address rewrites it, a removed node clears it. The selection carries between Structure's tabs and **never opens anything by itself**: the builder writes `seat=` and `unit=` on every selection, so a reload, a Back or a seat page's crumb lands on an address the builder wrote. **A request is its own word in the address**: `editor=open` beside `seat=` or `unit=` opens that node's editor (`EDITOR_OPEN` in `app/routes.ts`, which the seat page's Edit in org sends), and `add=unit|agent|human` opens the Add (under `unit=`, or at the top level), once, as soon as the builder can edit (loaded, in edit mode, not paused). The request then leaves the address, as it does when the reader moves the selection first (`editWiring.test.tsx`). (`seat=` alone as the request reopened an editor nobody asked for on every return.)
  - The toolbar carries the selected node's own actions, because a canvas tree item may contain no tab stops of its own. They are the card's and row's own list (`nodeActions.nodeMenu`), not a copy: same entries, order, names, icons, Edit reports included. Open seat is offered only for a seat the saved company has.
  - **The company's node has no Edit** (`nodeActions.editsInPlace`): no pencil on its card or row, and Enter and a double-click do nothing, because its mission, vision and standing policies are written on Company › Principles alone and a pencil on the root would read as editing the node. Once the company exists, the toolbar's menu for it offers that page (`BuilderApi.principles`, `openPrinciples`): in edit (`?edit=mission`) named **Edit principles** for a reader the page's gate admits (`useMayWriteCharter`), else **Open principles**; the card's and row's menus leave it out. The name, the one company field the model writes (`model/document.ts`'s `COMPANY_FIELDS`), is **Rename company** on every surface's menu, also for a company the draft is still creating.
  - The model refuses a change to the principles at its recording door, a kept log holding one is unreadable, `buildPatch` never names them, and an engine problem about one is listed at document level with **Open Principles**.
  - What the engine says about no node is two banners over the chart: refusals in the danger tone, and warnings (a valid setting with a consequence, which the engine runs) in the warning tone under "The engine runs this company, with *n* warnings to know about", each linking to where it is set where the builder authors none of it (a model entry's or the sandbox default's cell: **Open Models**).
  - A node's key is its IDENTITY (a seat's handle, a unit's key, carried by every stored node), so the base is keyed as it loads and a rename never moves a key. Only a node the draft created moves, from its minted key to the handle or key it was given, once a save has created it. The reducer lists what moved (`state.rekeyed`); the selection and an open dialog read their node through that list in the very render the keys change. Each dialog is mounted once per opening, never keyed by its node, so a moving key keeps an open editor's drawer, form and focus.
- **One polite live region** says what each operation, undo and redo did (undo and redo name themselves, since the operation's own sentence is past tense), and focus moves to the touched node through the mounted view's registered handle (`useBuilderView`).
- **Undo and redo are Ctrl or Command with Z**, and Shift with it, anywhere in the builder except a text field, and never under a modal.
- **A newer revision is an update, never an overwrite.** A check answering `409` (or a dry run validated against another base) halts checking and offers Update my draft. A draft holding no work is updated at once (an update of nothing, confirmed as it lands), never by re-reading the configuration: a plain read replaces the draft whole, losing an open editor's node and typed form and clearing the selection. The update is read only from a node serving the conflict's revision or a descendant, with the engine's description of it (a lead's from the unit the node serves, since a lead reads no history). `UpdateDraftDialog.tsx` shows what still applies, what is dropped and every conflict with its three values; confirming waits for a choice on each. Values are shown as a person reads them: the model tags a conflict over its own structures with their shape, so a node key reads as the node's name, a removed node as the fields that changed, a credential's mask as "A literal value is set (hidden)", never the marker or JSON.
- **Only the operation log is kept, and nothing is written before it is decided.** `useDraftKeeping.ts` reads the kept draft once the base is loaded, offers Keep or Discard for the same revision (and, for a lead, the same unit; read-only until answered), restores through the update flow for another, and discards one kept for the other mode or another unit. A lead's builder opens the unit a kept draft was made of while they still lead it (`persistence.keptScope`, read before the unit is chosen and deciding nothing), so another unit means one they no longer lead. It writes nothing before the decision, because the plan for an empty log is to clear. A change of reader or a refused credential clears it and withdraws an offer, but not a step-up the reader declined (the same person choosing not to confirm yet); a sign-out empties the tab's storage before it reloads. A draft with changes asks the browser's prompt before the tab goes (session storage does not outlive the tab); one storage cannot keep at all asks before the builder is left; a move within the builder asks nothing.
- **A save is the checked write, signed, and never believed blindly.** `useSave.ts` sends the model's save request with the audit summary signed by a write id minted when the review opens and kept while the draft does not change, so a second press after a lost answer carries the same id.
  - A lost answer is settled from the revision history before anything else (a lead's by reading the unit back), and while unknown the builder records nothing.
  - A write in flight is never aborted; a save landing after the builder was left still records the revision and clears the kept draft.
  - The kept log is marked with the write id before the save is sent and unmarked once the save is known not to have landed, so an answer lost after the builder was left, or across a reload, is settled on the next visit (`useSave.resume`) before the kept log is offered: replayed onto its own revision it would apply every change twice.
  - A save this page still has out when the builder opens again is waited for first (the engine may not have stored it yet, and settling then would read as not landed). It is not the draft on screen, so its revision is read like any newer revision, not made the base.
  - A save of the draft on screen makes that draft the base, keyed by the save's answer; the stored document is then read back, never over an edit made while that read is out, which already stands on the saved revision.
  - `ReviewSaveDialog.tsx` states every change and consequence and gates the irreversible ones on an acknowledgement, whose sentences (`dialogParts`'s `ACKNOWLEDGEMENT_TEXT`) the editor's company rename shares.
- **Create mode is a form, one template operation, and a create-only write.** `CreateCompany.tsx` collects the company's name, the starting shape and a seat for the operator, **Add a seat for yourself**, ticked from the start and named "Founder": every person holds a human seat and is invited or created onto one from the org chart, so a company started without one is one nobody, the operator included, can join until somebody adds one. Unticking is a deliberate answer (an agents-only company run through API tokens). It records the model's `applyTemplate` (refused outside create mode), so the start is a single undo and is checked like any draft. The save is `PUT` with `If-None-Match: *`; a company that appeared meanwhile is offered instead, and the draft is discarded rather than replayed onto it.
- **A revision this node applied asks every read again.** A config write answers once its revision is active, before this node applies it, and many answers (`llm_entries`, `limits`, `settings`, `sign_in_policy`) are read from what it applied, so the read a write fires may come back older than the write. The store says each rise of the node's `applied_epoch`, from the health push or a snapshot, and every `useQuery` and `useRest` that asks again on a reconnect asks again (`APPLIED_REVISION`, `protocol/session.ts`); a read that opted out of reconnects (a transcript, a code search) does not.
- **A save is not an apply, and the screen says so.** `AfterSaveStrip.tsx` keeps `{revision_id, epoch}` in a tab-lived store outside any screen (`savedRevision.ts`), reads this node's `applied_epoch` and `config_attempt` off the health push (both every five seconds, nothing to poll) and the `fleet` query on `recheck.ts`'s cadence, and resolves to Applied, Applied on N of M nodes, the node that refused it with a link to Settings › Nodes, or "Revision … has been activated since".
  - **One rule for both wires** (`lib/nodeStanding.ts`, `fleetNodeStanding` beside `nodeStanding`, one predicate over the facts both carry): a fleet row's `config_applied_epoch` is the push's `applied_epoch`; its `config_epoch`, `config_revision_id` and `config_status` are the push's `config_attempt`. An Admin and a lead are told the same of the same node; the row's one fact more is the revision a node runs.
  - **Applied** only on evidence: its attempt at that epoch on that revision went ok, or it has applied that epoch or a later one (a node that applied 5 and refused 6 has applied a save at 4), or it runs that revision (`config_serving_revision_id`).
  - **Passed**: a node that attempted a later epoch without applying the save's (two activations inside one reconcile tick are never attempted one by one) is neither applied nor waited on. Once every node has applied or passed it and one passed it, the strip settles on "activated since", not Applied for a save no node may run.
  - A report at the same epoch on another revision (one number names two once a rebuilt coordination store restarts the count) is that revision's, neither this save applied nor refused.
  - **A save whose answer was lost** carries no epoch: it takes the fleet activation's only while that names the saved revision, never `target_epoch`, which is the newest activation's whatever it names (0 for none). An activation naming another revision settles the strip on "Revision … has been activated since" (said as since, not as a replacement, because the history walk that found the save finds it as readily beneath a revision built on it); no activation keeps it applying and asking.
  - **A reader without Admin** reads no fleet and follows a save by this node's push alone (`lib/nodeStanding.ts`, the rule a ceiling's mark and a charter card follow their own writes by too). Order: the last attempt first, applied when it names that revision at that epoch and went ok, refused when it failed there (the applied epoch cannot say it: a failed attempt leaves it where it was and, from a pointer before a rebuilt coordination store, it can stand above the save's); then applied once the applied epoch reaches the save's, or passed once it attempted a later epoch first. A lost-answer save takes its epoch from that attempt only while it names the saved revision, else it is told it cannot be followed from here, not that it is applying (nothing would correct that). An epoch an answer supplied is pinned to the save in the store (`pinSavedEpoch`), so the next activation does not turn an applied or refused save into one that cannot be followed.
  - **Known limits**, both left to the engine under [#322](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/issues/322). A node holding an applied epoch from the previous pointer above the save's that has not attempted the save yet reads as applied, on push and row alike, since an epoch orders activations within one pointer only; telling the two apart takes the applied activation whole, which #322 has the engine keep. Neither wire keeps the applied epoch across a RESTART: `applied_epoch` and `config_applied_epoch` restart at 0 and move only on the next ok apply, while a node with the `data` role boots on the revision it applied before (one without it boots on nothing, runs no company, and has truly passed the save until it applies one). Until then a restarted node that refused a later activation reads as having passed the save: on its push alone when it booted on the saved revision (its row says it runs it), on both when it booted on a revision activated after the save. So a verdict from before the restart can turn from "Applied." into "activated since" (a lead's on the next push, an Admin's on the fleet read a reconnect makes), since neither wire carries the epoch the restarted node booted on, so the dashboard cannot tell this node from one that never ran the save; carrying it across a restart belongs with #322 too (an activation's identity across pointer lifetimes).
  - **Followers read this node's LAST push** (`lib/useLastHealth.ts`), never the store's live health slice: a dropped socket clears that and is no news of the save, and read as a standing it turned the verdict back into applying for as long as the socket was down. The TAB keeps that push (`StoreState.lastHealth`, written with every frame and left by a drop), not each follower, because the strip mounts afresh on every return to Structure and a follower mounting during a drop would say the save was applying.
  - The Builder's toast says the same of the same save: one settled beneath a later revision (`Landed.activeRevisionId`) names that revision as active now. Its View changes opens the saved revision against its parent (`against=`), since against the active revision a save that is active now differs from nothing; the conflict banner's Show what changed is the newer revision against the draft's base for the same reason. Both, and Copy as YAML, read the company document, so none is offered without Admin.
  - Structure draws the saved organization at once (every node answers the configuration with the saved revision); what each seat is doing comes from what this node runs, so a seat the save added has no state until it is applied and placed.
- **The status is the last answer about the current draft**, whoever asked: a save's refusal is placed on the nodes like a check's, and the check machine decides the status only while a check is out or before any answer.
- **A read-only builder records nothing.** The guarded posture, a conflict, a kept draft awaiting Keep or Discard, and a save whose outcome is unknown or still out all refuse operations at the one door every view goes through, and say why in the live region; so does a lead's draft for each operation reaching outside its unit. Actions are DISABLED rather than hidden, so a reader without Admin still sees what the builder does; Edit and Open seat change no draft and stay available. A refused check or save is worded by the refusal's code, in the sentence every writer of the company document uses (`configGuardedReason`): only access the reader lacks says "Needs Admin access"; a declined step-up (a configuration write asks for one, so an hour-old session meets it) says so and offers Check again, which resends the check and so asks them to confirm who they are.

### The org builder draws the engine's organization

Structure shows the draft as an Org chart and a Table, both reading one module (`routes/org/builder/chartModel.ts`), so they never disagree about where a seat is drawn, who leads a unit or who a seat reports to.

- **The document gives the shape, the engine gives the meaning.** Units, their seats and children are drawn as the draft holds them, because that is what an operation edits. Every derived fact comes from the last check's `derived` block, read through the document that check was sent:
  - a root seat the engine placed in a unit by its `unit:` reference is drawn in that unit, marked "Declared at the root with a unit reference";
  - a reference naming no unit stays at the root, marked with the engine's warning;
  - a unit with no lead of its own shows the lead it inherits;
  - a seat shows its primary manager, which follows from the whole organization, so only from a check of the draft as it stands.
  - A derived fact is shown only while the draft still holds the values the check saw (for an inherited lead, including where each unit above sits); after an edit the chart says it is waiting for the check rather than showing an unconfirmed placement or lead. A value not yet given reads "Reports to: known after the check" or "Manager after the check", never that a check is running: whether one is on its way or the engine is unreachable is the toolbar's check status to say, which a card cannot know.
  - A seat's handle and a unit's key are written in the document (every stored one carries the engine's, a new node the one typed into its form), so nothing waits on a check to name one, and the editor, dialogs and `chartModel.ts` read the same address.
  - The Reporting view, drawn from the last check while the draft has moved past it, says so in a note over the canvas.
- **The canvas is a tree of nodes.** The Org chart has the company at the root, with root seats and units hanging off it; every seat is a node hanging off its unit like the unit's child units, joined by the design system's elbow branches. The Reporting view is the engine's forest: seats with no manager at the top, marked "No manager", and seats managing each other in a loop under one "Reporting cycle" group, each loop drawn from its first seat in the engine's order. It is read-only, because a reporting line is not written anywhere as such: "Edit reports" (and Enter on a reporting card) opens the seat's editor at its Manages field, where `manages` is. The Builder's `openEditor` names the part of the form to start on (`EditorSectionName`), so an action about one field lands on it: a Reports to pill's "Choose another seat" opens the unit's editor at its Reports to field.
- **The node editor is a sheet of tabs, and the head names the node only.** It is the kit's 560px sheet (`Modal variant="sheet" flush`) with a 72px head (the node's mark, its live name, then the handle and kind or the unit's type, never where it reports: that is the **Work** tab's), a sticky band of underline `Tabs`, and one panel at a time, at fixed sizes: a 20px inset with 32px below, 24px between groups, 16px between fields, 30px controls, 32px fact rows.
  - The panel is the active tab's `tabpanel`; the form's state is the editor's, so an unmounted tab loses nothing.
  - Each tab carries one `TabsMarker`, the most urgent of a problem count, a warning and a change, mapped from a problem's path or an edit part's path by the longest tab prefix; a field that blocks Apply counts as a problem on its tab.
  - Help lines show on focus (`helperOnFocus`). What the builder shows and does not edit is a `FactList` row with a lock whose reason is a hover tooltip and is read inline by a screen reader; no info icons.
  - A connected tool is a card with its `VendorMark` and the `integrations` roll-up's own label and tone (`lib/toolState.ts`, shared with the Integrations screen), so a tool has one status word everywhere; a seat's own app state is a row in the card. Tools nobody connected are one line.
  - A seat's kind is a locked fact: there is no kind-change operation, because the kinds share almost no fields, so the editor ends in **Delete**.
- **A node holds no control a keyboard has to reach.** Each node is a `treeitem` with its level, position and expansion, and one roving tab stop moves among them: the arrows, Home, End and type-ahead walk the tree, Enter edits, Delete or Backspace deletes, and the ContextMenu key or Shift+F10 opens the node's menu. The buttons a pointer uses (expand, Add, More and the Reports to pill) sit beside the treeitem, hidden from assistive technology and out of the tab order, and open the same menus. **Nothing in a hidden strip ever holds focus**: a press on one of those buttons focuses the node instead, so a screen reader always has something to announce and a closing menu hands focus back to a card, not a button nobody can reach. Focus moves with `preventScroll` and the canvas then pans to reveal the node, opening a collapsed unit on the way. The Builder decides which node is focused after an add, a delete, a move, an undo or a redo; the mounted view performs it.
- **An agent seat is toned, and nothing else is.** This is the console org chart's drawing and the colour rule's second, bounded exception (see "The one rule"): every agent seat takes the colour its profile icon names (purple until its author chooses), on its card, the branch into it and its table row; every other node is neutral. No hue is made from a seat's key (a legend nobody could decode); the editor offers an agent's character and colour in one `AvatarPicker`, in its head and under **Profile icon**, and a person's and a unit's editor offers neither. A seat leads with the console chart's mark, not a badge: the agent's own character for an agent, a person's glyph in a dashed ring for a person (drawn alone in a table row).
  - A dashed edge on a node means only "a place nothing fills yet": the ghost of a node being added, and a unit's lead slot while no lead is set.
  - A reference that names nothing takes the caution tone; the Datadog fallback seat carries a neutral mark while Datadog is enabled, the only time the engine routes an alert to it.
- **One line round every box.** A card is framed once: the selected node's card takes the accent on its own boundary rather than a ring inside it, its focus ring is drawn over that boundary, a toned card has no halo, and a set lead is a raised pill with no frame of its own. The chart stands on a dotted field, which says it pans before anybody drags it.
- **A click on nothing puts the selection down**, on the chart's field, round the table or on the page under either (`ui/clickOnNothing.ts`). A click on a node, a row or a control is that thing's own, and a pan keeps the selection.
- **A chart node says what it is and what it is doing, never a count.** A seat's card says its live state under its name, the state's dot and word then its kind and handle ("● Working · agent · @pm"), read from the running company, not the draft; a person's card says its kind and handle alone. No problem count (an empty box beside every node with nothing wrong). The Table's Status column writes the state as one calm line (`StatusLine`), in a cell that neither grows nor wraps, so a push changes a word and never a row's height; the Table's Problems column and the toolbar's status count the problems. A mark the engine gave (a lead or a unit reference that names nothing) is held by the chart like a placement while the node still writes what the check warned about, rather than leaving with each check and returning with its answer.
- **The table is a treegrid of rows.** The same structure as rows with navigable cells: Name (a select box before it, the kind and handle or the type and size under it), Status, Reports to, Problems, Controls and Edit.
  - Columns follow the grid's own width, not the window's: Reports to and Problems drop first, then Status, whose words move under the name.
  - A row's keys are a card's keys; Right opens a row or steps into its cells, Left steps back out, Up and Down keep the column, and a cell holding a control (a Reports to chip, a run-time control, the actions menu, an add pill) focuses the control, which becomes the grid's one tab stop. A press that opens such a control moves that tab stop too, because the control keeps the focus and hands it back when its menu closes; the row's chevron, hidden from assistive technology, takes no focus and hands the press to the row. Navigation keys are the grid's before the control's, so ArrowDown on a menu button moves to the next row rather than opening the menu.
  - The grid scrolls sideways in its own box at narrow widths, which is the containing block of everything in it: a scroller clips only descendants placed inside it, and a screen-reader label placed against the frame gave the page a sideways overflow as wide as the grid. A box that scrolls on one axis clips on both, so a row's menus open in a `.popup-layer` over the grid, placed from their trigger, following a sideways scroll (or closing once the trigger has left the frame), not cut off under the last rows.
  - The company's row and each unit's carry an add pill beside the name ("Add to *team*") that splits into the three kinds.
  - Alt+Up and Alt+Down move a row among its siblings of the same kind, past the row drawn beside it: a root seat the engine placed in a unit by its reference is drawn in that unit, so the root seats around it step over it rather than make a move nobody can see.
  - The engine's primary manager is the first seat that lists a seat, so the reporting lines the next check reports are compared with the ones before, and a changed primary manager is announced.

---

## Rules a change has to keep

1. **Colour is state, never a derived identity.** No hash-to-hue, no tint the
   dashboard picks for an agent, no per-category chip colour. To tell two
   things apart, use their names. The eight bounded exceptions (see "The one
   rule" above): third-party app marks in `@crewlethq/icons`; the toned agent
   nodes of Company › Structure's chart and Table; an agent's own profile icon;
   a Crewlet character in its author's colour; a QR code's black on white
   (`@crewlethq/ui`'s `QrCode`, inks are the fixed `color.qr` tokens); a
   collaborator's presence colour in an artifact; a colour value's swatch
   (`ColorChip`); code read in Gitlet (the kit's code host colours) and a diff's
   lines. **Every diff is tinted, never in a state's hue**: a line's kind is
   its glyph, the diff family's tint and, on an edited line, an underline (see
   [Every diff is tinted](#every-diff-is-tinted)). The character and colour
   lists are the contract's (`contract/avatar.ts`), held to the engine's and the
   design system's; `lib/avatar.ts`'s `avatarOf` draws a part this build does
   not know as the default part, not as nothing.
   **A seat's identity badge is `Avatar`, everywhere but Structure, through
   `SeatAvatar`** (`ui/SeatAvatar.tsx`; `seatBadge` for a kit component that
   draws the badge itself). Structure's chart and Table draw the console
   chart's marks instead, `ui/orgNodes.tsx`'s `seatMark` (see "An agent seat is
   toned, and nothing else is"). It is handed the seat's `avatar` wherever the
   chart holds the seat, so an agent is its own character, and a person, or a
   seat the chart does not hold, is initials from its name or handle. For an
   AGENT a leading word "agent" is dropped before the initials, because the
   squircle already says it: "Agent CEO" and "Agent CTO" are `CE` and `CT`, not
   `AC`. A screen reader still hears the whole name. The `kind` is the OUTLINE,
   a circle for a person and a squircle for an agent, the one cue telling them
   apart: who holds a seat is structural, so a shape, not a hue. A kind the
   chart does not hold is read from the writer's recorded kind where the screen
   has one (a write of kind `operator` is a person no chart lists), else the
   kit's default, the agent squircle. No hand-rolled robot glyph: it draws the
   KIND, which the roster already gives, in the slot that says WHO.
   `ring="brand"` (the accent as a ring round the neutral badge, meaning
   *selected*) is only for the badge that IS the reader: the sidebar's own
   account row (unless it wears a `mark`, whose notch is cut from the outline
   the ring would follow), and the reader's own face among a change row's
   reviewers (where a verdict corner takes its place), a change's merge-box
   reviewers, rail reviewers and participants. The kit's `CharacterPicker` wears
   it on the chosen character, the same meaning. What a seat is DOING is its
   `status` (`statusOf`), the kit's corner glyph, never a ring or a coloured
   edge on its card; a row that draws it says the state in words too where it
   has room.
2. **No new colour, size, radius or spacing literal.** If a component needs
   one, add the TOKEN.
3. **A fill step is never text and an `-ink` step is never a background.** The
   palette suite measures both; an inline `background:` carrying a hue token is
   the mistake it catches. Gitlet's open pill stands on
   `--color-change-open-fill`, the success ink, which the package measures as
   that pill's ground (`styles/codehost.test.ts`).
4. **Nothing animates on a data push.** Only entrances, control states and the
   steady-state pulse on something live now; under reduced motion every pulse
   is static and every entrance ends on its first frame
   (`styles/motion.test.ts`).
5. **Every list sorts through `tsKey` with a three-way comparator**, and every
   keyed row uses an identity that survives the row's own lifecycle.
6. **Every empty state says why it is empty** and what would fill it, and
   distinguishes "nothing happened" from "nothing could be read".
7. **A write says what happened, and is made as you**: the principal your
   session resolves to, through `POST /operator/act`, never "the dashboard". A
   change to the company's work goes through `act` (`protocol/act.ts`) from
   `useAct` (`lib/useAct.ts`) and nowhere else (`app/writeGate.test.tsx` holds
   that and renders every write control for an anonymous, an unbound and a bound
   reader); a change to its configuration through `protocol/configWrite.ts`.
   Nothing outside `src/protocol/` reaches the network
   (`protocol/transport.test.ts`). Every write reports its outcome: a toast when
   it landed, a persistent notice with Retry when nobody can say, and the
   engine's refusal beside the control that caused it. A write control is never
   hidden and never optimistic (see "Acting, as yourself"); a button whose
   result is invisible gets pressed twice.
8. **No screen renders a credential it read back.** The setup dialog shows the
   `${VAR}` a field points at, or, for a hand-written literal, an empty box
   whose PLACEHOLDER is dots saying one is held. Never a value (no route
   returns one), and never dots as the value: a placeholder cannot be
   submitted, and a sentinel recognised on the way out is one an edit can
   defeat. The one exception is a secret the engine has just MINTED for the
   person looking, to be written down: a second factor's key at enrolment (with
   Copy, and a QR code of its `otpauth://` URI beside the link that opens it)
   and a set of recovery codes (with Copy and Download). Each is shown once,
   never stored by the page, never read back, and the screen says so. A token
   typed on the sign-in screen is sent once and kept nowhere.
9. **A directory line carries no control, and a card one.** Company ›
   Integrations lists every tool and service as one link with its mark, name
   and state, because a list is read in one glance. A card on its home carries
   exactly one action (the one fix it owes, or Open); everything else a tool
   offers is on its page, beside the reason for each.
10. **Every screen, section and filter is in the URL**, and obeys the
    push/replace table above.
11. **A screen subscribes to the slices it reads and no others.**
12. **Numbers are tabular**, and an absent number is a MARKED absence, not a
    zero: zero is a measurement. `EmptyValue` draws the mark and says what the
    absence means ("Not reported", "Not measured"), because a bare dash is read
    aloud as "dash" or skipped; a value still arriving is another fact, which a
    tile reports by being busy. **There is exactly ONE absent mark, and it is
    `EmptyValue`'s**: its en dash in JSX, its `EMPTY_VALUE` constant in a string
    a module returns. No module spells one itself (a local `Dash` is an em dash,
    which the design system "does not use anywhere", and two glyphs for one fact
    sit in one viewport). `cells.test.tsx` scans the tree for a string literal
    or JSX text node that is nothing but a dash; an em dash inside prose is
    house punctuation and not what it looks for.
13. **A control reports its own outcome**, especially an invisible one (a copy,
    a download, a write, a revoke), in text a screen reader reaches as well as
    an icon. A refusal is reported too and OUTLASTS the confirmation, so a
    reader who looked away for three seconds can still learn it did not land: a
    failed state holds until the next click, a successful one settles back.
14. **Per-subject state is keyed on its subject.** A hash change re-renders the
    route switch rather than remounting it, so on `#/live/turns/A` →
    `#/live/turns/B` anything the screen remembers about A (a held refusal, an
    open disclosure, a selected tab) describes B until something clears it.
    Every id-bearing route carries `key={id}`.
15. **A screen head's controls wrap.** A button does not break its own label,
    so a head with several overflows a phone's line instead of taking a second.
    The page header and `ObjectHeader` take their badges and actions as slots
    that wrap, and any row built beside one wraps too.
16. **A link reads as a link at every size, and a rule under the words is not
    how.** A text-register class on an `<a>` that overrides its colour makes a
    navigation decoration; `.t-link` is the caption-sized register that keeps
    the accent. Hover is a step within the text rungs, not a rule under the
    words. Two exceptions: (1) WCAG 1.4.1, PERMANENT not hover-only (a hover
    mark is invisible to keyboard, touch and anyone who has not guessed): an
    anchor that is a word in a running sentence takes `.prose-link`, and
    `.prose.md a` and `.int-form-note a` get it without asking; (2)
    `forced-colors: active`, where the rung step cannot be seen at all. See *A
    link is a colour* above for all three.
16a. **And every anchor register answers the pointer.** A register that pins
    its own colour silently takes the `a:hover` step away (`.work-col-foot a`
    and `.int-form-note a` are (0,1,1) exactly as the step is, and the later
    sheet wins), and one already `--color-text-primary` at rest, like
    `.cell-seat` and `.wl-who`, is handed a step to `--color-text-primary` that
    moves nothing. A register whose rest colour is the accent ink steps to
    `--color-text-primary`; one that is `--color-text-primary` at rest steps to
    the accent ink, which says *this name* is the link rather than the row
    around it. Nothing in `styles/` can check this today: it needs a real
    cascade, not a parse.
16b. **Text takes the ink, never the fill.** Every status family is three
    rungs: the base is what a thing is painted *with* (a primary button, a
    status dot, a meter bar), the `-soft` is the ground it tints, and the `-ink`
    is the only text colour. The design system measures the pairs it publishes;
    only `styles/rungs.test.ts` measures which rung this application spends
    where, and both mistakes are silent. `--color-brand-accent` as text gives
    3.09:1 on its own soft ground and 3.71 on the page, against the 4.5 small
    text needs; the ink gives 5.96 and 7.15. An `-ink` **on** its family's solid
    fill is the one pairing never measured (it gave 1.72:1 on a 9px digit, so
    the unread count rendered as a dot). The workspace attention badge is the
    ACCENT's ink on the accent's soft ground: a count of things waiting for the
    reader is "act here", never a caution.
16c. **The faint rung is decoration, and that is a contrast rule.**
    `--color-text-muted` is about 3:1 against the ground in *both* themes, the
    floor for a non-text mark, not the 4.5 a word needs. A word takes
    `--color-text-tertiary` (6.1–6.6:1). Ten marks remain on the faint rung (two
    tree characters, a breadcrumb slash, four icons, three icon-only controls),
    each named in `styles/rungs.test.ts` with the reason it is one.
17. **Run `make dashboard` and commit every tree it writes with the change —
    `git add -A -- static/dashboard static/artifacts static/protocol`, not
    `git add -u`.** CI rebuilds and fails on a diff AND on an untracked file in
    any of them (`make dashboard-check`): a lazy chunk is a NEW hashed file each
    time its source changes, so `git add -u` stages the entry that imports it
    and leaves the chunk behind, and a binary built from that commit serves a
    screen whose code is not in it.
18. **Everything the page runs or loads is its own bundle.** The engine serves
    the shell under a Content-Security-Policy allowing scripts, styles, fonts,
    images and connections from this origin only (images also as `data:`), and
    no inline script or `<style>` block
    ([API endpoints](api-endpoints.md#security-headers-on-every-response)). A
    `style` prop is fine, because React applies it through the CSSOM; a `style`
    attribute set as a string in markup, an injected `<style>`, an `eval`, or a
    font, image or request from another host is refused by the browser, leaving
    only a console violation. A form may post to this origin or to an `https:`
    host (the GitHub App manifest flow needs it).
    **Everything under `assets/` is content-hashed, because the engine caches
    it for good.** `/static/dashboard/assets/*` is served
    `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so a browser never re-asks; that is
    correct only because the build names each file `<name>-<hash>.<ext>`, so
    different bytes are a different URL. A fixed-name file anywhere but
    `assets/` (the fonts, notices and brand marks) is served `no-cache` and
    revalidated on every load, like the shell. `TestEveryFileUnderAssetsIsContentHashed`
    fails on an unhashed name under `assets/`. The engine gzips text once per
    file at the best level for a client that asks, so nothing is pre-compressed
    and no proxy is needed ([API endpoints](api-endpoints.md#wiring)).
19. **Tokens for what agents spend; money only a vendor's, through the kit.**
    Every figure of what agents spend is a token count: on Spend, a seat's
    profile, a task's cost, a turn's phases and the landing screen's pulse. The
    engine records a price only where one is reported, and only a subscription
    harness reports one, so a currency figure covers the minority of calls
    while the token count beside it covers all, and reads as the company's
    spend while being a fraction. So no screen draws a model price, and the
    client declares no price field at all, since a field `protocol/types.ts`
    declares is one line from being drawn. The engine's price stays on its API
    ([API endpoints](api-endpoints.md#token-spend-breakdown)).
    The one money a screen draws is a growth integration's own: a vendor
    account's ad spend, earnings, proceeds and spending caps, in the account's
    currency as the vendor reports it. It is drawn only by the design system's
    `Money` (`formatMoney`), from integer micros, never through a float and
    never summed across currencies, and only the growth modules
    (`contract/growth.ts`, `components/growth/`, `routes/growth/`) name a
    currency, as data; none spells a code or a sign or asks `Intl` for a
    currency format itself.
    Two other places a price can be read on a screen: a record shown
    **verbatim**, as stored (an event's own payload), because dropping a field
    would misreport the record, and nothing there is drawn as a figure; and an
    artifact sheet's own cells, where a number column whose schema declares a
    currency is the author's data, drawn by the design system's sheet model in
    the author's format, never an engine-recorded figure. Three gates, each
    over a different artefact: the SOURCE, where `src/money.test.tsx` parses
    every shipped module (comments excluded, so a note can name what it
    forbids) and admits a currency's name in the growth modules alone; the
    SCREENS, where the same suite renders the landing screen, Spend, a task, a
    seat's Overview and Activity tabs and a turn over wire fixtures carrying a
    price everywhere the engine puts one, and reads text and attributes back
    for any trace; and the BUNDLE, where `TestTheDashboardRendersNoPrice` scans
    every module the engine serves, lazy chunks included, and admits exactly
    the sheet model's currency format and the signs it strips from typed
    input, and `Money`'s formatter and its ISO 4217 table, each written as the
    whole construct, because the committed bundle is what a browser runs.
